docs.title: Risk & Decisioning documentation
docs.text:
This site documents two related but separate systems in Merchant Solutions Risk, plus a proposed platform to monitor them:

  • Underwriting Decisioning — a real-time, synchronous scoring service on AWS that turns an underwriting request into a decision.
  • Feature Risk Monitoring — a batch, Snowflake-native feature store pipeline that builds the feature library the risk-monitoring models train and score on.
  • Monitoring Kickoff — the meeting and whiteboard where the monitoring project was handed over: what the manager asked for, and why.
  • Data Quality Monitoring — a proposed (BRD-stage) platform to monitor input data, features and scores across Underwriting, Risk Monitoring and Clover Capital.
  • After the BRD: Next Steps: the 1:1 that followed the BRD. Socialise the templates, build end to end on a stand-in table, then add fixed-layout reports and hourly Lambda + SNS alerts.
  • DQ Framework: How It Works: the framework that was built (Great Expectations on Snowflake, in an AWS Lambda): how it is set up, configured and run, and what each module does.
  • DQ Framework: Lift & Shift to AWS: what to ask for, and the steps to move it from LocalStack into a real AWS account.
  • DQ Framework Blueprint — the architecture and phased delivery plan for building that platform on Great Expectations, starting with input monitoring.

The two systems share some terminology ("primitive vs composite") but have separate code, data and tooling.

docs.title: Underwriting Decisioning
docs.text:
The UW (Underwriting) Real-Time Decisioning Service receives an underwriting request from an external service, runs it through a set of fraud, identity-theft and credit models on AWS, and returns a decision in real time, while Snowflake acts as both the source of reference/config data and the historical store of every decision made.

Sources

Everything here is derived from two inputs:

1. Photos of *Real-Time Decisioning Service Architecture.pdf* ("UW AWS Architecture").
2. A meeting transcript explaining what happens *before* the Snowflake config tables.

Where something is my interpretation rather than stated in those sources, it is marked **(inferred)**.

docs.title: The system in one picture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    UI["Admin console UI<br/>(governed, 1 row at a time)"] --> CFG[("Snowflake<br/>config tables")]
    BATCH["Monthly batch<br/>(MCC-level stats)"] --> CFG
    CFG -- "SF2AWS Config Table Pipe<br/>Lambda (fingerprint check)" --> S3REF[("S3<br/>reference cache")]

    EXT["External service<br/>(MRD, RASI, ...)"] -- "1. API request" --> ALB[ALB]
    ALB --> PL["Post-ALB Lambda"]
    PL -- "2. invoke" --> SM{{"Step Functions<br/>state machine"}}
    S3REF -- "3. read reference data" --> SM
    SM -- "4. run models + rules" --> RE["Rules Engine<br/>Lambda"]
    SM -- "6. response" --> PL
    PL --> ALB -- "7. API response" --> EXT

    RE -- "5a. write Full UW output" --> S3LOG[("S3<br/>transaction logs")]
    S3LOG -- "5b. new output file event" --> TLP["AWS2SF Trans Log<br/>Pipe Lambda"]
    TLP -- "5c. load" --> HIST[("Snowflake<br/>historical table")]

docs.title: Three processes, one service
docs.text:
Process Timing What it does Config caching (top band) Asynchronous Copies Snowflake config/reference tables into S3 so the real-time path never queries Snowflake. Decisioning (middle band) Real-time, synchronous API request in, models + rules run in a state machine, decision out. Transaction logging (bottom band) Asynchronous Every decision is written to S3 and then piped into a historical Snowflake table.

The key design idea: Snowflake is never on the hot path. The real-time request only touches AWS (ALB, Lambda, Step Functions, S3). Snowflake is fed and read asynchronously on both sides.

docs.title: End-to-end data flow
docs.text:
The diagram is split into three horizontal bands inside the AWS boundary. The numbers below match the numbered arrows on the diagram.

flowchart TB
    EXT["External service<br/>(MRD, RASI, ...)"]:::ext
    SFcfg[("Snowflake<br/>config tables")]:::snow
    SFhist[("Snowflake<br/>historical table")]:::snow

    subgraph AWS["UW AWS Architecture"]
        direction TB

        subgraph BAND1["Asynchronous process — config caching"]
            direction LR
            L1["SF2AWS Config Table<br/>Pipe Lambda"]:::lambda
            S3ref[("S3<br/>reference bucket")]:::s3
        end

        subgraph BAND2["Real-time process — decisioning"]
            direction LR
            ALB["ALB"]:::alb
            POST["Post-ALB Lambda"]:::lambda
            SM["Step Functions<br/>state machine<br/><i>(orchestration)</i>"]:::sfn
            RE["Rules Engine Lambda<br/><i>(final orchestration step)</i>"]:::lambda
        end

        subgraph BAND3["Asynchronous process — transaction logging"]
            direction LR
            S3log[("S3<br/>transaction log bucket")]:::s3
            L2["AWS2SF Trans Log<br/>Pipe Lambda"]:::lambda
        end
    end

    %% Band 1: config caching (read side, async)
    SFcfg -->|ingest reference data from config tables| L1
    L1 -->|cache reference data in S3| S3ref

    %% Band 2: real-time decisioning
    EXT -->|1 - API request| ALB
    ALB -->|2 - state machine invocation| POST
    POST --> SM
    S3ref -->|3 - read reference data| SM
    SM -->|4 - state machine runs| RE
    SM -.->|6 - state machine response| POST
    POST -.-> ALB
    ALB -.->|7 - API response| EXT

    %% Band 3: transaction logging (write side, async)
    %% 5a now originates from the Rules Engine Lambda, not the state machine construct
    RE -->|5a - write Full UW output structure| S3log
    S3log -->|5b - new output file triggers async write| L2
    L2 -->|5c - write Full UW output to Snowflake| SFhist

The Step Functions state machine above expands into the layered orchestration described in Decisioning lanes & layers.

The model team's view of the same flow

The Implementation Support Document describes the request path as ten steps, from MRD collecting the data to the response on screen, with the owner and failure handling of each.

docs.title: Band 1: Asynchronous config caching (top)
docs.text:
Arrow From → To What happens Ingest reference data from config tables Snowflake config tables → SF2AWS Config Table Pipe Lambda Lambda runs each query from its state file against Snowflake. Cache reference data in S3 Lambda → S3 (reference bucket) Changed results (by fingerprint) are written as files to S3.

This runs independently of any request (scheduled or triggered, (inferred): the trigger is not shown).

docs.title: Band 2: Real-time decisioning (middle)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant X as External service (MRD, RASI...)
    participant A as ALB
    participant P as Post-ALB Lambda
    participant S as Step Functions state machine
    participant RE as Rules Engine Lambda (in state machine)
    participant R as S3 reference cache
    participant T as S3 transaction logs
    X->>A: API request
    A->>P: forward
    P->>S: start execution (state machine invocation)
    S->>R: read reference data
    S->>S: run Normalizer → lane models → aggregates
    S->>RE: Rules Engine (render final UW decision)
    RE->>T: 5a. write Full UW output structure
    RE-->>S: decision
    S-->>P: state machine response
    P-->>A: response
    A-->>X: API response (UW decision)
  1. API Request: an external service (the diagram lists MRD, RASI, etc.) sends an underwriting request (e.g. a merchant application) to the Application Load Balancer.
  2. State Machine Invocation: the ALB forwards to the Post-ALB Lambda, which validates/shapes the payload (inferred) and starts the AWS Step Functions state machine.
  3. Read Reference Data: the state machine reads the cached config from S3 (mappings such as TMX code categories, MCC stats).
  4. State Machine runs: orchestration of the decisioning layers. The normalizer runs first, then the three lanes in parallel, then the rules engine. See lanes & layers for the concepts and Inside the state machine for every state and Lambda.
  5. 5a. Write Full UW output structure: the Rules Engine Lambda (the final step in the orchestration) writes the full UW output structure — inputs, scores and decision — directly to the S3 transaction-log bucket. (Updated: this write now originates from the Rules Engine Lambda itself, not from the state-machine construct.)
  6. State Machine Response: the result returns to the Post-ALB Lambda.
  7. API Response: the decision goes back through the ALB to the caller.

Because the response returns synchronously, the Step Functions workflow is most likely an Express workflow invoked synchronously (inferred).

docs.title: Band 3: Asynchronous transaction logging (bottom)
docs.text:
The request is logged too

Per the manager, the API request (step 1) is also written to a Snowflake table, although the diagram doesn't show it. That table is the input for data quality monitoring; the 5c historical table is the output. See What to monitor.

Arrow From → To What happens 5a Rules Engine Lambda → S3 (transaction log bucket) The Rules Engine writes the full UW output structure per decision. (Updated: previously drawn from the state machine.) 5b S3 → AWS2SF Trans Log Pipe Lambda A new output file (S3 event notification) triggers the async write. 5c Lambda → Snowflake historical table The full UW output is written to a historical table for analytics, monitoring and model retraining.

    classDef lambda fill:#BC5618,stroke:#B5531E,color:#fff;
    classDef s3 fill:#54802D,stroke:#4C7A26,color:#fff;

Layers map to the rows above: the Normalizer is the Normalization Layer; the per-source boxes are the Primitive Model Layer; the per-lane Aggregate boxes are the Composite Model Layer ("score of scores"); and the Rules Engine is the Rules Engine Layer, which takes all lane scores into account.

The Rules Engine performs the 5a write

As the final step in the orchestration, the Rules Engine Lambda writes the full UW output structure directly to the S3 transaction-log bucket (step 5a) — see the end-to-end data flow. (Updated: this write previously came from the state-machine construct.)

docs.title: The four layers
docs.text: Layer Definition from the diagram Plain English Normalization Layer All cleaning, scaling and feature generation that is shared across models & rules. Turn the raw request + reference data into a clean feature set once. Primitive Model Layer Source-specific models. Model-specific encoders and normalization sit with primitive model images. One model per data source; each brings its own encoders. Composite Model Layer Also known as "score of scores"; uses scenario-specific model objects (depending on sources available). Combine the per-source scores into one lane score, picking the right model for whichever sources returned data. Rules Engine Layer Final set of rules that takes into account all scores and data to render a final UW decision. Business rules produce approve / decline / refer etc. (outcome values inferred).

docs.title: The three lanes
docs.text:
The three lanes (Merchant Fraud, Identity Theft, Credit) are the columns in the diagram above. Each lane runs its own set of source models and rolls them up into a lane aggregate:

Source model Merchant Fraud (MF) Identity Theft (IDT) Credit Internal App GNF ✅ ✅ ✅ Experian Consumer / Commercial ✅ ✅ ✅ Lexis Neustar ✅ ✅ Lexis TMX (ThreatMetrix) ✅ ✅ Aggregate MF Aggregate IDT Aggregate Credit Aggregate

Confirmed by the state-machine definition

In the PDF the Rules Engine is drawn under the IDT lane. The real Step Functions graph confirms what the legend implied: all three aggregates feed one Rules Engine (uw-rules-engine-cert), and it runs only after every lane has finished. The lanes do run in parallel, in a Parallel state named ScoreLanes. The source models inside each lane run in parallel too. See Inside the state machine for every state and Lambda name.

docs.title: What the data sources are
docs.text:
The full list

The Implementation Support Document lists every source MRD collects (application, TINCheck, GNF, RNF, Mastercard MATCH, LexisNexis with Emailage and ThreatMetrix, Neustar, Experian bureau and BIZ ID; Equifax to replace Experian bureau), the component models per source, and the score-of-scores combinations.

  • Internal App GNF: features from the application data and Fiserv's Global Negative File (GNF, negative history on merchant accounts). The internal Restricted Name File (RNF) is used too.
  • Experian Consumer / Commercial: credit bureau data on the owner (consumer) and the business (commercial).
  • Lexis Neustar: LexisNexis / Neustar identity and phone/contact verification signals.
  • Lexis TMX: LexisNexis ThreatMetrix device and digital-identity signals. The TMX code categories config table in the transcript maps raw TMX codes into categories used by these models.

docs.title: Inside the state machine
docs.text:
This page walks through the actual Step Functions definition behind step 4 of the end-to-end flow, state by state. It is taken from the state-machine graph in the AWS console (CERT environment). The lanes & layers page describes the same thing conceptually; this page shows how it is really wired.

What is confirmed vs inferred

The state names, state types, Lambda function names and their order are read straight from the console graph. Why a state exists (for example, why there are three Merge states) is my interpretation and is marked (inferred). The state-machine JSON (ASL) would confirm these.

docs.title: The whole state machine at a glance
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    START((Start)):::term --> CIP["CaptureInitialPayload<br/><i>Pass</i>"]:::pass
    CIP --> NORM["uw-normalizer-cert<br/><i>Lambda</i>"]:::lambda
    NORM --> SL

    subgraph SL["ScoreLanes — Parallel: 3 lanes run at the same time"]
        direction LR
        MF["<b>Merchant Fraud</b><br/>ScoreMfPrimitives (4 Lambdas)<br/>MergeMf1 → 2 → 3<br/>mf-aggregate-cert<br/>EmitMfLane"]:::lane
        IDT["<b>Identity Theft</b><br/>ScoreIdtPrimitives (4 Lambdas)<br/>MergeIdt1 → 2 → 3<br/>idt-aggregate-cert<br/>EmitIdtLane"]:::lane
        CR["<b>Credit</b><br/>ScoreCreditPrimitives (2 Lambdas)<br/>MergeCredit1<br/>credit-aggregate-cert<br/>EmitCreditLane"]:::lane
    end

    SL --> B1["BuildRulesPayload1<br/><i>Pass</i>"]:::pass
    B1 --> B2["BuildRulesPayload2<br/><i>Pass</i>"]:::pass
    B2 --> B3["BuildRulesPayload3<br/><i>Pass</i>"]:::pass
    B3 --> RE["uw-rules-engine-cert<br/><i>Lambda</i>"]:::lambda
    RE --> END((End)):::term
    RE -. "5a: write Full UW output" .-> S3[("S3<br/>transaction log bucket")]:::s3

    classDef lambda fill:#BC5618,stroke:#B5531E,color:#fff;
    classDef pass   fill:#e8eef5,stroke:#7a8ca3,color:#1a1c1e;
    classDef lane   fill:#fdf1e6,stroke:#E8864A,color:#1a1c1e;
    classDef term   fill:#f2e2b8,stroke:#b59a4a,color:#3a2e05;
    classDef s3     fill:#54802D,stroke:#4C7A26,color:#fff;

The run has five phases:

# Phase States Layer 1 Keep the request CaptureInitialPayload (setup) 2 Normalize uw-normalizer-cert Normalization layer 3 Score the three lanes ScoreLanes and everything inside it Primitive model + Composite model layers 4 Build the rules input BuildRulesPayload1 → 2 → 3 (glue) 5 Decide uw-rules-engine-cert Rules engine layer

docs.title: The three state types you will see
docs.text:
Type Icon in the console What it does here Lambda: Invoke orange λ Runs a Lambda function: the normalizer, a model, an aggregate or the rules engine. All the real computation happens in these. Pass split arrow Runs no code. It only reshapes the JSON passing between states: copies, merges or renames fields. Parallel fork Starts several branches at the same time and waits for all of them. Its output is an array with one element per branch.

The last row matters most. Because a Parallel state returns an array, every Parallel state here is followed by Pass states that flatten the array back into one object. That is what the Merge* and BuildRulesPayload* states are for.

docs.title: Phase 1: CaptureInitialPayload (Pass)
docs.text:
The first state keeps a copy of the incoming request, as it arrived from the Post-ALB Lambda.

Why (inferred): each later state replaces its input with its output by default. Without a saved copy, the original application data would be gone by the time the rules engine runs. The rules engine needs both the scores and the original request fields, so the request is stashed at the start.

docs.title: Phase 2: uw-normalizer-cert (Lambda)
docs.text:
This is the Normalization layer. One Lambda cleans the request, scales values and builds the features that are shared by every model and rule, so this work is done once rather than once per model.

Where the S3 reference data is read

There is no separate state for step 3 of the end-to-end flow ("read reference data"). So the S3 reference cache must be read inside the Lambdas. The normalizer is the most likely reader, since it builds the shared features (for example, mapping raw TMX codes to categories) (inferred). Models with their own lookups may read S3 too. To confirm which ones do, check the Lambda code or its CloudWatch logs.

docs.title: Phase 3: ScoreLanes (Parallel)
docs.text:
ScoreLanes starts three branches at the same time, one per lane. Each branch gets the normalizer's output as its input. The state finishes only when all three branches have finished, so the slowest lane sets the time for this phase.

Every lane has the same five-part shape:

  1. Score<Lane>Primitives (Parallel): runs that lane's source models at the same time. This is the Primitive model layer.
  2. Merge<Lane>1…n (Pass): flattens the array of model outputs into one object.
  3. <lane>-aggregate-cert (Lambda): the lane's "score of scores". This is the Composite model layer.
  4. Emit<Lane>Lane (Pass): shapes the lane's final result for the next phase.

So there are two levels of Parallel: lanes run at the same time as each other, and within each lane the source models run at the same time too.

docs.title: Why the number of Merge states matches the number of sources
docs.text:
Look at the counts: 4 sources → 3 merges (MF, IDT) and 2 sources → 1 merge (Credit). It is always sources − 1.

That fits how Step Functions merges JSON. Its built-in merge function, States.JsonMerge, combines exactly two objects at a time. Folding n results into one therefore takes n − 1 merges (inferred from the counts; the ASL would confirm it):

ScoreMfPrimitives output: an array, one element per branch
  [ {gnf result}, {experian result}, {neustar result}, {tmx result} ]

MergeMf1:  merge( [0], [1] )        → {gnf + experian}
MergeMf2:  merge( previous, [2] )   → {gnf + experian + neustar}
MergeMf3:  merge( previous, [3] )   → {gnf + experian + neustar + tmx}

mf-aggregate-cert receives ONE flat object holding all four primitive scores

The same reasoning explains BuildRulesPayload1–3 in phase 4.

docs.title: What the Emit*Lane states do
docs.text: EmitMfLane, EmitIdtLane and EmitCreditLane are the last state in each branch, so their output becomes that lane's element in the ScoreLanes result. Most likely they wrap the lane's result under its own key (for example mf, idt, credit). Then the three lanes can be merged in phase 4 without their fields overwriting each other (inferred).

docs.title: Phase 4: BuildRulesPayload1 → 2 → 3 (Pass)
docs.text:
ScoreLanes returns an array of three lane results. The rules engine needs one object that holds all three lane results plus the original request saved in phase 1. That is four pieces, which takes three pairwise merges (inferred):

BuildRulesPayload1:  merge( lane result A, lane result B )
BuildRulesPayload2:  merge( previous, lane result C )
BuildRulesPayload3:  merge( previous, captured initial payload )   ← from CaptureInitialPayload

The exact order of the pieces may differ. Only the ASL can show it.

docs.title: Phase 5: uw-rules-engine-cert (Lambda), then End
docs.text:
The Rules engine layer. It receives the combined payload: all three lane aggregates, their primitive scores and the original request. It applies the business rules and produces the final UW decision.

Two things happen here:

  • It writes the full UW output structure to the S3 transaction-log bucket (step 5a). This triggers the asynchronous logging to Snowflake (5b and 5c). See Band 3.
  • Its return value becomes the state machine's output. That goes back to the Post-ALB Lambda and on to the caller (steps 6 and 7).

It is the last state, so the execution reaches End right after it.

docs.title: How the data changes from state to state
docs.text:
What the JSON looks like after each phase (conceptual, (inferred)):

After state The data is… CaptureInitialPayload the original request, plus a saved copy of it uw-normalizer-cert the shared, normalized feature set Score<Lane>Primitives an array of that lane's model outputs, one per source Merge<Lane>n (last) one object with all of that lane's primitive scores <lane>-aggregate-cert the lane's composite ("score of scores") result Emit<Lane>Lane the lane result under its lane key ScoreLanes an array of 3 lane results BuildRulesPayload3 one object: 3 lane results + the original request uw-rules-engine-cert the final UW decision (also written to S3 as the full UW output)

Using Merchant A from the worked example (illustrative values), the rules-engine input would look roughly like this:

{
  "mf":     { "aggregate_score": 0.11, "primitives": { "internal_app_gnf": "…", "experian": "…", "neustar": "…", "tmx": "…" } },
  "idt":    { "aggregate_score": 0.08, "primitives": { "…": "…" } },
  "credit": { "aggregate_score": 0.79, "primitives": { "internal_app_gnf": "…", "experian": "…" } },
  "request": { "merchant": "Downtown Coffee LLC", "mcc": "5812", "…": "…" }
}

The field names are invented to show the shape. They are not the real schema.

docs.title: Timing: what runs at the same time
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant SM as State machine
    participant N as uw-normalizer-cert
    participant MF as MF lane
    participant IDT as IDT lane
    participant CR as Credit lane
    participant RE as uw-rules-engine-cert
    participant S3 as S3 transaction log
    SM->>SM: CaptureInitialPayload
    SM->>N: invoke
    N-->>SM: normalized payload
    par ScoreLanes
        SM->>MF: 4 primitives in parallel → MergeMf1-3 → mf-aggregate → EmitMfLane
    and
        SM->>IDT: 4 primitives in parallel → MergeIdt1-3 → idt-aggregate → EmitIdtLane
    and
        SM->>CR: 2 primitives in parallel → MergeCredit1 → credit-aggregate → EmitCreditLane
    end
    MF-->>SM: MF lane result
    IDT-->>SM: IDT lane result
    CR-->>SM: Credit lane result
    SM->>SM: BuildRulesPayload1 → 2 → 3
    SM->>RE: invoke with combined payload
    RE->>S3: 5a: write Full UW output
    RE-->>SM: final UW decision

Rough latency: normalizer + the slowest lane + rules engine. Within a lane, the slowest source model sets the time, plus the merges and the aggregate. Pass states take almost no time.

docs.title: All the function names
docs.text:
Every Lambda follows <lane>-<source>-<environment>. The -cert suffix is the environment (CERT, the certification / pre-production stage). In other environments the suffix is likely different, for example -prod (inferred).

Source Merchant Fraud Identity Theft Credit Internal App GNF mf-internal-app-gnf-cert idt-internal-app-gnf-cert credit-internal-app-gnf-cert Experian Consumer / Commercial mf-experian-consumer-commercial-cert idt-experian-consumer-commercial-cert credit-experian-consumer-commercial-cert Lexis Neustar mf-lexis-neustar-cert idt-lexis-neustar-cert (none) Lexis TMX mf-lexis-tmx-cert idt-lexis-tmx-cert (none) Aggregate mf-aggregate-cert idt-aggregate-cert credit-aggregate-cert

Shared across all lanes: uw-normalizer-cert (first) and uw-rules-engine-cert (last).

Totals: 15 Lambda functions, 4 Parallel states (ScoreLanes + 3 Score*Primitives), 14 Pass states. 33 states in all.

docs.title: What this means for support
docs.text:
• Every source model runs on every request. There is no Choice state that skips a source. If a source has no data for a merchant (for example, TMX finds no device), its Lambda still runs and returns an empty or "no signal" result. The lane's aggregate then picks the right scenario model (inferred).
  • One failing Lambda can fail the whole run. In Step Functions, if any branch of a Parallel state fails, the whole Parallel state fails, unless the definition has Retry or Catch rules. The console graph does not show whether these exist. Confirm this in the ASL, because it decides whether, for example, a Neustar outage stops every decision.
  • Finding a failure: open the execution in the Step Functions console. The failed state is marked in red, and you can see each state's input and output. If it failed inside a Lambda, the error is that function's (for example idt-lexis-tmx-cert), and its CloudWatch logs have the details.
  • Finding the slow part: the execution timeline shows how long each state took. Look at the slowest lane, then the slowest primitive inside it.
  • Wrong reference data: there is no separate read state, so check the logs of the Lambda that reads S3 (most likely the normalizer).

See also the Support engineer guide.

docs.title: Support engineer guide
docs.text: How to reason about issues in this system, organised by the three processes.

docs.title: 1. "My config change isn't being used"
docs.text:
Walk the chain left to right:

Check Where What to look for Row approved? Admin console UI The row is in an approved/decisioned state. Data in Snowflake? Snowflake config schema SELECT the table; confirm the new value exists. Cache job ran? CloudWatch Logs for the SF2AWS Config Lambda Recent invocation, no errors, Snowflake connection OK. Fingerprint changed? State file Fingerprint for that table's row updated after the change. If the query in the query column doesn't select the changed column/row, the hash won't change. S3 file updated? S3 reference bucket LastModified timestamp and contents of the object. State machine reads it? CloudWatch Logs of the Lambda that reads S3 (most likely uw-normalizer-cert) There is no separate read state; the S3 read happens inside a Lambda. Confirm it loaded the expected object/version. Watch for Lambda-level caching of reference data across warm invocations (inferred risk). 
-- Example: confirm the value landed in Snowflake (adjust names)
SELECT * FROM <db>.<config_schema>.TMX_CODE_CATEGORIES WHERE key = '<code>';

# Example: confirm the cached object refreshed
aws s3api head-object --bucket <reference-bucket> --key <path/to/file>
aws logs tail /aws/lambda/<sf2aws-config-lambda> --since 1h

docs.title: 2. "The API is slow / erroring"
docs.text:
Symptom Likely place 5xx from ALB, no Lambda logs ALB target health / Lambda permissions for ALB. 502 from ALB Post-ALB Lambda returned a malformed response or timed out. Timeouts One slow primitive model or third-party source. Lanes run in parallel, so the slowest lane sets the time. In the execution timeline, find the slowest lane, then the slowest *-cert primitive inside it. Execution failed Open the execution in the Step Functions console; the failed state is red. A failing primitive fails its whole Parallel state unless Retry/Catch is defined (confirm in the ASL). See Inside the state machine. Wrong decision Compare the transaction log for that request with the expected config; check which composite model scenario was chosen (sources available).

Useful places: ALB access logs, CloudWatch metrics for each Lambda (Duration, Errors, Throttles, ConcurrentExecutions), Step Functions execution history.

docs.title: 3. "Decisions missing in Snowflake history"
Key design facts to remember
docs.text:
• Snowflake is never in the real-time path; Snowflake outages affect freshness and history, not live decisions.
  • The real-time path depends on S3 reference data being present and valid; an empty or malformed cached file can break every request.
  • Most config tables are still empty today (per the transcript), so expect missing-config issues while they are being populated.
  • Monthly MCC stats tables may be manually updated for now; confirm their freshness when MCC-based features look stale.

docs.title: Before the config tables
docs.text: The architecture diagram starts at Snowflake Config Tables. The transcript answers the question "what is upstream of those tables?"

docs.title: Short answer
docs.text:
For the true config tables, nothing technical is upstream except people's decisions. They are parameters for the service: mappings, categories and lookups that the models and rules need. They are entered through a governed admin console UI, not produced by a data pipeline.

flowchart LR
    A["Analysis / business decision<br/>(e.g. 'map TMX codes differently')"] --> B["Admin console UI<br/>(new MRV / visual app)"]
    B -- "one row at a time,<br/>approved & decisioned" --> C[("Snowflake<br/>config tables")]
    M["Underwriting developers'<br/>upstream processes (unclear)"] -.-> D[("Monthly batch tables<br/>MCC-level stats")]
    C --> E["SF2AWS Config Table Pipe Lambda"]
    D --> E
    E --> F[("S3 reference cache")]

docs.title: 1. Someone identifies a need for config
docs.text: Example from the transcript: a data scientist (Arjen) identified that three new config tables were needed for multiple models. The modelling team supplies the "starting place for the data", and the engineering team puts it into Snowflake.

docs.title: 2. Config is defined in the admin console
docs.text:
In the admin console of the new app, each true config table is a governed key/value view. The example shown was TMX code categories:

key value a TMX code the category it maps to

Properties called out in the meeting:

  • Governed: rows are approved and decisioned.
  • One row at a time: you cannot bulk-update with a Snowflake process; each change is an ad-hoc, deliberate edit.
  • Relatively static: changes over time, but not on a regular schedule.
  • Work in progress: Sachin has been setting many of these up; most are still empty and need to be populated.

docs.title: 3. The tables live in Snowflake
docs.text: Today the tables sit in a config schema in Snowflake. Over time they will migrate to the UI-governed style (like TMX code categories).

docs.title: 4. Monthly batch tables (missing from the diagram)
docs.text:
The diagram only shows "config tables", but there is a second category:

  • Monthly batch tables holding MCC-level statistics (MCC = Merchant Category Code).
  • These do have something upstream, owned by the underwriting developers; the full picture was not known in the meeting.
  • For now they may be updated manually; a proper deployed process is planned later.

docs.title: 5. Cache to S3 (the "yellow dotted line")
docs.text: The team's concern is simply: whatever is in Snowflake must be cached to S3. That is done by the SF2AWS Config Table Pipe Lambda using a state file.

docs.title: How the caching job decides what to refresh
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant L as SF2AWS Config Lambda
    participant St as State file
    participant SF as Snowflake
    participant S3 as S3 reference bucket
    L->>St: read rows (one per table / S3 file)
    loop for each row
        L->>SF: run the SQL in the row's "query" column
        SF-->>L: result set
        L->>L: hash result -> new fingerprint
        alt fingerprint changed
            L->>S3: write/overwrite the cached file
            L->>St: store new fingerprint
        else unchanged
            L->>L: skip (no write)
        end
    end
  • Each row of the state file corresponds to one file that lands in S3.
  • The row has a query column (the SQL to run) and a fingerprint (hash of the last result).
  • Because config changes rarely, most runs are no-ops; S3 is only rewritten when the data really changed.

Why this matters for support

If a config change made in the UI does not show up in decisions, the chain to check is: UI row approved → Snowflake table updated → Lambda ran → fingerprint changed → S3 file updated → state machine reading the new file. See the support guide.

docs.title: Worked example: two merchants end to end
docs.text:
This page traces two underwriting requests through the whole service so you can see what is shared and what is per-merchant. It is the best place to start if the data flow still feels abstract.

The merchant data and scores below are illustrative

Nothing here is a real application or a real model output. The names, MCCs, device codes and scores are invented to make the flow concrete. They are (illustrative). Treat the shape of the flow as the lesson, not the numbers.

docs.title: First, clear up one common misconception
docs.text:
A natural assumption is:

"For each merchant run, the service retrieves that merchant's data, caches it in AWS, and the state machine reads it from there."

That is not how it works. There are two very different kinds of data, and only one of them is cached:

Data Example Per-merchant? Cached in S3? When it is fetched Reference / config data TMX code categories, MCC-level stats, lookup mappings ❌ shared ✅ yes — the reference cache bucket Asynchronously, long before any request The merchant's own data the application, the owner's details, source/bureau signals ✅ per-run ❌ no — it flows through the request live At decision time, inside the request The decision (output) scores + final UW decision for this merchant ✅ per-run ✅ yes — the transaction log bucket (later) After the decision, for history/analytics

So:

  • The reference cache is the same for every merchant. Merchant A and Merchant B read the identical cached files (same TMX category map, same MCC stats). It is refreshed on its own schedule by the SF2AWS Config Lambda, not per request.
  • The merchant-specific data arrives in the API request and is normalized and scored in real time. It is never pre-cached.
  • The only per-merchant thing written to S3 is the transaction log, and that happens after the decision (steps 5a–5c), into a different bucket, purely for history — it is never fed back into the models for that same request.
flowchart LR
    subgraph SHARED["Shared, cached ahead of time"]
        REF[("S3 reference cache<br/>TMX categories, MCC stats")]
    end
    subgraph PERREQ["Per-merchant, live in the request"]
        REQ["Merchant request<br/>(application + source signals)"]
    end
    REF --> SM{{"Step Functions<br/>state machine"}}
    REQ --> SM
    SM --> DEC["Decision for this merchant"]
    DEC -.->|"after, for history"| LOG[("S3 transaction log")]

docs.title: The two merchants at a glance (illustrative)
docs.text:
Attribute Merchant A — Downtown Coffee LLC Merchant B — QuickCash Online Comes in via MRD RASI MCC 5812 (eating places) 5967 (direct marketing / inbound teleservices) Internal App GNF ✅ present ✅ present Experian Cons/Comm ✅ returned ✅ returned Lexis Neustar ✅ returned ✅ returned Lexis TMX ✅ returned (device recognised) ⚠️ no match / thin → treated as missing Illustrative outcome Approve Refer (manual review)

The difference is deliberate: Merchant B is missing one source (TMX), which is exactly the case the Composite Model Layer is designed to handle by picking a scenario-specific model. Watch for that below.

docs.title: 0. (Earlier, asynchronously) the reference cache is already warm
docs.text: Long before Merchant A applies, the SF2AWS Config Lambda has already cached the shared reference files into S3 — for example a tmx_code_categories file and an mcc_stats file. Nothing about this step involves Merchant A; it would have happened anyway.

docs.title: 1. API request
docs.text: MRD sends Merchant A's underwriting request to the ALB. The payload carries Merchant A's data (business details, owner details, and the source signals the caller has — Internal App GNF, Experian, Lexis Neustar, Lexis TMX). (Exactly which signals are in the payload vs. fetched later is not stated in the sources — inferred.)

docs.title: 2. State machine invocation
docs.text: The ALB forwards to the Post-ALB Lambda, which validates/shapes the payload (inferred) and starts the Step Functions state machine.

docs.title: 3. Read reference data (the shared cache)
docs.text:
The state machine reads the shared cached files from S3 — the same files any other request uses:

  • tmx_code_categories → used to turn Merchant A's raw TMX device code into a category. Say Merchant A's device code maps to category trusted (illustrative).
  • mcc_stats for MCC 5812 → a low baseline-risk profile for eating places (illustrative).

docs.title: 4. State machine runs (Normalizer → lanes → aggregates → Rules Engine)
docs.text:
Inside the state machine the layers and lanes execute on Merchant A's data:

  1. Normalizer cleans/scales Merchant A's features once (using shared reference data where needed).
  2. Primitive models score each source. All four sources are present, so every lane runs its full set:
  3. Merchant Fraud lane: GNF, Experian, Neustar, TMX → MF Aggregate = 0.11 (illustrative, low).
  4. Identity Theft lane: GNF, Experian, Neustar, TMX → IDT Aggregate = 0.08 (illustrative, low).
  5. Credit lane: GNF, Experian → Credit Aggregate = 0.79 (illustrative, good).
  6. Composite models roll each lane's primitive scores into that lane aggregate. Because all sources returned, the "all-sources" scenario model object is used (inferred mechanism).
  7. Rules Engine takes all three aggregates plus the data and renders the final decision → Approve (illustrative).
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant X as MRD
    participant A as ALB
    participant P as Post-ALB Lambda
    participant S as State machine
    participant RE as Rules Engine Lambda
    participant R as S3 reference cache (shared)
    participant T as S3 transaction logs
    X->>A: Merchant A request
    A->>P: forward
    P->>S: start execution
    S->>R: read tmx_code_categories, mcc_stats (5812)
    Note over S: Normalizer → 3 lanes (all 4 sources) → aggregates
    S->>RE: Rules Engine → APPROVE
    RE->>T: 5a. write Merchant A full UW output
    RE-->>S: decision = Approve
    S-->>P: decision = Approve
    P-->>A: response
    A-->>X: Approve

docs.title: 5a–5c. Log the decision (asynchronous, after the fact)
docs.text: The inputs, scores and the Approve decision are written to the transaction log bucket (5a). A new-file event triggers the AWS2SF Trans Log Lambda (5b), which loads the record into the Snowflake historical table (5c) for analytics and model retraining. This does not affect Merchant A's own response — it already went out.

docs.title: 6–7. Response
docs.text: The decision returns through the Post-ALB Lambda (6) and back out through the ALB to MRD (7): Approve.

docs.title: Merchant B — step by step (where it diverges)
docs.text: Steps 1–3 look the same in shape: RASI sends the request, the Post-ALB Lambda starts the state machine, and the state machine reads the same shared reference files. The differences start at the data itself.

docs.title: 3. Read reference data — same cache, different lookups hit
docs.text:
The state machine reads the identical cached files, but Merchant B's data lands on different entries:

  • mcc_stats for MCC 5967 → a higher baseline-risk profile (illustrative).
  • tmx_code_categories → Merchant B's TMX call returned no recognised device (thin signal), so there is effectively no TMX source to categorise.

docs.title: 4. State machine runs — the composite layer adapts
docs.text:
This is the key teaching point. One source (TMX) has no data, so the lanes that use TMX are missing one input:

  1. Normalizer runs on the data that is present.
  2. Primitive models: all four MF and IDT source models still run. The state machine has no step that skips a source (see Inside the state machine). But mf-lexis-tmx-cert and idt-lexis-tmx-cert have no device signal to score, so they return an empty or "no signal" result (inferred). The Credit lane never used TMX, so it is unaffected.
  3. Composite models — scenario-specific: because TMX is absent, each affected lane's composite picks the model object trained for the "no-TMX" scenario instead of the all-sources one. This is exactly the "score of scores … depending on sources available" behaviour from the Composite Model Layer.
  4. MF Aggregate = 0.63 (illustrative, elevated).
  5. IDT Aggregate = 0.41 (illustrative, medium).
  6. Credit Aggregate = 0.55 (illustrative, thin-but-ok).
  7. Rules Engine combines all aggregates + the higher-risk MCC profile and renders → Refer (send to a human) rather than an outright Approve/Decline (illustrative; outcome values inferred).
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant X as RASI
    participant A as ALB
    participant P as Post-ALB Lambda
    participant S as State machine
    participant RE as Rules Engine Lambda
    participant R as S3 reference cache (shared)
    participant T as S3 transaction logs
    X->>A: Merchant B request
    A->>P: forward
    P->>S: start execution
    S->>R: read tmx_code_categories, mcc_stats (5967)
    Note over S: TMX missing → composite uses<br/>"no-TMX" scenario models → higher aggregates
    S->>RE: Rules Engine → REFER
    RE->>T: 5a. write Merchant B full UW output
    RE-->>S: decision = Refer
    S-->>P: decision = Refer
    P-->>A: response
    A-->>X: Refer

docs.title: 5a–7. Log + response
docs.text: Same as Merchant A: the decision and its scores are logged to S3 → Snowflake history (5a–5c), and Refer is returned synchronously to RASI (6–7).

docs.title: Side-by-side: what actually differed
docs.text: Step Merchant A Merchant B Reference files read Same shared cache Same shared cache Which cache rows mattered MCC 5812 (low), TMX cat trusted MCC 5967 (higher), no TMX category (missing source) Sources available All four Three (no TMX) Composite model chosen "all-sources" scenario "no-TMX" scenario (inferred) Final decision Approve (illustrative) Refer (illustrative) Written to transaction log ✅ after decision ✅ after decision

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. The S3 cache is shared reference data, not per-merchant. Both merchants read the exact same files; what differs is their own request data and which reference entries that data touches.
  2. Merchant data is live, not cached. It enters with the request, is normalized and scored in the state machine, and the decision returns synchronously. The only per-merchant S3 write is the after-the-fact transaction log.
  3. The composite layer adapts to whatever sources returned. Missing a source (like TMX for Merchant B) doesn't break the request — it selects a scenario-specific model instead, which is why two merchants can take structurally different paths through the same pipeline.

Where this is inferred

The step skeleton (1–7, 5a–5c), the three lanes, the four layers and the scenario-specific composite behaviour come from the architecture diagram and transcript. The specific merchants, MCCs, device-code categories, scores and the Approve/Refer outcomes are illustrative and the exact decision values are (inferred) — confirm real thresholds and outcome labels with the team.

docs.title: Data Quality Monitoring: overview
docs.text:
This section explains a draft Business Requirements Document (BRD) for a proactive Model & Rule Monitoring Platform: a data-quality framework in the spirit of Great Expectations. It covers what the BRD asks for, how each type of check works, and how it could be built.

Sources and labels

This section is based on screenshots of the BRD ("Model and Rules Performance BRD, Part 1: Input Monitoring", file Input Data Monitoring BRD_4.1, Version 1.0, September 2026, still marked @TEMPLATE) and its companion requirements spreadsheet (tabs Input Monitoring and Feature_Scores Monitoring). The pages use three labels:

- Unlabelled statements about requirements come **from the BRD**.
- **(inferred)**: my reading of something the BRD does not state.
- **(suggestion)**: an implementation idea that is **not** in the BRD.

What's next

The After the BRD section covers what the manager asked for once the BRD was written: who fills in the templates, which UW tables to monitor, the report layout and hourly alerting.

docs.title: The problem the BRD is solving
docs.text:
Today, decisions in Underwriting, Risk Monitoring and Clover Capital are monitored reactively. Problems only come to light when a business stakeholder notices something odd in a rule, such as a sudden rise in how often a rule fires. The BRD lists five specific gaps:

  • Underwriting and risk monitoring are reactive. Problems are found only when the business reports a rise in a rule.
  • There is no systematic monitoring of input data, features, scores, or model/rule performance.
  • Business stakeholders see only rule outcomes, not the scores or features behind them.
  • There is no feedback loop connecting model performance back to real account outcomes.
  • Monitoring must eventually cover Risk Monitoring and Clover Capital as well as Underwriting, without a separate build for each.

The goal is to catch bad data before it turns into bad decisions, and to build that capability once, in a modular way, so all three business areas can reuse it.

docs.title: The BRD series
docs.text:
The BRD is the first in a planned series. Each part covers one layer of monitoring:

flowchart LR
    P1["<b>Part 1</b><br/>Input Monitoring<br/><i>(this BRD)</i>"]:::now
    P2["<b>Next</b><br/>Feature & Score<br/>Monitoring"]:::next
    P3["<b>Next</b><br/>Rule<br/>Monitoring"]:::next
    P4["<b>Next</b><br/>Model Performance<br/>Monitoring"]:::next
    P5["<b>Next</b><br/>Reusable Monitoring<br/>Architecture"]:::next
    P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4
    P5 -. "underpins all parts" .-> P1 & P2 & P3 & P4

    classDef now  fill:#f2d492,stroke:#c99a2e,color:#3a2e05;
    classDef next fill:#e8eef5,stroke:#7a8ca3,color:#1a1c1e;

Only Part 1 has written requirements so far. The spreadsheet already has a second tab, Feature_Scores Monitoring, so the next part is partly drafted. This section covers both.

docs.title: Business objective (Part 1)
docs.text:
ID Objective Expected outcome BO-01 Input Data Monitoring Potential issues are identified before they affect business outcomes, through proactive alerts and reports. Track applications, LN (LexisNexis), TMX, Bureau etc. data for availability and validity before it is used by models.

The data sources named here are the same ones that feed the Underwriting decisioning lanes: the internal application (GNF), Lexis Neustar, Lexis TMX and Experian (the bureau).

docs.title: How the platform fits together
docs.text:
The BRD does not include an architecture diagram. That is reserved for the later Reusable Monitoring Architecture part. Below is how the requirements fit together (inferred from the parameters in the spreadsheet):

flowchart LR
    subgraph SRC["Data in Snowflake"]
        direction TB
        IN[("Raw inputs<br/>applications, LN, TMX, Bureau")]:::src
        FS[("Features & scores<br/>FICO, IDT score, ...")]:::src
        BM[("Benchmark population<br/>(a fixed date range)")]:::src
    end

    CFG[("Check definitions<br/>variable × check type × threshold<br/>(the spreadsheet)")]:::cfg
    RUN["Check runner<br/>(hourly)"]:::step
    RES[("Results<br/>PASS / FAIL per variable per check")]:::out
    AL["Alerts<br/>(email, hourly)"]:::alert
    REP["Report<br/>(weekly)"]:::out

    IN --> RUN
    FS --> RUN
    BM -. "features/scores only" .-> RUN
    CFG --> RUN
    RUN --> RES
    RES -- "FAIL and Alerts Sent = Yes" --> AL
    RES --> REP

    classDef src   fill:#127EA6,stroke:#1877A3,color:#fff;
    classDef cfg   fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#5e4e8a,color:#fff;
    classDef step  fill:#f2d492,stroke:#c99a2e,color:#3a2e05;
    classDef out   fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;
    classDef alert fill:#e08a7b,stroke:#a8503f,color:#2b0c08;

Where \"Snowflake Path\" fits in this picture

The BRD's Snowflake Path parameters are the addresses of the three blue boxes on the left. Each is the full name of a Snowflake table, DATABASE.SCHEMA.TABLE, that the check runner reads. The draft leaves them as "Link" placeholders, so no table has been chosen yet. See What "Snowflake Path" means.

Four ideas recur throughout the BRD:

  1. Each variable–check pair is configured separately. For every variable you choose which checks apply, the threshold that counts as a failure, and whether a failure sends an alert.
  2. Every result is binary: PASS or FAIL.
  3. There are two schedules. Alerts are evaluated hourly; a report is produced weekly.
  4. Inputs and features are judged differently. Input checks look only at the data itself. Feature and score checks compare an active population with a benchmark population, to detect drift.

docs.title: Input monitoring vs feature & score monitoring
docs.text: Input monitoring Feature & score monitoring Looks at Raw input fields (Merch ID, Enquiry Date, Avg Ticket, ...) Model inputs and outputs (FICO Score, Phone Health, IDT Score, ...) Question asked "Is this data present and valid?" "Has this data's distribution shifted from what the model was built on?" Compared with Nothing; only the data itself A benchmark/base population from a chosen date range Typical checks Missing values, field population, acceptable range, format Same checks, plus CSI/FSI and PSI stability indices Data window Hourly alerts, weekly report Active population daily; hourly alerts, weekly report

docs.title: Where this connects to the rest of the site
docs.text:
• Where the BRD came from: the monitoring kickoff meeting. See From kickoff to BRD for what the draft covers and what it still misses.
  • Underwriting: the inputs to monitor are the source data behind the lane primitives. Snowflake is not on the real-time path, so this monitoring would most likely run on data after it has been logged to Snowflake, not as a check that blocks a live decision. Whether it should block decisions is an open question. See Review notes.
  • Risk Monitoring: the feature store outputs are natural targets for feature monitoring. Its -999 sentinel value is exactly what the Placeholder Value check type is for.

docs.title: Pages in this section
docs.text:
• Input monitoring: the Part 1 requirements, each check type explained, and a worked example.
  • Feature & score monitoring: the drift checks (benchmark vs active), with CSI and PSI worked out step by step.
  • Implementation guide: how to build it with Great Expectations or natively in Snowflake.
  • Review notes & open questions: gaps in the draft worth raising.

docs.title: Feature & score monitoring
docs.text:
The spreadsheet's second tab, Feature_Scores Monitoring, drafts the next BRD in the series. It moves from raw inputs to the features and scores the models use and produce, for example FICO Score, Bank Verification, Phone Health, KYB Verification and IDT Score.

Input monitoring asks "is this data valid?". Feature & score monitoring adds a second question: "does this data still look like the data the model was built and validated on?" A model can get inputs that are each perfectly valid and still drift, if the overall mix of values shifts.

docs.title: Two populations
docs.text:
The main difference from input monitoring is that two datasets are compared:

Parameter Value Meaning Benchmark / Base Population Date A fixed reference period, for example the data the model was developed on. Snowflake Path: Benchmark (link) The Snowflake table holding that reference data. Active Population Daily Recent production data, refreshed every day. Snowflake Path: Active (link) The Snowflake table holding that recent data. Scheduled Yes Reporting Freq (Scheduled = Y) Weekly Alert Freq Hourly

What the two Snowflake Paths are

Each one is a table's full name in Snowflake, DATABASE.SCHEMA.TABLE: the data the comparison reads. This tab needs two because it compares two populations. Both are still "Link" placeholders in the draft. They will most likely both point at the historical table of model-service output, possibly the same table with different date filters (inferred). Full explanation: What "Snowflake Path" means.

flowchart LR
    B[("Benchmark population<br/>fixed date range")]:::bm
    A[("Active population<br/>refreshed daily")]:::act
    B --> CMP["Compare distributions<br/>per feature / score"]:::step
    A --> CMP
    CMP --> R{"Deviation beyond<br/>alert criteria?"}
    R -- "No" --> P["PASS"]:::ok
    R -- "Yes" --> F["FAIL → alert if enabled"]:::bad

    classDef bm   fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#5e4e8a,color:#fff;
    classDef act  fill:#127EA6,stroke:#1877A3,color:#fff;
    classDef step fill:#f2d492,stroke:#c99a2e,color:#3a2e05;
    classDef ok   fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;
    classDef bad  fill:#e08a7b,stroke:#a8503f,color:#2b0c08;

docs.title: Check types
docs.text:
This tab has the same nine check types as input monitoring, plus two stability indices:

Check type Applied to What it measures Feature Stability Indicator (FSI / CSI) Each feature (input to a model) How much one feature's distribution has shifted between benchmark and active. CSI = Characteristic Stability Index. Population Stability Indicator (PSI) A model score How much the score distribution has shifted between benchmark and active.

In this tab the criteria column is labelled "Deviation (Alert Criteria)" rather than "Alert Criteria". Criteria here describe a change compared with the benchmark, not an absolute limit.

docs.title: The variable matrix (as drafted)
docs.text:
The Missing Values column is hidden behind the dropdown in the screenshot, so it is left out:

Feature / Score Value Length Deviation Alert? FSI / CSI Deviation Alert? FICO Score No No Yes Dec > 10% Yes Bank Verification No No No Phone Health No No No KYB Verification No No No … (row 17) Yes Length ≠ 8 char Yes Yes Inc > 5% Yes … (row 18) No No Yes Dec > 5% No … (rows 19–20) No No No IDT Score No No No

The variable names give useful context. Phone Health most likely comes from the Lexis Neustar source, and IDT Score from the Identity Theft lane aggregate (idt-aggregate-cert) (inferred). So this tab covers both features and model scores.

docs.title: How CSI and PSI are calculated
docs.text:
CSI and PSI use the same formula. The only difference is what it is applied to: CSI to one feature, PSI to a score.

  1. Split the benchmark values into bins, often 10 bins with equal numbers of records.
  2. Use the same bin edges to count the active values.
  3. For each bin, take the share of benchmark records (E, expected) and active records (A, actual).
  4. Add up (A − E) × ln(A / E) across all bins.
PSI = Σ over bins of  (A_i − E_i) × ln(A_i / E_i)

The result is always ≥ 0: 0 means no shift, and bigger means more shift. Movement in either direction raises it. A common industry rule of thumb (not from the BRD):

PSI / CSI value Usual reading < 0.10 Stable, no action needed 0.10 – 0.25 Moderate shift, investigate > 0.25 Significant shift, act

docs.title: Worked example 1: a small shift (illustrative)
docs.text:
FICO Score in 4 bins. The benchmark is spread evenly; the active population has drifted slightly upward.

Bin (FICO) Benchmark E Active A A − E ln(A/E) (A − E) × ln(A/E) < 620 0.25 0.20 −0.05 −0.2231 0.0112 620 – 679 0.25 0.25 0 0 0 680 – 739 0.25 0.25 0 0 0 ≥ 740 0.25 0.30 +0.05 +0.1823 0.0091 Total 1.00 1.00 0.020 → stable

docs.title: Worked example 2: a real shift (illustrative)
docs.text:
Same bins, but the active population has moved a lot. For example, a new marketing channel brings in more high-score applicants.

Bin (FICO) Benchmark E Active A A − E ln(A/E) (A − E) × ln(A/E) < 620 0.25 0.10 −0.15 −0.9163 0.1374 620 – 679 0.25 0.20 −0.05 −0.2231 0.0112 680 – 739 0.25 0.30 +0.05 +0.1823 0.0091 ≥ 740 0.25 0.40 +0.15 +0.4700 0.0705 Total 1.00 1.00 0.228 → moderate shift

How \"Dec > 10%\" fits with CSI

The draft gives FSI/CSI criteria as directional percentages: Dec > 10%, Inc > 5%. But the CSI value is never negative and goes up whichever way the data moves. It doesn't "decrease by 10%" in any meaningful way. These criteria most likely mean something else, such as "the mean of the feature fell by more than 10% compared with the benchmark", or "the share of records in some key bin fell by 10%". Either is a reasonable check, but it isn't CSI. See Review notes.

docs.title: Value Length on a feature: "Length ≠ 8 char"
docs.text: Row 17 checks that a value is exactly 8 characters. That is typical for codes or dates in YYYYMMDD form (inferred). A sudden change in length usually means an upstream format change, for example a vendor switching date formats. Such a change can make a feature silently fail to parse.

docs.title: What changes from input monitoring
docs.text:
Aspect Input monitoring Feature & score monitoring Datasets One (the data being checked) Two (benchmark + active) Kind of criteria Absolute ("missing > 30%") Change from benchmark ("Dec > 10%"), or index value Extra check types (none) FSI/CSI, PSI Needs a stable baseline No Yes: choosing the benchmark period matters

Choosing the benchmark period

The benchmark should be data the model behaved well on: usually its development or validation sample, or a recent stable period. If it's too short, the bins are noisy. If it covers an unusual time (seasonal peaks, an incident), every comparison against it is skewed. Record the chosen date range with each result so a PSI value can be traced back.

Next: Implementation guide.

docs.title: Implementation guide
docs.text:
The full blueprint

This page is a short summary of the options. The detailed, phased design (architecture, data model, Phase 1 sprint plan, reference code, operations and roadmap) is in the DQ Framework Blueprint.

The BRD defines what to monitor. It deliberately leaves how to a later part (Reusable Monitoring Architecture). Everything on this page is therefore (suggestion): a way to build what the BRD describes, using the same config-driven pattern the feature store pipeline already uses.

Code on this page is a sketch

The examples show the shape of the solution. Check the Great Expectations and Snowflake syntax against the versions your team actually installs before running anything.

docs.title: The core idea: the spreadsheet is the config
docs.text:
The requirements spreadsheet is already a configuration table: a variable, a check type, a threshold, and an alert flag. Store that as a Snowflake table and write one generic runner that reads it. Then adding a check, or extending monitoring to Risk Monitoring or Clover Capital, means inserting rows, not writing code. That directly meets the BRD's requirement of "no separate build for each".

The feature store already works this way: Transaction Array Definitions and Feature Definitions are config tables that drive generic code.

flowchart LR
    XL["BRD spreadsheet<br/>(business-owned)"] -->|"load / sync"| CFG[("DQ_CHECK_DEFINITIONS")]:::cfg
    CFG --> RUN["Generic check runner<br/>(hourly)"]:::step
    SRC[("Source tables<br/>(Snowflake Path)")]:::src --> RUN
    BM[("Benchmark tables")]:::src -.-> RUN
    RUN --> RES[("DQ_RESULTS<br/>one row per check per run")]:::out
    RES --> ALR["Alert job (hourly)<br/>FAIL + alert flag → email"]:::alert
    RES --> RPT["Weekly report<br/>(dashboard / email)"]:::out

    classDef cfg   fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#5e4e8a,color:#fff;
    classDef src   fill:#127EA6,stroke:#1877A3,color:#fff;
    classDef step  fill:#f2d492,stroke:#c99a2e,color:#3a2e05;
    classDef out   fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;
    classDef alert fill:#e08a7b,stroke:#a8503f,color:#2b0c08;

docs.title: Config table: DQ_CHECK_DEFINITIONS
docs.text:
One row per variable × check, a direct translation of the spreadsheet:

create table DQ_CHECK_DEFINITIONS (
    check_id        number autoincrement,
    domain          varchar,   -- 'UW', 'RM', 'CLOVER'          (reuse across business areas)
    monitor_type    varchar,   -- 'INPUT' or 'FEATURE_SCORE'
    source_table    varchar,   -- the BRD's "Snowflake Path": DATABASE.SCHEMA.TABLE to check
    benchmark_table varchar,   -- "Snowflake Path: Benchmark" (feature/score checks only)
    timestamp_col   varchar,   -- column used to select each run's window, e.g. the last hour
    variable        varchar,   -- e.g. 'AVG_TICKET'
    check_type      varchar,   -- 'MISSING_VALUES', 'ACCEPTABLE_RANGE', 'CSI', ...
    params          variant,   -- e.g. {"max_pct": 0.30} or {"min": 0, "max": 10000}
    alert_enabled   boolean,   -- the "Alerts Sent?" column
    severity        varchar,   -- (suggestion) 'HIGH' for the "sensitive fields" the BRD mentions
    active          boolean
);

Where the Snowflake Path goes

The BRD's Snowflake Path values become source_table (and benchmark_table for feature/score checks), written as DATABASE.SCHEMA.TABLE. The runner puts that name after FROM in every check. See What "Snowflake Path" means.

The Avg Ticket row of the spreadsheet becomes three config rows:

variable check_type params alert_enabled AVG_TICKET MISSING_VALUES {"max_pct": 0.30} true AVG_TICKET FIELD_POPULATION {"min_pct": 0.70, "placeholders": [-999]} false AVG_TICKET ACCEPTABLE_RANGE {"min": 0, "max": 10000, "exclusive": true} false

docs.title: Results table: DQ_RESULTS
docs.text:
Every run writes one row per check. The weekly report and the alerts both read from this table:

create table DQ_RESULTS (
    run_ts        timestamp_ntz,
    check_id      number,
    window_start  timestamp_ntz,
    window_end    timestamp_ntz,
    row_count     number,          -- how many records were checked (also catches "no data")
    metric_value  float,           -- e.g. 0.33 for 33% missing, 0.228 for a PSI
    result        varchar,         -- 'PASS' / 'FAIL'
    alerted       boolean
);

docs.title: Option A: Great Expectations (GX Core)
docs.text: GX is an open-source Python library. You declare "expectations" about your data (for example, "this column is not null in at least 70% of rows"), run them against a dataset, and get PASS/FAIL results plus human-readable HTML reports ("Data Docs"). It can run its checks as SQL directly in Snowflake.

docs.title: Mapping BRD check types to GX expectations
docs.text: BRD check type GX expectation (GX 1.x class name) Notes Missing Values ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeNull(mostly=0.70) mostly is the share that must pass: "> 30% missing fails" means mostly=0.70. Field Population ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeNull + ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeInSet(placeholders) Two expectations together = "populated with a real value". Acceptable Range ExpectColumnValuesToBeBetween(min_value, max_value, strict_min, strict_max) strict_* handles the ≤ / < question. Accepted Values ExpectColumnValuesToBeInSet(value_set) Expected Format ExpectColumnValuesToMatchRegex(regex) Dates can also be checked by regex. Duplicate Values ExpectColumnValuesToBeUnique / ExpectCompoundColumnsToBeUnique Value Length ExpectColumnValueLengthsToEqual(8) / ...ToBeBetween Value Type ExpectColumnValuesToBeOfType / ...InTypeList Placeholder Value ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeInSet([-999, 'N/A', ...], mostly=…) CSI / PSI No built-in PSI. Write a custom expectation, or compute it in SQL (below) and check the result. GX has a KL-divergence expectation, but KL isn't the same as PSI. Volume / Freshness ExpectTableRowCountToBeBetween; freshness via max timestamp Covers the "availability" gap.

docs.title: Sketch: building a GX suite from the config table
docs.text:
import great_expectations as gx

context = gx.get_context()
ds = context.data_sources.add_snowflake(name="uw", connection_string=SNOWFLAKE_URL)
asset = ds.add_table_asset(name="uw_inputs", table_name="UW_INPUTS_LAST_HOUR")
batch = asset.add_batch_definition_whole_table("last_hour")

# one translator per BRD check type: config row → GX expectation
BUILDERS = {
    "MISSING_VALUES":   lambda v, p: gx.expectations.ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeNull(
                            column=v, mostly=1 - p["max_pct"]),
    "ACCEPTABLE_RANGE": lambda v, p: gx.expectations.ExpectColumnValuesToBeBetween(
                            column=v, min_value=p["min"], max_value=p["max"],
                            strict_min=p.get("exclusive", False), strict_max=p.get("exclusive", False)),
    "ACCEPTED_VALUES":  lambda v, p: gx.expectations.ExpectColumnValuesToBeInSet(
                            column=v, value_set=p["values"]),
    "VALUE_LENGTH":     lambda v, p: gx.expectations.ExpectColumnValueLengthsToEqual(
                            column=v, value=p["length"]),
    "PLACEHOLDER":      lambda v, p: gx.expectations.ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeInSet(
                            column=v, value_set=p["placeholders"], mostly=1 - p["max_pct"]),
}

suite = context.suites.add(gx.ExpectationSuite(name="uw_input_monitoring"))
for row in load_config(domain="UW", monitor_type="INPUT"):       # SELECT from DQ_CHECK_DEFINITIONS
    suite.add_expectation(BUILDERS[row.check_type](row.variable, row.params))

result = context.validation_definitions.add(
    gx.ValidationDefinition(name="uw_inputs_hourly", data=batch, suite=suite)
).run()

write_results_to_snowflake(result)                                # → DQ_RESULTS, PASS/FAIL per check

docs.title: Option B: Snowflake-native
docs.text:
All the data already lives in Snowflake, so the checks can also run inside Snowflake with no separate Python service.

Plain SQL and Tasks. Each check type is one SQL template; a scheduled Task runs them hourly:

-- Missing Values for one variable over the last hour
-- (Snowflake allows reusing the alias "metric" later in the same SELECT)
select 'AVG_TICKET'                                    as variable,
       'MISSING_VALUES'                                as check_type,
       count(*)                                        as row_count,
       count_if(avg_ticket is null) / nullif(count(*), 0) as metric,
       iff(metric > 0.30, 'FAIL', 'PASS')              as result
from <uw_inputs_table>
where event_ts >= dateadd(hour, -1, current_timestamp());

-- PSI for a score: benchmark vs active, with bins taken from the benchmark (sketch)
with bins as (select bin_id, lo, hi, benchmark_share from FICO_BENCHMARK_BINS),
active as (
    select b.bin_id, count(*) / sum(count(*)) over () as active_share
    from <active_scores> s join bins b on s.fico >= b.lo and s.fico < b.hi
    group by b.bin_id
)
select sum((a.active_share - b.benchmark_share)
           * ln(a.active_share / b.benchmark_share)) as psi
from bins b join active a using (bin_id);
-- note: a bin with zero active records makes ln() fail; floor shares at a small epsilon

Data Metric Functions (DMFs). Snowflake has built-in data-quality metrics that can be attached to a table and run on a schedule, for example SNOWFLAKE.CORE.NULL_COUNT, DUPLICATE_COUNT, ROW_COUNT and FRESHNESS. You can also write your own. Results go to a system view. DMFs require Enterprise edition or higher; check what your account supports.

alter table <uw_inputs_table> set DATA_METRIC_SCHEDULE = '60 MINUTE';
alter table <uw_inputs_table> add data metric function SNOWFLAKE.CORE.NULL_COUNT on (avg_ticket);

Alerts. A Snowflake ALERT can check DQ_RESULTS every hour and send email through a notification integration:

create or replace alert DQ_HOURLY_ALERT
  warehouse = <warehouse>
  schedule  = '60 MINUTE'
  if (exists (
        select 1 from DQ_RESULTS r join DQ_CHECK_DEFINITIONS d using (check_id)
        where r.result = 'FAIL' and d.alert_enabled
          and r.run_ts > dateadd(hour, -1, current_timestamp())))
  then call SYSTEM$SEND_EMAIL('<email_integration>', '<team@company.com>',
                              'DQ check failures', 'See DQ_RESULTS for the last hour.');

docs.title: Choosing between them
docs.text:
Great Expectations Snowflake-native (SQL / DMFs / Alerts) Check library Large set of ready-made expectations Write SQL templates (DMFs cover the basics) Where it runs Python job (GitLab CI, Airflow, Lambda, ...) that sends SQL to Snowflake Entirely in Snowflake Reports Data Docs (HTML) out of the box Build a dashboard on DQ_RESULTS PSI / CSI Custom expectation or SQL SQL Extra infrastructure A Python runtime and a scheduler None beyond Snowflake Fit with the team today New dependency Matches the Snowflake-native feature store

(suggestion) Neither option is clearly better. A practical split: use GX if the team wants a standard framework, with its check library and Data Docs, that is reusable across UW, RM and Clover Capital, which is what the BRD hints at. Use Snowflake-native if you want the fewest moving parts. In both cases, keep the config table and results table above. They are what make the platform reusable, whichever engine runs the checks.

docs.title: One hourly run, end to end
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant SCH as Scheduler (hourly)
    participant RUN as Check runner
    participant CFG as DQ_CHECK_DEFINITIONS
    participant SRC as Source table (Snowflake Path)
    participant RES as DQ_RESULTS
    participant AL as Alert job
    participant TEAM as On-call / data owner
    SCH->>RUN: trigger
    RUN->>CFG: load active checks (domain, monitor type)
    loop each variable × check
        RUN->>SRC: run check SQL over the last window
        SRC-->>RUN: metric + row count
        RUN->>RES: write PASS / FAIL
    end
    AL->>RES: any FAIL with alert_enabled in this run?
    alt yes
        AL->>TEAM: email (variable, check, metric, threshold)
    end
    Note over RES: weekly report reads all of DQ_RESULTS

docs.title: A phased plan
docs.text:
1. Settle the definitions. Resolve the questions in Review notes. In particular, define each check type precisely, and decide whether monitoring can block decisions or only runs after the fact.
  2. Build the config and results tables and load the spreadsheet into them.
  3. Start with UW input monitoring on a few high-value sources (applications, TMX, bureau). Add volume and freshness checks, which catch vendor outages, the most damaging failure.
  4. Run it quietly for a few weeks, writing results with alerts turned off. Use real FAIL rates to tune thresholds, so the first alerts aren't noise.
  5. Turn on alerts for the fields marked sensitive.
  6. Add feature & score monitoring once benchmark periods are agreed.
  7. Extend to RM and Clover Capital by adding config rows with a new domain.

docs.title: Input monitoring (BRD Part 1)
docs.text: Input monitoring checks the raw data coming in: application fields and responses from LexisNexis, TMX and the bureau. The question for every field is: is this data present and valid?

docs.title: Ground rules from the BRD
docs.text:
• Input monitoring covers raw data only.
  • It checks the quality of the input itself. There is no comparison between a benchmark/base population and the active population. That comparison belongs to feature & score monitoring.
  • Every check on every variable produces PASS or FAIL against its configured criteria.
  • The reporting frequency is decided (see below). The alert channel (email) and alert frequency are still under discussion. The draft suggests a set of sensitive or important fields whose alerts could be sent at the end of the day or on another schedule. (That sentence is cut off in the screenshot.)

docs.title: Required parameters
docs.text:
These are set once for the monitoring job:

Parameter Value Meaning Snowflake Path (link) Which data to check: the Snowflake table or view the checks run against. Explained below. Scheduled Yes The checks run on a schedule, not on demand. Reporting Freq (Scheduled = Y) Weekly A summary report is produced every week. Alert Freq Hourly Failures are evaluated, and alerts sent, every hour.

docs.title: What "Snowflake Path" means
docs.text:
In short

Snowflake Path is the address of the data the checks run against: one table or view in Snowflake, written as its full three-part name DATABASE.SCHEMA.TABLE. It answers the question "which data are we checking?". Despite the word "path", it is not a folder or a file location.

The three parts. Snowflake organises data as database → schema → table, and a table's full name joins all three with dots. A real example from the feature store:

Part Example Think of it as Database GBS_PROD_CRANALYTICS the top-level container Schema CRAGGR a group of related tables inside it Table CR_AGG_RMI_INFO the actual data Path GBS_PROD_CRANALYTICS.CRAGGR.CR_AGG_RMI_INFO all three joined

What the BRD actually says. In the draft, every Snowflake Path value is just the word "Link": a hyperlink placeholder, most likely meant to open the table in Snowflake's web UI (inferred). No real table has been named yet. Until it is, the checks have nothing to run against.

How many paths, and what they should point to:

BRD tab Parameter Should point to Input Monitoring Snowflake Path The raw input data. Per the kickoff, the A1 dataset on Day 1, then one table per source (LexisNexis, GNF, application, ...) on Day 2 (inferred). For UW, the 1:1 named the API request table (details). Feature_Scores Snowflake Path: Benchmark The reference population: features and scores from a fixed past period. Feature_Scores Snowflake Path: Active Recent production features and scores, refreshed daily.

For features and scores, both paths will most likely point into the Snowflake historical table loaded from the model service's JSON output (step 5c). In that case Benchmark and Active could be the same table filtered to different date ranges (inferred).

What the path alone doesn't tell you. To run hourly checks, each path also needs:

  • A timestamp column, to select "the last hour" of records.
  • The environment: sandbox (e.g. AP_SBX_...) or production. These are different databases.
  • Read access for whatever role runs the checks.

In SQL, the path is simply what goes after FROM:

select count(*)                                   as row_count,
       count_if(avg_ticket is null) / count(*)    as pct_missing
from   <DATABASE>.<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>                -- ← the Snowflake Path
where  <event_ts> >= dateadd(hour, -1, current_timestamp());

In the implementation guide it is stored in the source_table and benchmark_table columns of the config table.

docs.title: The check types
docs.text:
The spreadsheet offers nine check types in a dropdown. The BRD does not define them, so the definitions below are (inferred). Each one should be confirmed and written into the BRD itself (see Review notes).

Check type What it asks Typical criteria Example Missing Values What share of records have this field null? FAIL if missing > X% Avg Ticket null in > 30% of records Field Population What share of records have a real, usable value (not null, not blank, not a placeholder)? FAIL if populated < X% Enquiry Date usable in < 70% of records Acceptable Range Are numeric or date values inside the allowed bounds? FAIL if outside [min, max] Avg Ticket must be > $0 and < $10,000 Accepted Values Is the value one of an allowed list? FAIL if not in the set Account status in {01, 02, 03, 13} Expected Format Does the value match a pattern? FAIL if it doesn't match the regex/format Date is YYYY-MM-DD; ID is all digits Duplicate Values Is a value that should be unique repeated? FAIL if duplicates > X The same application ID appears twice in an hour Value Length Is the string length as expected? FAIL if length ≠ N (or outside range) Merchant ID must be N characters Value Type Is the data type correct? FAIL if the type is wrong Numeric field arriving as text Placeholder Value Is the field filled with a "fake" default? FAIL if placeholder share > X% -999, 9999, N/A, UNKNOWN, 1900-01-01

Placeholders hide missing data

A field filled with -999 is not null, so a Missing Values check passes it. The data is still effectively missing. That is why Field Population and Placeholder Value exist alongside Missing Values. The feature store uses -999 this way, so any monitoring of its outputs must count -999 as "not populated".

docs.title: The variable matrix (as drafted)
docs.text:
The spreadsheet is a grid: one row per variable, three columns per check type:

  • Check? (Yes/No): whether this check applies to the variable.
  • Alert criteria: the threshold that makes it FAIL.
  • Alerts Sent? (Yes/No): whether a FAIL sends an alert, or only shows up in the report (inferred).

What the screenshot shows so far (the … rows are still placeholders in the draft):

Variable Missing Values Criteria Alert? Field Population Criteria Alert? Acceptable Range Criteria Alert? Merch ID Yes > 30% No No Yes (<=0 >=15) Yes Enquiry Date Yes > 30% No Yes < 70% Yes No (<=2025 >=2026) Avg Ticket Yes > 30% Yes Yes < 70% No Yes (<=$0 >=$10000) No … (4 rows) some No mixed < 80% No No Client ID Yes > 30% No Yes < 80% No No

docs.title: How to read a row
docs.text:
Take Avg Ticket:

  • Missing Values: Yes, > 30%, alert Yes. If more than 30% of records in the window have no Avg Ticket, the check FAILs and an alert goes out.
  • Field Population: Yes, < 70%, alert No. If fewer than 70% have a real value, it FAILs, but this only shows up in the weekly report.
  • Acceptable Range: Yes, (<=$0 >=$10000), alert No. Read as: a value ≤ $0 or ≥ $10,000 is out of range. That reading is (inferred): the notation lists the failing boundaries.

Some criteria in the draft are ambiguous. For example, (<=0 >=15) on Merch ID, a range check on an ID field. Those are covered in Review notes.

docs.title: Worked example: one hour of application data
docs.text:
Illustrative. In one hour, 200 applications arrive. The checks configured for Avg Ticket and Enquiry Date run against those 200 records:

Variable Check Measured Criteria Result Alert? Avg Ticket Missing Values 66 null of 200 = 33% > 30% FAIL Yes → email Avg Ticket Field Population 120 usable of 200 = 60% (66 null + 14 -999) < 70% FAIL No (report only) Avg Ticket Acceptable Range 3 values ≥ $10,000 ≤$0 or ≥$10,000 FAIL (if any one value counts) No Enquiry Date Missing Values 10 null of 200 = 5% > 30% PASS (n/a) Enquiry Date Field Population 190 usable of 200 = 95% < 70% PASS (n/a)

Two things this example shows:

  • Only one email goes out this hour (Avg Ticket, Missing Values), even though there are three FAILs. The other two wait for the weekly report.
  • The Acceptable Range result depends on a rule the BRD hasn't set yet: does one bad value make the check FAIL, or does it take more than some percentage? With 3 out of 200 (1.5%), the answer flips from FAIL to PASS depending on that rule.

docs.title: What happens on each run
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    T["Hourly trigger"] --> L["Load the last window of input data<br/>(Snowflake Path)"]
    L --> C["For each variable × check type<br/>where Check? = Yes"]
    C --> M["Compute the metric<br/>(e.g. % missing)"]
    M --> D{"Breaches the<br/>alert criteria?"}
    D -- "No" --> P["PASS"]:::ok
    D -- "Yes" --> F["FAIL"]:::bad
    P --> R[("Store result")]
    F --> R
    F --> A{"Alerts Sent? = Yes"}
    A -- "Yes" --> E["Send alert email"]:::bad
    A -- "No" --> R
    R --> W["Weekly report<br/>(all results)"]

    classDef ok  fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;
    classDef bad fill:#e08a7b,stroke:#a8503f,color:#2b0c08;

docs.title: Coverage gap: "availability" isn't checked yet
docs.text:
Objective BO-01 asks for availability and validity. Every check type above is about validity: whether the values are good. None is about availability: whether the data arrived at all. If a TMX outage means zero TMX responses arrive in an hour, there is nothing to measure "% missing" against, and every check can quietly pass. (suggestion) Add two more check types:

  • Volume: row count in the window compared with what's expected. For example, FAIL if TMX responses drop below 50% of the same hour last week.
