  • Freshness: time since the newest record. For example, FAIL if no bureau data has arrived for 2 hours.

Next: Feature & score monitoring.

docs.title: Review notes & open questions
docs.text: The BRD is a Version 1.0 draft (it is still marked @TEMPLATE, and several matrix rows are placeholders). Below are gaps and ambiguities worth raising with its author, roughly in order of importance. Each one includes a suggested resolution, marked (suggestion).

docs.title: 1. Blocking check or after-the-fact monitoring?
docs.text:
BO-01 says data should be checked "for availability and validity before being consumed by models". But the parameters (a Snowflake path, hourly alert frequency, weekly reports) describe batch monitoring of stored data. In Underwriting, Snowflake is never on the real-time path. Data reaches Snowflake only after the decision, through the transaction log (steps 5a–5c).

So there are two very different designs:

Design How it works Implication Blocking check Checks run inside the decision flow (e.g. in the normalizer Lambda) and can stop or flag a decision Real protection, but adds latency and new ways for live decisions to fail After-the-fact monitoring Checks run hourly on data already logged to Snowflake No risk to live decisions; issues are caught within the hour, not prevented

(suggestion) Make the BRD say which one it means. The parameters fit after-the-fact monitoring. If so, reword BO-01 to something like "detected within one hour of arrival" rather than "before being consumed by models".

docs.title: 2. Define every check type precisely
docs.text:
The check types are listed in a dropdown but never defined. Two of them overlap as drafted:

  • Missing Values > 30% and Field Population < 70% describe the same condition if "populated" just means "not null": 30% missing is 70% populated.

(suggestion) Add a definitions table to the BRD. For example: Missing Values = null only; Field Population = not null and not blank and not a placeholder. Then the two checks differ, and the placeholder list for each field (e.g. -999) becomes part of its configuration.

docs.title: 3. Tighten the alert criteria
docs.text:
• The range notation is ambiguous. Does (<=$0 >=$10000) describe the failing values or the allowed ones, and are the bounds inclusive? The draft relies on the reader guessing.
  • Some ranges look misplaced. (<=0 >=15) on Merch ID is a numeric range on an identifier. It is probably meant to be a length check (Value Length) instead.
  • Hard-coded years will go stale. (<=2025 >=2026) on Enquiry Date stops making sense once the calendar moves on. (suggestion) Use relative rules such as "not in the future and not older than N days".
  • One bad value or a percentage? For range, format and accepted-value checks, say whether a single violating record makes the check FAIL, or only more than X% of records (GX calls this mostly).
  • Criteria with the check switched off. Enquiry Date's Acceptable Range says No but still lists criteria. Clarify whether it is meant to be on.

docs.title: 4. Clarify what the FSI/CSI criteria measure
docs.text:
The criteria Dec > 10% and Inc > 5% are directional percentages. But CSI and PSI are never negative and go up whichever way the data moves (see the worked examples). (suggestion) Decide which of these is meant:

  • CSI/PSI index thresholds, for example FAIL if CSI > 0.10, warn above 0.25; or
  • Directional change in a summary statistic, for example FAIL if the mean FICO falls by more than 10% compared with the benchmark.

Also define the binning (how many bins, and are the edges set from the benchmark?), and how the benchmark date range is chosen and refreshed.

docs.title: 5. Add availability checks
docs.text: BO-01 asks for availability, but every check type measures validity. A vendor outage that sends zero records can pass every percentage-based check. (suggestion) Add Volume (row count against expected) and Freshness (time since the last record) check types. See Input monitoring.

docs.title: 6. Small windows make noisy percentages
docs.text: Alerts run hourly. In a quiet hour with 12 applications, 4 missing values is already 33%, a FAIL. (suggestion) Set a minimum row count below which a check reports "insufficient data" rather than PASS/FAIL. Or evaluate over a rolling window, for example the last 24 hours, re-checked every hour.

docs.title: 7. Alerting details still open
docs.text:
The BRD itself flags these as undecided:

  • Channel: email is proposed. Is there also Teams/Slack, or a ticket?
  • Recipients and ownership: who receives an alert for each data source, and who fixes it?
  • Repeat suppression: a problem that lasts 10 hours would send 10 identical emails. (suggestion) Send an alert on the first FAIL and a "resolved" note on the first PASS afterwards.
  • Sensitive fields: the draft mentions a set of important fields with their own alert timing. Name them, perhaps as a severity in the config.
  • PASS/FAIL only: consider adding a WARN level between them, so thresholds can be tuned without paging anyone.

docs.title: 8. Scope and data locations
docs.text:
• Snowflake paths (what they are) are still placeholder links. For each data source (applications, LN, TMX, Bureau), give the exact DATABASE.SCHEMA.TABLE in each environment, the timestamp column for windowing, and the role that can read it. For feature/score monitoring, say whether Benchmark and Active are two tables or one table with two date ranges.
  • "Alerts Sent? = No": confirm this means "shown in the weekly report only", not "check disabled".
  • Clover Capital is in scope for reuse, but none of its data sources are described yet.
  • Matrix rows marked … need their variable names filled in before the matrix can be implemented.

docs.title: Summary for the author
docs.text: # Topic Ask 1 Blocking vs after-the-fact State which one; align BO-01 wording with the hourly Snowflake design. 2 Check definitions Define each check type; separate Missing Values from Field Population. 3 Alert criteria Fix notation, relative dates, and the "one bad value vs %" rule. 4 FSI/CSI criteria Index thresholds or directional change? Define bins and benchmark. 5 Availability Add Volume and Freshness checks. 6 Noisy windows Minimum row count or rolling window. 7 Alerting Channel, owners, repeat suppression, sensitive fields, WARN level. 8 Scope Real Snowflake paths, meaning of "No", Clover Capital sources.

docs.title: Lift and shift to AWS
docs.text:
This section is the plan for moving the framework from the laptop and LocalStack into a real AWS account. Two things keep the move small:

  • There is nothing to rewrite. The code, the configuration and the CloudFormation template that run in LocalStack today are the ones that go to AWS. One template parameter changes: Target=localstack becomes Target=aws.
  • Most of the work is asking for access. The steps are networking, a Snowflake service user, and permission to deploy. Ask for these early, because they take days; the deployment itself takes minutes.
Page This page What changes, what gets created, and what to ask for Step by step The deployment, in order, with commands and checks Hosting the report Keeping the Streamlit report running for the team, and linking it from the alerts After go-live Changing rules and code, watching it, costs, rollback, troubleshooting

docs.title: What changes between LocalStack and AWS
docs.text: LocalStack (today) AWS Code src/dqf/ Same Configuration config/dq_config.yaml, sample table Same file; its sources point at the real tables Template infra/cloudformation.yaml, Target=localstack Same file, Target=aws Lambda package Mounted folder (LocalStack has no ECR) Container image in ECR, built from the Dockerfile (the dependencies are ~490 MB, over the 250 MB zip limit) Snowflake login Secrets Manager in LocalStack, filled from .env Secrets Manager in AWS, created once by hand Snowflake user DQF_SVC on the sandbox account A service user on the production account Network Laptop → internet → Snowflake Lambda → (VPC, NAT or PrivateLink) → Snowflake Alerts SNS (read from a queue) and SMTP to Gmail SNS → email subscribers. No SMTP password anywhere Schedules Off; invoked by hand EventBridge: hourly at :20, daily at 01:30 UTC Error alarm Not created CloudWatch alarm on Lambda errors → the same SNS topic GX report LocalStack S3 The stack's private S3 bucket, data_docs/ Streamlit report make app on the laptop Streamlit in Snowflake, not AWS (Hosting the report); the alerts link to it

docs.title: What gets created
docs.text:
infra/deploy.sh creates or uses these. If your team uses Terraform or deploys through the console instead of CloudFormation, this list is what to create; the settings are in the template.

flowchart LR
    subgraph ACC["Your AWS account (one region, ideally the Snowflake account's region)"]
        ECR[("<b>ECR</b><br/>dqf image")]:::cfg -.-> L
        EB1["<b>EventBridge rule</b><br/>hourly :20"]:::aws --> L["<b>Lambda</b> dqf-run<br/>2 GB, 10 min"]:::aws
        EB2["<b>EventBridge rule</b><br/>daily 01:30"]:::aws --> L
        ROLE["<b>IAM role</b><br/>least privilege"]:::cfg -.-> L
        S3[("<b>S3 bucket</b><br/>dq_config.yaml, GX report<br/>private, versioned")]:::cfg <--> L
        SM[("<b>Secrets Manager</b><br/>Snowflake login<br/>(you create it)")]:::cfg -.-> L
        L --> SNS["<b>SNS topic</b><br/>dqf-alerts"]:::alert --> MAIL["email subscribers"]:::alert
        CW["<b>CloudWatch alarm</b><br/>Lambda errors"]:::alert --> SNS
    end
    L == "HTTPS 443" ==> SF[("<b>Snowflake</b>")]:::snow

    classDef aws fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3e10,color:#fff;
    classDef cfg fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#57498a,color:#fff;
    classDef alert fill:#a8503f,stroke:#7a3527,color:#fff;
    classDef snow fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;
Resource Name Notes ECR repository dqf Created by deploy.sh if missing; scan on push Lambda function <stack>-run Container image, x86_64, 2048 MB, 600 s timeout IAM role generated Read the one secret; read the bucket; write only data_docs/; publish only to the topic; logs; VPC access if in a VPC. Optional permissions boundary and KMS key S3 bucket <stack>-config-<account>-<region> The configuration and the GX report. Public access blocked, versioned SNS topic <stack>-alerts Plus an email subscription if ALERT_EMAIL is set EventBridge rules hourly, daily Can be deployed off (SCHEDULES=DISABLED) CloudWatch alarm on the Lambda's Errors A run that crashes (not a check that fails) alerts the same topic Secrets Manager secret dqf/snowflake Created by you, once, not by the template

docs.title: What to ask for, and from whom
docs.text:
Send these requests first. Everything else depends on them.

# Request Usually from Why 1 An AWS account / environment and a region (preferably the Snowflake account's region) Cloud platform team Where it runs 2 Permission to deploy CloudFormation with IAM role creation, ECR, Lambda, S3, SNS, EventBridge, CloudWatch, and to create one secret. Or: a pipeline that does it Cloud platform team deploy.sh needs these. Ask whether a permissions boundary is required on new roles and whether tags are mandatory 3 Private subnets with outbound HTTPS to Snowflake (NAT, a proxy, or Snowflake PrivateLink), plus a security group allowing outbound 443 Network team The Lambda must reach Snowflake. Give them the output of select system$allowlist(); from Snowflake: the exact hosts and ports 4 Access from those subnets to Secrets Manager, S3 and SNS (through the NAT, or VPC endpoints) Network team A Lambda in a VPC has no AWS API access by default 5 A Snowflake service user (key pair), a role with SELECT on the monitored tables, a warehouse, and a schema for the results table Snowflake admins Run sql/01_setup.sql with production names. If the account uses network policies, allow the NAT's egress IPs for this user 6 The real table names for the A1 record (and the full response table), and for each feature-store view Data owners For the sources in dq_config.yaml 7 An email address for alerts (a distribution list is better than a person) Your team The SNS subscription. Some company mail filters hold AWS confirmation emails: tell IT to expect one

Ask for the network first

Reaching Snowflake from inside a VPC (item 3) is the step most likely to be slow. The AWS2SF Lambda already reaches Snowflake from AWS, so ask to reuse its subnets and security group. That is usually the fastest route.

docs.title: Ready-to-go checklist
docs.text:
Before you run the deployment, you should have:

  • [ ] AWS CLI logged in to the target account and region (aws sts get-caller-identity)
  • [ ] Docker running on the machine that builds the image (or a CI pipeline that builds it)
  • [ ] The production Snowflake user, role, warehouse and results schema, and the private key file
  • [ ] SELECT granted on every table in the configuration
  • [ ] Subnet IDs and a security group ID with a route to Snowflake and to Secrets Manager, S3, SNS
  • [ ] dq_config.yaml updated to the real tables, and make validate passing
  • [ ] An alert email address
  • [ ] If required: the permissions boundary ARN, the KMS key ARN, the mandatory tags

Then follow Step by step.

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
The order matters: each step can be checked before the next one starts. Run all commands from dq-framework/.

flowchart LR
    A["1. Snowflake<br/>user, role, grants"]:::s --> B["2. Network<br/>route to Snowflake"]:::s
    B --> C["3. Secret<br/>the login"]:::s
    C --> D["4. Configuration<br/>real tables"]:::s
    D --> E["5. Deploy<br/>schedules off"]:::d
    E --> F["6. Verify<br/>check, run, alert"]:::d
    F --> G["7. Go live<br/>schedules on"]:::g

    classDef s fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#57498a,color:#fff;
    classDef d fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3e10,color:#fff;
    classDef g fill:#54802D,stroke:#3a5a1e,color:#fff;

docs.title: 1. Snowflake
docs.text:
On the production Snowflake account, with an admin:

  1. Make a new key pair for production. Don't reuse the sandbox key.

    mkdir -p keys/prod && cd keys/prod && openssl genrsa 2048 | openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -nocrypt -out dqf_prod.p8 \
  && openssl rsa -in dqf_prod.p8 -pubout -out dqf_prod.pub && cd ../..

  2. Run sql/01_setup.sql with the production names (database, schema, warehouse, role, user) and the new public key. Leave out the line that grants the role to your own user if that is not allowed.

  3. Grant read access on each monitored table:

    grant usage on database <DB> to role DQF_ROLE;
grant usage on schema <DB>.<SCHEMA> to role DQF_ROLE;
grant select on table <DB>.<SCHEMA>.<TABLE> to role DQF_ROLE;     -- each table / view in the configuration

  4. Note the account identifier: select current_organization_name() || '-' || current_account_name();.

  5. Get the hosts the network team must allow: select system$allowlist();.

Check: from your laptop, put the production values in a copy of .env, then run make check.

docs.title: 2. Network
docs.text:
The Lambda runs in private subnets and needs outbound HTTPS (443) to:

Destination Through Snowflake (the hosts from system$allowlist(), including the OCSP host) NAT gateway or proxy; or Snowflake PrivateLink if the account uses it Secrets Manager, S3, SNS NAT, or VPC endpoints: Secrets Manager (interface), S3 (gateway), SNS (interface)

Lambda logs go to CloudWatch without a VPC route, so no endpoint is needed for them.

If the Snowflake account uses PrivateLink, use its PrivateLink account identifier in the secret (the …privatelink… form your Snowflake admin gives you).

Without a VPC

If the account allows Lambdas outside a VPC and Snowflake accepts connections from the internet, leave SUBNET_IDS empty. The Lambda then reaches everything directly, and this step is skipped. Many company accounts do not allow this.

Check: step 6's check action is the real test.

docs.title: 3. The secret
docs.text:
Write the login to a temporary file. The private key goes in as one line, with \n for line breaks:

python3 - <<'EOF' > secret.json
import json
print(json.dumps({
    "account": "ORGNAME-ACCOUNTNAME", "user": "DQF_SVC", "role": "DQF_ROLE", "warehouse": "DQF_WH",
    "database": "DQF_DB", "schema": "DQF", "auth": "keypair",
    "private_key": open("keys/prod/dqf_prod.p8").read()}))
EOF
aws secretsmanager create-secret --name dqf/snowflake --secret-string file://secret.json \
    [--kms-key-id <your KMS key ARN>]
rm secret.json

Note the secret's ARN from the output. If you used your own KMS key, pass its ARN to the deployment as SECRET_KMS_KEY_ARN.

Check: aws secretsmanager describe-secret --secret-id dqf/snowflake shows the secret's details without the value.

docs.title: 4. The configuration
docs.text:
Point the sources in config/dq_config.yaml at the real tables, adjust the checks, limits and business rules, then:

make validate    # every problem, with where it is
.venv/bin/dqf run hourly --no-alerts     # optional, from the laptop with the production .env

The copy in the image is only a fallback. The Lambda reads the copy in S3, which deploy.sh uploads. To deploy an Excel workbook instead, set CONFIG_FILE=config/dq_config.xlsx.

docs.title: 5. Deploy, with schedules off
docs.text:
STACK=dqf \
SNOWFLAKE_SECRET_ARN=arn:aws:secretsmanager:<region>:<account>:secret:dqf/snowflake-AbCdEf \
RESULT_TABLE=DQF_DB.DQF.DQ_RESULT \
ALERT_EMAIL=dq-alerts@yourcompany.com \
SUBNET_IDS=subnet-aaa,subnet-bbb \
SECURITY_GROUP_IDS=sg-ccc \
SCHEDULES=DISABLED \
infra/deploy.sh

Optional settings, if your account needs them:

Variable When PERMISSIONS_BOUNDARY_ARN New IAM roles must carry a boundary policy SECRET_KMS_KEY_ARN The secret uses your own KMS key TAGS="CostCenter=1234 Owner=risk-analytics" Tags are mandatory REPO=team/dqf A required ECR repository name SKIP_BUILD=1 IMAGE_URI=<uri> Your CI pipeline builds and pushes the image; the script only deploys AWS_REGION A region other than your CLI default REPORT_URL=<address> The Streamlit report's address, linked from every alert. See Hosting the report

The script:

  1. builds the image (linux/amd64) and pushes it to ECR;
  2. deploys infra/cloudformation.yaml with Target=aws;
  3. uploads dq_config.yaml to the stack's bucket;
  4. prints the test commands.

If your team deploys only through a pipeline, the pipeline needs to do the same three things: build the Dockerfile, deploy the template with these parameters, and copy dq_config.yaml to S3.

docs.title: 6. Verify
docs.text:
Run these in order. Each one tests one more part.

F=dqf-run
invoke() { aws lambda invoke --function-name $F --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out --payload "$1" /dev/stdout; }

# a) Login, network, secret, configuration. Runs no checks, writes nothing, sends nothing.
invoke '{"action": "check"}'

# b) A real run, stored in the results table, without alerts
invoke '{"schedule": "hourly", "send_alerts": false}'
invoke '{"schedule": "daily", "send_alerts": false}'

# c) The alert path: confirm the SNS subscription email first, then
invoke '{"action": "test_alert"}'
Step Good result If it fails a "ok": true, with the Snowflake account, user and role, and the configuration counts snowflake: FAILED … timeout: network (step 2). JWT token is invalid: the key (step 1). AccessDenied on the secret: the ARN or the KMS key. config: FAILED: S3 access or a problem in the configuration b Counts of checks; rows appear in the results table A check with ERROR: a missing SELECT grant or a wrong column c An email from AWS Notifications No email: the subscription is not confirmed, or a mail filter is holding it

The Lambda's log: aws logs tail /aws/lambda/dqf-run --since 15m.

docs.title: 7. Go live
docs.text:
SCHEDULES=ENABLED SKIP_BUILD=1 IMAGE_URI=<the image from step 5> \
STACK=dqf SNOWFLAKE_SECRET_ARN=... RESULT_TABLE=... ALERT_EMAIL=... SUBNET_IDS=... SECURITY_GROUP_IDS=... \
infra/deploy.sh

(The same command as step 5, plus SCHEDULES=ENABLED. It reuses the image instead of building a new one.)

Optional history. To give the reports and the alert logic a starting history, backfill from the laptop with the production .env: .venv/bin/dqf backfill hourly 24 and .venv/bin/dqf backfill daily 7. This sends no alerts.

From now on the Lambda runs at 20 past every hour and at 01:30 UTC every day.

docs.title: Making changes
docs.text:
Change What to do Redeploy code? A check, a limit, a new source, alert on/off Edit dq_config.yaml, make validate, then aws s3 cp config/dq_config.yaml s3://<bucket>/dq_config.yaml No. The next run reads it A new business rule Add it to the rules: section of dq_config.yaml and use it from a check; then the same as above No A custom check, for logic field conditions cannot express (rare) A developer adds a custom GX expectation to src/dqf/expectations.py, tests it, then infra/deploy.sh Yes Code Test (make test, LocalStack), then infra/deploy.sh Yes Alert recipients Add or remove SNS subscriptions (console or aws sns subscribe) No Schedule times HourlySchedule / DailySchedule template parameters Stack update only Rotate the Snowflake key alter user DQF_SVC set rsa_public_key_2 = '…', update the secret, check, then unset the old key No

The bucket is versioned: to undo a configuration change, restore the previous version of dq_config.yaml, or upload the previous version from Git.

Test a configuration change in LocalStack first (make local-deploy, make local-invoke). It runs the same code against the same Snowflake.

docs.title: Watching it
docs.text:
What Where Data problems The alert emails; the Streamlit report; the GX report in S3 (data_docs/site/index.html) The framework itself crashed The CloudWatch alarm emails the same topic (Lambda Errors ≥ 1 in an hour) A check could not run ERROR in the email and the results table, with the reason Each run's summary CloudWatch Logs /aws/lambda/dqf-run: one JSON line per run with the counts Duration and memory The REPORT line in the log. Raise MemorySize in the template if Max Memory Used nears 2048 MB

To read the GX report: aws s3 sync s3://<bucket>/data_docs/site ./site, then open site/index.html. To share it with the team without downloads, put the bucket behind CloudFront with company sign-in, or use the Streamlit report in Snowflake.

docs.title: Costs (rough)
docs.text: Item Estimate Lambda About 750 runs a month × ~30 s × 2 GB: under $1 a month S3, SNS, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch, EventBridge A few dollars a month; the secret is about $0.40 ECR Cents. Delete old images now and then Snowflake warehouse The main cost. An X-Small warehouse resumed 25 times a day for about a minute each: roughly 0.4 credits a day. It grows with the size of the tables and the number of sources. Share an existing warehouse if allowed

docs.title: Rolling back
docs.text: Problem Undo A bad configuration Restore the previous S3 version of dq_config.yaml (or upload the previous one from Git) A bad code release Re-run deploy.sh with SKIP_BUILD=1 IMAGE_URI=<previous image tag>. Every image is kept in ECR with its timestamp tag Alerts too noisy Set ALERT = No on the noisy checks; or disable the schedules (SCHEDULES=DISABLED) Remove it entirely aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name dqf. Empty the bucket first; the secret, the ECR repository and the Snowflake objects stay until removed by hand

docs.title: Troubleshooting in AWS
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix check times out on Snowflake No route from the subnets to Snowflake, or the OCSP host is blocked Network team: allow the system$allowlist() hosts; check the NAT or PrivateLink check times out on the secret or the configuration A Lambda in a VPC with no route to AWS APIs NAT, or VPC endpoints for Secrets Manager and S3 AccessDeniedException reading the secret Wrong ARN, or a custom KMS key Deploy with the right SNOWFLAKE_SECRET_ARN; set SECRET_KMS_KEY_ARN Incoming request with IP … is not allowed A Snowflake network policy Add the NAT's egress IPs to the policy for DQF_SVC Stack fails creating the role A permissions boundary is required, or IAM is not allowed PERMISSIONS_BOUNDARY_ARN; or ask the platform team for a deployment pipeline Lambda: Runtime.InvalidEntrypoint or exec format error The image was built for ARM Build with --platform linux/amd64 (deploy.sh does) Lambda times out Very large tables or many sources in one run Raise Timeout (max 900 s) or the warehouse size; add a ROW_FILTER; split sources across schedules No alert emails SNS subscription not confirmed, or held by a mail filter aws sns list-subscriptions-by-topic; confirm; ask IT to allow no-reply@sns.amazonaws.com Every check ERROR The role lost SELECT, or a table was renamed Re-grant; update dq_config.yaml

docs.title: Hosting the report
docs.text:
The Streamlit report is not part of the Lambda. The Lambda runs for about 30 seconds each hour and stops; a report has to keep running so people can open it at any time. The two share only the results table in Snowflake:

flowchart LR
    L["<b>Lambda</b> (AWS)<br/>runs ~30 s an hour"]:::aws -- "writes" --> T[("<b>DQ_RESULT</b><br/>Snowflake")]:::snow
    T -- "reads" --> R["<b>Streamlit report</b><br/>always on"]:::out
    L -- "alert email<br/>with a link" --> P["People"]:::alert
    P -- "click" --> R

    classDef aws fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3e10,color:#fff;
    classDef snow fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;
    classDef out fill:#54802D,stroke:#3a5a1e,color:#fff;
    classDef alert fill:#a8503f,stroke:#7a3527,color:#fff;

docs.title: Where to host it
docs.text:
Option Runs on Login and access Cost Verdict Streamlit in Snowflake Snowflake Company Snowflake sign-in; access by Snowflake role. No keys: the app uses its own session Warehouse time only while someone has it open Recommended ECS Fargate or App Runner A container in AWS Needs the key from Secrets Manager and a sign-in in front (ALB + company SSO) Runs, and costs, all the time Only if it must be in AWS A laptop (make app) Your machine Your .env — Development only

Streamlit in Snowflake is the easiest option. The report reads only Snowflake, so hosting it there needs no servers, no network work, no secrets and no sign-in setup. Everyone who can open Snowsight with the right role can open it. The app file already supports it: in Snowflake it uses the app's own session instead of a key.

docs.title: Publishing it to Streamlit in Snowflake
docs.text:
1. Once, as ACCOUNTADMIN: run sql/03_report_app.sql in Snowsight. It lets DQF_ROLE create a stage and a Streamlit app in DQF_DB.DQF.

  2. From dq-framework/:

    make report-publish

    This uploads app/streamlit_app.py (and an environment.yml with its packages) to the stage DQF_DB.DQF.DQF_APP. It then creates or updates the app DQF_DB.DQF.DQ_REPORT, owned by DQF_ROLE, and prints its address:

    https://app.snowflake.com/<org>/<account>/#/streamlit-apps/DQF_DB.DQF.DQ_REPORT

  3. Let the team open it (as ACCOUNTADMIN or the schema owner):

    grant usage on database DQF_DB to role <TEAM_ROLE>;
grant usage on schema DQF_DB.DQF to role <TEAM_ROLE>;
grant usage on streamlit DQF_DB.DQF.DQ_REPORT to role <TEAM_ROLE>;

    The app runs with its owner's rights (DQF_ROLE), so viewers do not need access to the results table itself.

Re-run make report-publish after changing the app.

For production, do the same on the production Snowflake account.

docs.title: Linking it from every alert
docs.text:
Every alert email has an Open the data quality report button when DQF_REPORT_URL is set.

Where Set Laptop runs DQF_REPORT_URL=… in .env (default http://localhost:8501) LocalStack The same .env value; make local-deploy passes it to the Lambda AWS REPORT_URL=… for infra/deploy.sh (the template's ReportUrl parameter)

The link opens the report on the run the email is about: the email adds ?schedule=hourly&window=2026-10-17 12:00, and the report selects that schedule and window. A Snowsight address keeps its route after #, where extra parameters would be lost, so for Streamlit in Snowflake the link opens the report on the latest run. The email names the window, and the report's sidebar lists every window.

docs.title: If it has to run in AWS
docs.text:
If policy requires the report in AWS rather than Snowflake, run the same file in a container:

  • Image: python:3.12-slim with streamlit, pandas and snowflake-connector-python, plus app/streamlit_app.py. Run it with streamlit run streamlit_app.py --server.port 8501 --server.headless true.
  • Login: the same SNOWFLAKE_* settings, with the private key from Secrets Manager. Write it to a file at start-up, or extend the app to read the secret.
  • Hosting: ECS Fargate (one task) behind an internal Application Load Balancer with company SSO (OIDC), or App Runner with private access.
  • Link: set REPORT_URL to the load balancer's address. Deep links then work, because there is no # route.

This is more to build and run than Streamlit in Snowflake, and nothing in it is automated yet.

docs.title: Data Quality Framework blueprint
docs.text:
This section is the architecture and delivery plan for a modular data quality framework built on Great Expectations (GX Core). It covers the three monitoring phases agreed in the kickoff and drafted in the BRD:

  1. Input Monitoring: is the raw data present and valid? This is the current priority.
  2. Features & Scores Monitoring: has what the models see and produce shifted?
  3. Model & Rule Performance Monitoring: are our decisions still separating good from bad?

Status: proposed design

Nothing on these pages has been approved yet. It is a blueprint for the team and reviewers to react to. Three labels are used throughout:

- **Recommendation**: the proposed approach, with the reasoning.
- **Decision needed**: a choice the team or a stakeholder must make before or during the build.
- **(inferred)**: something not confirmed by the sources (BRD, kickoff, system docs).

docs.title: What the framework must achieve
docs.text:
These goals come from the kickoff meeting and the BRD:

Goal What it means in practice Proactive detection We find data and model problems before the business reports an "uptick in a rule". Build once, reuse everywhere The same platform serves Underwriting, Risk Monitoring and Clover Capital. Configuration, not code A new data source, field or check is a config change, never a code change. Alerts people trust The right person gets an alert, at the right time, and not too many of them. Stakeholder reporting A scheduled weekly report, plus a report anyone can generate on demand.

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
These eight principles drive every decision in the blueprint:

  1. Configuration over code. A reference registry (source → fields → checks) drives everything. The feature store already works this way, which the kickoff called out as the model to follow.
  2. Monitor what matters. Only fields used in a model or a rule. Start with the top 5 per source, then widen. TMX alone sends ~2,000 fields, of which ~50 are used.
  3. Validate contracts, not raw payloads. GX reads curated, typed monitoring views that expose just the monitored fields, never raw JSON or vendor dumps.
  4. GX is the engine; Snowflake is the system of record. Configuration, results and alert state live in Snowflake tables. GX runs in an ephemeral context built fresh from that config on every run.
  5. Push the work down to Snowflake. GX turns checks into SQL that Snowflake executes. Only aggregates come back, so no bulk or personal data leaves Snowflake.
  6. Never in the decision path. Monitoring runs on data after it is logged. A monitoring outage can never slow or block an underwriting decision.
  7. Alerts are a product. Alerts carry state: one notification when a problem starts, one when it ends, and nothing in between. They are routed by severity and kept within a volume budget.
  8. Everything versioned and auditable. Config lives in Git and is reviewed before release. Each result records the config version and GX version it ran with.

docs.title: One platform, three phases
docs.text:
Each phase adds new metric producers on top of the same platform. The runner, results store, alerting and reporting are built once, in Phase 1.

docs.title: Timeline at a glance
docs.text:
Roughly six months end to end, consistent with the kickoff's "four to six months". Phase 3 data preparation starts early because outcomes take months to mature. See the roadmap.

Weeks Work 1–10 Phase 1: Input monitoring. Shadow mode by week 6, alerts live by week 10. 5–24 Phase 3 groundwork: find outcome data, define "bad", build the outcome-labelling job. 9–16 Phase 2: Features & scores. Can start once the new model's JSON output is in Snowflake. 15–24 Phase 3: Performance metrics, as soon as mature outcome cohorts exist.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text: Page Read it for Architecture Components, data model, runtime, security, and the key decisions. Phase 1: Input monitoring The detailed design and sprint plan to start with. Reference implementation Repository layout and code sketches for the runner, checks and alerts. Phase 2: Features & scores Baselines, PSI/CSI, score sanity, rule activity. Phase 3: Model & rule performance Outcome labelling, performance metrics, rule performance. Operations & alerting Alert lifecycle, routing, runbooks, service levels. Roadmap & governance Timeline, responsibilities, risks, open decisions, first two weeks.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This page describes the target architecture shared by all three phases: the components, the data model, how configuration is managed, where the framework runs, and the architecture decisions behind it.

docs.title: System context
docs.text:
The framework sits beside the systems it monitors and never inside them. It reads from Snowflake and writes its own results back to Snowflake.

flowchart LR
    subgraph PROD["Systems being monitored"]
        direction TB
        UW["Underwriting<br/>model service (AWS)"]:::sys
        RM["Risk Monitoring<br/>feature store"]:::sys
        CC["Clover Capital<br/>(later)"]:::sys
    end

    SF[("Snowflake<br/>inputs, model output history,<br/>feature store, outcomes")]:::snow

    UW -- "logged after each decision<br/>(UW step 5c)" --> SF
    RM --> SF
    CC -.-> SF

    DQF["<b>DQ framework</b><br/>GX runner + registry<br/>+ alerting + reporting"]:::dqf
    SF -- "read-only SQL" --> DQF
    DQF -- "results, alert state" --> SF

    DQF --> TEAM["Data / model team<br/>(alerts)"]:::ppl
    DQF --> BIZ["Business stakeholders<br/>(reports)"]:::ppl

    classDef sys  fill:#2E3B4E,stroke:#1a2330,color:#fff;
    classDef snow fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;
    classDef dqf  fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3f12,color:#fff;
    classDef ppl  fill:#e8eef5,stroke:#7a8ca3,color:#1a1c1e;

Recommendation: monitoring stays after the fact. The kickoff pointed at the model service's JSON output as the data to monitor, and that output only exists once a decision has been made. Keeping monitoring outside the decision path also means it can never add latency to, or break, a live decision. This resolves BRD review note #1.

docs.title: Logical architecture
docs.text:
The framework is split into five groups of components, each with one job:

flowchart LR

        direction TB
        GIT["Git repo<br/>YAML config + SQL views"]:::cfg
        CI["CI pipeline<br/>validate + deploy"]:::cfg
        REG[("Registry tables<br/>DQ_SOURCE, DQ_FIELD,<br/>DQ_CHECK, DQ_BASELINE")]:::cfg
        GIT --> CI --> REG
    end

    subgraph DP["Data plane: what is checked"]
        direction TB
        RAW[("Source tables<br/>A1, per-source, JSON history")]:::snow
        VW[("Monitoring views<br/>DQ_VW_*: typed,<br/>monitored fields only")]:::snow
        MET[("Metric tables<br/>PSI, performance")]:::snow
        RAW --> VW
        VW --> MET
    end

    subgraph EP["Execution plane: running checks"]
        direction TB
        SCH["Scheduler"]:::eng
        RUN["DQ runner<br/>Python + GX Core<br/>(ephemeral context)"]:::eng
        SCH --> RUN
    end

    subgraph RP["Results plane: what happened"]
        direction TB
        RUNS[("DQ_RUN")]:::out
        RESU[("DQ_RESULT")]:::out
        ALS[("DQ_ALERT")]:::out
    end

    subgraph XP["Consumption"]
        direction TB
        AM["Alert manager"]:::alert
        NOTI["Email / Teams"]:::alert
        RPT["Weekly + on-demand<br/>reports"]:::out
        DOCS["GX Data Docs<br/>(technical drill-down)"]:::out
        AM --> NOTI
    end

    REG --> RUN
    VW --> RUN
    MET --> RUN
    RUN --> RUNS
    RUN --> RESU
    RESU --> AM
    AM --> ALS
    RESU --> RPT
    RUN --> DOCS

    classDef cfg   fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#5e4e8a,color:#fff;
    classDef snow  fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;
    classDef eng   fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3f12,color:#fff;
    classDef out   fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;
    classDef alert fill:#e08a7b,stroke:#a8503f,color:#2b0c08;
Component Responsibility Built in Git repo Source of truth for check config (YAML), monitoring views (SQL), and framework code. Phase 1 CI pipeline Lint and test code; validate config against the schema; apply database migrations; load config into the registry. Phase 1 Registry tables The deployed config: what to check, where, how, and who owns it. The runner reads these tables, never the YAML. Phase 1 Monitoring views (DQ_VW_*) A stable data contract per source: typed columns, an event timestamp, keys, and monitored fields only. This is what a BRD "Snowflake Path" should point to. Phase 1, more each phase Metric tables Pre-computed metrics GX checks cannot calculate itself: PSI/CSI (Phase 2), AUC/KS/bad rates (Phase 3). Phases 2–3 Scheduler Triggers runs: hourly (P1), daily (P2), monthly (P3). Phase 1 DQ runner Reads the registry, builds GX expectation suites, runs them against Snowflake, classifies the results, writes them. Phase 1 Results tables An append-only history of every run and every check result. Everything downstream reads from here. Phase 1 Alert manager Opens, de-duplicates, escalates and resolves alerts, and routes notifications by severity. Phase 1 Reports The weekly scheduled report and an on-demand "generate report". Phase 1 (basic), extended later

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
All framework tables live in one schema, called DQ_FRAMEWORK here. The database name is a Decision needed: the team's sandbox for development, and a production database for go-live.

erDiagram
    DQ_SOURCE ||--o{ DQ_FIELD : "has"
    DQ_SOURCE ||--o{ DQ_CHECK : "table-level checks"
    DQ_FIELD  ||--o{ DQ_CHECK : "field-level checks"
    DQ_CHECK_TYPE ||--o{ DQ_CHECK : "implements"
    DQ_RUN    ||--o{ DQ_RESULT : "produces"
    DQ_CHECK  ||--o{ DQ_RESULT : "evaluated as"
    DQ_CHECK  ||--o{ DQ_ALERT : "raises"
    DQ_SOURCE ||--o{ DQ_BASELINE : "phase 2"

    DQ_SOURCE {
        string source_id PK
        string domain "UW, RM, CLOVER"
        string phase "INPUT, FEATURE_SCORE, PERFORMANCE"
        string snowflake_object "DB.SCHEMA.VIEW"
        string timestamp_col
        string window "1h, 1d, 1mo"
        int min_rows
        string owner_team
        boolean active
    }
    DQ_FIELD {
        string field_id PK
        string source_id FK
        string field_name
        string data_type
        boolean in_model
        boolean in_rules
        int importance_rank
        boolean is_pii
        string placeholder_values
    }
    DQ_CHECK {
        string check_id PK
        string source_id FK
        string field_id FK "null for table-level"
        string check_type FK
        string params "JSON"
        string warn_threshold "JSON"
        string fail_threshold "JSON"
        string severity "HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW"
        boolean alert_enabled
        string config_version
    }
    DQ_CHECK_TYPE {
        string check_type PK
        string gx_expectation
        string param_schema "JSON schema"
        string description
    }
    DQ_RUN {
        string run_id PK
        string source_id FK
        timestamp window_start
        timestamp window_end
        string status
        int row_count
        string gx_version
        string config_version
    }
    DQ_RESULT {
        string run_id FK
        string check_id FK
        float metric_value
        string status "PASS, WARN, FAIL, INSUFFICIENT_DATA, ERROR"
        int element_count
        int unexpected_count
        string details "JSON, PII-safe"
    }
    DQ_ALERT {
        string alert_id PK
        string check_id FK
        string state "OPEN, ESCALATED, RESOLVED, SUPPRESSED"
        timestamp opened_at
        timestamp last_seen_at
        timestamp resolved_at
        int occurrences
    }
    DQ_BASELINE {
        string baseline_id PK
        string source_id FK
        string target "score or feature"
        string bin_edges "JSON"
        string expected_shares "JSON"
        date period_start
        date period_end
        string approved_by
    }

Key design points:

  • DQ_FIELD is the reference table the kickoff asked for. It lists each source's fields, whether each is used in the model or rules, and its importance rank. "Top 5 fields per source" is then just a filter on importance_rank.
  • Separate WARN and FAIL thresholds let a check warn early and only alert when it truly fails.
  • INSUFFICIENT_DATA is its own status. When a quiet hour has too few rows, the check says so instead of reporting a misleading PASS or FAIL. This addresses review note #6.
  • Results are append-only and versioned. Every result can be traced to the exact config and GX version that produced it.
  • details never stores personal data. For fields flagged is_pii, only counts are kept, never sample values.

docs.title: Configuration management
docs.text:
Updated after the 1:1

The manager asked for the Excel template to be the input, read by the code as a data frame. For the MVP, read the Excel directly. For production, keep Excel as the intake form and convert it into the YAML below. See Excel template vs YAML config.

Recommendation: check configuration is written as YAML in Git, reviewed through merge requests, validated in CI, and only then loaded into the registry tables. The BRD spreadsheet stays as the business-friendly way to propose checks. A YAML change in Git is what makes them live.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant AN as Analyst / engineer
    participant GIT as Git (merge request)
    participant CI as CI pipeline
    participant RV as Reviewer
    participant REG as Registry tables
    participant RUN as DQ runner
    AN->>GIT: edit config/sources/uw_a1.yml
    GIT->>CI: pipeline on merge request
    CI->>CI: validate YAML schema, check-type params, field names exist in view
    CI-->>GIT: pass / fail report
    RV->>GIT: review and approve
    GIT->>CI: merge to main
    CI->>REG: upsert config, stamp config_version
    Note over RUN,REG: the next scheduled run picks up the new config automatically

Why not let people edit the tables directly? Because a reviewed merge request gives an audit trail, a safe way to roll back, and automatic validation for free. Those are the governance properties a monitoring system needs. It also keeps threshold changes visible: no one can quietly raise a threshold to silence an alert.

docs.title: Runtime and deployment
docs.text:
Decision needed: where the runner runs. The runner is a small Python container that sends SQL to Snowflake, so it needs little compute.

Option Pros Cons Fit GitLab scheduled pipeline Already used by the team (feature store, UW models); fastest to start Not built for hourly production schedules; weak alerting if a run fails MVP / shadow mode AWS Lambda + EventBridge Scheduler + SNS The manager's direction (1:1). Serverless; hourly schedule; SNS email; the team already has an email Lambda and an AWS → Snowflake Lambda (AWS2SF) to copy 15-minute limit; GX + connector need a container image; needs a service account and a network path to Snowflake Chosen for the MVP and production AWS ECS Fargate + EventBridge Scheduler Production-grade scheduling, retries, CloudWatch logs; UW already runs on AWS; Secrets Manager for keys Needs infrastructure-as-code and an AWS account path Recommended for production Airflow / MWAA Rich scheduling and dependency management Heavy to stand up just for this Only if the team already has Airflow Inside Snowflake (Snowpark) No external runtime GX is not designed to run inside a Snowflake procedure; package support is uncertain Not recommended

Decision (after the 1:1): run the hourly checks in AWS Lambda, scheduled by EventBridge, and send alerts through SNS, as the manager directed (details). Package the runner as a container image so that the same code can move to ECS Fargate if a run ever needs more than Lambda's 15 minutes. Running from a laptop or a GitLab schedule is still fine while you wait for approvals.

Environments: sandbox (development and shadow mode against sandbox copies) → prod. Config files carry an environment overlay, so the same check definitions point at different databases.

Use versioned migrations, not drop-and-recreate

The feature store's DDL deploy drops and recreates its schema, which has wiped in-flight progress before (see the backfill runbook). The DQ framework holds history (results and alert state) that must never be lost. Use versioned, forward-only migrations (for example with a tool such as schemachange). Never drop results tables in a deploy.

docs.title: Security and access
docs.text: Concern Approach Authentication A Snowflake service user with key-pair authentication, the same pattern the feature store uses. The private key is kept in AWS Secrets Manager (production) or masked GitLab CI variables (MVP), and never in the repo. Least privilege Role DQ_RUNNER_ROLE: SELECT on the monitoring views only, read/write on DQ_FRAMEWORK. No access to raw source tables beyond what the views expose. Personal data Monitoring views expose only monitored fields. is_pii fields keep counts only, never sample values, in results, alerts or Data Docs. Separation of duties Config changes need an approved merge request. The runner role cannot change config tables, only CI's deploy role can.

docs.title: Cost and performance
docs.text:
• Push the work down to Snowflake. GX's Snowflake datasource runs metrics as SQL inside Snowflake. Only aggregates come back to the runner.
  • Read only one window of data per run. Each run reads one hour (Phase 1), never the whole table. The monitoring views should be clustered or filtered by the event timestamp, so Snowflake skips the data outside the window.
  • Read only the needed columns. Views expose monitored fields only, which keeps each query small.
  • Use a small warehouse. Start on an X-Small warehouse with a short auto-suspend. Keep it separate from heavy warehouses such as MSDESCI_EXT_HEAVY, so other teams' jobs never starve monitoring, and vice versa.
  • Watch the cost of the checks themselves. Track run duration and credits per run in DQ_RUN.

docs.title: Monitoring the monitor
docs.text:
A monitoring system that fails silently is worse than none, because the team believes it is protected.

  • Heartbeat: a separate check (a Snowflake alert) fires if no DQ_RUN has completed for a source in the last two expected intervals.
  • Run health: an ERROR result (a check that could not execute) is itself an alert. It is never treated as a pass.
  • Reported metrics: run duration, checks executed, errors, and alert counts per week. See Operations.

docs.title: Architecture decisions
docs.text: # Decision Status Rationale ADR-01 GX Core is the validation engine Agreed (kickoff) Named by the manager; a mature expectation library; Data Docs included. ADR-02 Config and results live in Snowflake tables; GX runs in an ephemeral context Recommendation One system of record; GX's own file-based stores would drift from it; results can be queried with SQL. ADR-03 Git YAML is the config source of truth, deployed by CI Recommendation Audit trail, review, validation, rollback. ADR-04 Runtime: AWS Lambda (container image) + EventBridge, alerts via SNS Decided (manager, 1:1) See the options table above; ECS Fargate is the fallback if runs outgrow 15 minutes. ADR-05 A custom stateful alert manager, not GX's built-in notification actions Recommendation GX actions fire on every failing run, which causes alert storms. Alerts need memory of what is already open. ADR-06 Metrics, then expectations for PSI and performance metrics Recommendation GX has no PSI/AUC/KS expectations. Compute metrics in SQL or Python, then let GX judge them. ADR-07 Monitoring is after the fact and non-blocking Recommendation Matches the JSON-output source; no risk to live decisions. ADR-08 GX validates curated monitoring views, not raw payloads Recommendation A stable data contract, typed columns, PII control, and cheap queries. ADR-09 Versioned migrations, never drop-and-recreate Recommendation Results and alert history are permanent records.

docs.title: Operations & alerting
docs.text: A monitoring platform succeeds or fails on its alerts. Too many, and people stop reading them. Too vague, and nobody knows what to do. This page answers the kickoff's three open questions, when to alert, who to alert, and how many alerts, and describes how the platform is run day to day.

docs.title: Severity and routing
docs.text:
Every check has a severity in its config. Severity decides how and how fast people hear about a failure.

Severity Use for On FAIL Escalates after Example HIGH Failures that will change decisions now Immediate notification to the source owner 4 hours unresolved A source stops arriving (FRESHNESS); no-hit rate spikes; final-score PSI ≥ 0.25 MEDIUM Real problems that can wait for working hours Included in an hourly digest to the team channel 24 hours unresolved New enumeration in a key field; duplicate applications; rule hit rate ×2 LOW Quality debt Weekly report only Not escalated A few out-of-range values in a minor field (WARN, any severity) Early warning Weekly report and dashboards; never notifies (none) Missing values at 15% against a 30% FAIL threshold (ERROR) The check itself couldn't run Platform channel (framework owners) 2 hours A SQL error after an upstream schema change

Who: every source has an owner_team and an alert_route in its config. Routing goes to a team, never to one named person, so alerts still reach someone during holidays. Recommendation: start with email to a team distribution list, as the BRD proposes, delivered through an SNS topic from the hourly Lambda (design). Add a Teams channel once alert volume is stable.

docs.title: Alert lifecycle
docs.text:
Alerts are stateful. A check that keeps failing produces one alert, not one per hour.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Healthy
    Healthy --> Open: first FAIL (notify)
    Open --> Open: still failing (no new message)
    Open --> Escalated: unresolved past the severity limit (notify)
    Escalated --> Escalated: still failing
    Open --> Resolved: 2 consecutive PASS (notify)
    Escalated --> Resolved: 2 consecutive PASS (notify)
    Resolved --> Healthy
    Healthy --> Suppressed: planned maintenance or known incident
    Open --> Suppressed: acknowledged known incident
    Suppressed --> Healthy: suppression window ends
Rule Why Notify on state changes only (opened, escalated, resolved) One problem means one thread of messages, not 24 a day Resolve after 2 consecutive passes Stops a check that flips between PASS and FAIL from spamming Suppression windows (DQ_SUPPRESSION: source, check, start, end, reason, who) Planned vendor maintenance or a known incident doesn't page anyone, and the record of it is kept Every alert is recorded in DQ_ALERT with timestamps This is how detection time and time-to-resolve are measured (KPIs below)

docs.title: What an alert says
docs.text:
Every notification should let the reader act without opening another tool first:

[DQ][HIGH][OPENED] uw_a1_input · EXPERIAN_HIT_STATUS · NO_HIT_RATE

What:      No-hit rate 14.2% in window 09:00–10:00 (FAIL threshold 11.0%;
           trailing same-hour median 6.0%)
Since:     09:00 (first failing window)  ·  occurrences: 1
Impact:    Bureau component score missing for more applications → IDT/MF/Credit
           lanes fall back to their "no bureau" scenario models
Check:     check_id uw_a1_input.EXPERIAN_HIT_STATUS.NO_HIT_RATE · config v3f9a2c
First steps: runbook https://<docs>/dq-framework/operations/#runbooks (NO_HIT_RATE)
Owner:     uw-data-eng   ·   Escalates at 13:00 if unresolved

docs.title: Alert budget
docs.text: Recommendation: treat alert volume as a budget: at most about 5 HIGH alerts per week across all sources to begin with. If shadow mode shows the budget would be exceeded, tune the thresholds or lower the severity before go-live, not after. Track the budget weekly. If it is persistently exceeded, review the checks rather than accepting the noise.

docs.title: Runbooks
docs.text:
One entry per check type: what the failure usually means, and what to look at first.

Check type Usually means First steps FRESHNESS / VOLUME Pipeline or vendor outage; a load job failed; a schedule changed Check the loader (for UW: the AWS2SF Lambda logs); check the vendor status; compare with the same hour last week SCHEMA / VALUE_TYPE An upstream column was renamed, dropped or retyped Compare the view with the source table definition; find the upstream release; update the view (a migration), not the checks MISSING_VALUES / FIELD_POPULATION / PLACEHOLDER Mapping broke, a vendor stopped sending a field, or defaults are being written Find when it started (DQ_RESULT history); check whether it hits all records or one channel; contact the source owner NO_HIT_RATE Bad request data sent to the vendor (formatting, IDs), a vendor issue, or a population shift Sample no-hit requests for formatting problems; check the vendor status; compare by channel or region NEW_ENUMERATION / ACCEPTED_VALUES A new code introduced upstream Confirm with the data owner. If legitimate, add it to the allowed values (a merge request) and tell the modelling team how the model handles unseen categories ACCEPTABLE_RANGE / TREND A unit change (cents vs dollars), a test data leak, or a real population shift Look at the extreme values; check recent upstream changes; if it is a real shift, hand over to Phase 2 analysis PSI / CSI (Phase 2) The population or a feature has shifted against the baseline Find which bands moved; check related input checks for the root cause; tell the model owner Rule hit rate (Phase 2) A rule input changed, or the population did Trace the rule's inputs through Phase 1 checks; confirm with the rule owner before the business notices Performance (Phase 3) The model or a rule is losing ranking power Confirm with confidence intervals; hand over to the model review process ERROR / heartbeat The framework itself is broken Runner logs; Snowflake query history; credentials; recent config deploys

docs.title: Change management
docs.text: Change How New source, field or check Merge request to config/; starts in shadow mode (alert_enabled: false) for 2 weeks Threshold change Merge request with justification (the evidence from DQ_RESULT); reviewed by the check owner Turning alerts on Merge request after the shadow period shows the check stays within the alert budget New baseline (Phase 2) Modelling team approves; new baseline_id; the old one is kept Performance definition (Phase 3) Reviewers approve; new label_version; old labels are kept

docs.title: Service levels and KPIs
docs.text:
These numbers show whether the framework is doing its job. They are reported in the weekly report.

KPI Definition Target (proposed) Run completeness Scheduled runs completed ÷ scheduled runs ≥ 99% Run timeliness Hourly runs finished by :30 past the hour ≥ 95% Coverage Fields used in a model or rule that have at least one active check ÷ all such fields Top 5 = 100% at go-live; all fields by the end of Phase 1 Detection lead time Alert time − incident start time ≤ 2 hours (inputs); before the business reports it Alert precision Alerts the owner marks actionable ÷ all alerts ≥ 80% Alert volume HIGH alerts per week ≤ ~5 (the budget) MTTA / MTTR Mean time to acknowledge / to resolve, from DQ_ALERT Tracked from go-live; targets set after 1 month Business-first incidents Data incidents the business noticed before an alert Trending to zero, the headline goal from the kickoff

docs.title: Phase 1: Input monitoring
docs.text: Priority: start here. Phase 1 builds the shared platform (registry, runner, results, alerts, reports) and uses it to monitor raw input data: the fastest early-warning signal the team has.

docs.title: Objective and success criteria
docs.text:
Detect a broken or changed input data source within two hours, before the business notices it through a rule.

Success criterion Target (proposed) Coverage 100% of the top 5 fields per source by go-live; all fields used in the model or rules by end of phase Detection time Injected faults are detected in the first run after they appear (at most ~2 hours) Alert precision At least 80% of HIGH alerts are actionable (measured during and after shadow mode) Alert volume At most ~5 HIGH alerts per week across all sources (alert budget, tuned in shadow mode) Modularity Onboarding a new Day 2 source takes config changes only, with no code changes Reliability At least 99% of scheduled runs complete; a missed run raises a heartbeat alert

docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph P1A["Phase 1a: weeks 5-8"]
        A1[("A1 dataset<br/>top 5 fields<br/>+ table-level checks")]:::now
    end
    subgraph P1B["Phase 1b: weeks 8-10"]
        A1ALL[("A1 dataset<br/>all fields used in<br/>model or rules")]:::next
    end
    subgraph P1C["Phase 1c: Day 2, when available"]
        LN[("LexisNexis")]:::later
        GNF[("GNF response")]:::later

    classDef now   fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;
    classDef next  fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;
    classDef later fill:#e8eef5,stroke:#7a8ca3,color:#1a1c1e;

Added after the blueprint

A stakeholder email adds reconciliation (compare MRD's raw data with the input payload) and stresses no-activity alerts after A1 received no applications from 10 October. It also says A1 is today's API structure and A2 follows in the January timeframe. See Requirements update.

In scope: the A1 dataset on Day 1, then per-source tables on Day 2. Only fields used in a model or a rule, starting with the top 5 per source by importance. Both validity checks (is each value OK?) and availability checks (did the data arrive?). Lightweight trend checks on a few key fields. Hourly alerting, a weekly report, and an on-demand report.

Out of scope for Phase 1: formal distribution drift (PSI/CSI) and score monitoring (Phase 2), and performance metrics (Phase 3).

How this settles the input-drift question

The kickoff asked for drift analysis on inputs such as average ticket and annual sales. The BRD moved benchmark comparisons out of Part 1 (the conflict). Recommendation: Phase 1 includes simple trend checks: compare this window's median and no-hit rate with the same hour over the last four weeks. Formal PSI/CSI on a frozen baseline stays in Phase 2. Inputs get an early drift signal, and formal drift is not built twice.
