docs.title: The monitoring view: the data contract
docs.text:
Every source gets a view that is the only thing GX reads. It renames, types and trims the source table into a stable contract. If the upstream table changes, only the view changes and the checks don't. The column names below are illustrative: the real ones come from the A1 field inventory.

create or replace view DQ_FRAMEWORK.DQ_VW_UW_A1_INPUT as
select
    application_id                         as APPLICATION_ID,    -- key
    load_ts::timestamp_ntz                 as EVENT_TS,          -- window column
    merch_id::varchar                      as MERCH_ID,
    client_id::varchar                     as CLIENT_ID,
    try_to_date(enquiry_date)              as ENQUIRY_DATE,
    try_to_number(avg_ticket, 18, 2)       as AVG_TICKET,
    try_to_number(annual_sales, 18, 2)     as ANNUAL_SALES,
    mcc::varchar                           as MCC,
    upper(experian_hit_status)             as EXPERIAN_HIT_STATUS -- e.g. HIT / NO_HIT
from <A1_DATABASE>.<A1_SCHEMA>.<A1_TABLE>;

Why try_to_* and not plain casts

A hard cast fails the whole query on one bad value. try_to_number turns a bad value into NULL, so the Value Type and Missing Values checks catch it and report it, rather than the run crashing.

docs.title: Check catalog
docs.text: Each BRD check type maps onto a GX expectation. Where GX has no built-in expectation, the framework adds a derived 0/1 indicator column to the window query and checks its mean with a built-in GX expectation. That way every check reports a measured value (see the derived-column pattern). The thresholds below are suggested starting points, to be tuned during shadow mode.

docs.title: Table-level checks (availability)
docs.text: Check type What it catches GX implementation Suggested thresholds VOLUME A source silently stops sending, or suddenly sends far too much ExpectTableRowCountToBeBetween; the runner computes the bounds from the trailing median for the same hour of the week WARN below 70%, FAIL below 50% or above 200% of the trailing median FRESHNESS Data stopped arriving: a pipeline or vendor outage ExpectColumnMaxToBeBetween on a probe query returning minutes since the newest EVENT_TS FAIL if no new data for 2× the load interval SCHEMA An upstream column was dropped, renamed or retyped ExpectTableColumnsToMatchSet + ExpectColumnValuesToBeOfType FAIL on any mismatch DUPLICATES The same application loaded twice ExpectCompoundColumnsToBeUnique (keys) FAIL if more than 0.1% duplicates

docs.title: Field-level checks (validity)
docs.text:
Check type (BRD name) What it catches GX implementation Suggested thresholds MISSING_VALUES Nulls rising ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeNull(mostly=1 - fail_pct) WARN above 10%, FAIL above 30% (BRD) FIELD_POPULATION Values that are present but useless (null, blank or placeholder) ExpectColumnMeanToBeBetween(min_value=…) on a derived 0/1 "is populated" column (not null, not blank, not a placeholder) FAIL below 70% populated (BRD) PLACEHOLDER_VALUE Defaults like -999 creeping in ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeInSet(placeholders, mostly=…) FAIL above 5% ACCEPTABLE_RANGE Out-of-range numbers or dates ExpectColumnValuesToBeBetween(min, max, strict_min, strict_max, mostly=…) FAIL if more than 1% out of range ACCEPTED_VALUES / NEW_ENUMERATION A category value never seen before ExpectColumnValuesToBeInSet(allowed_values); the details record the new values WARN on any new value; FAIL if new values exceed 1% of rows EXPECTED_FORMAT IDs or dates in the wrong pattern ExpectColumnValuesToMatchRegex(regex, mostly=…) FAIL if more than 1% don't match VALUE_LENGTH A code changes length (e.g. "≠ 8 characters") ExpectColumnValueLengthsToEqual / …ToBeBetween FAIL if more than 1% VALUE_TYPE A numeric field arriving as text ExpectColumnValuesToBeOfType + try_to_* nulls in the view FAIL on a type mismatch NO_HIT_RATE The vendor returns "no record" more often (the kickoff's Experian example) ExpectColumnMeanToBeBetween(max_value=…) on a derived 0/1 "is no-hit" column; the limit is the trailing same-hour median + the allowed increase WARN at +3 percentage points, FAIL at +5 points above trailing TREND (lightweight) The median of a key field drifts (avg ticket, annual sales) ExpectColumnMedianToBeBetween, with bounds from the trailing 4-week median WARN at ±20%, FAIL at ±35%

Why some checks compare against the past

A fixed threshold such as "no-hit rate above 12%" either fires constantly or never, because normal rates vary by hour and by day of the week. Relative checks (volume, no-hit rate, trend) compare each window with the same hour of the week over the last four weeks. Those trailing values come from DQ_RESULT history, which the framework already stores. Until four weeks of history exist (a cold start), these checks only produce WARN, never FAIL.

docs.title: How a result becomes a status
docs.text:
GX gives a single pass or fail per expectation. The framework turns that into five statuses:

flowchart TB
    S["Run the check"] --> E{"Did the check<br/>execute?"}
    E -- "no: SQL error, timeout" --> ERR["ERROR<br/>(alerts as a platform issue)"]:::err
    E -- "yes" --> R{"Rows in window<br/>at least min_rows?"}
    R -- "no" --> INS["INSUFFICIENT_DATA<br/>(no alert; VOLUME check<br/>covers the gap)"]:::ins
    R -- "yes" --> F{"Breaches FAIL<br/>threshold?"}
    F -- "yes" --> FAIL["FAIL"]:::fail
    F -- "no" --> W{"Breaches WARN<br/>threshold?"}
    W -- "yes" --> WARN["WARN"]:::warn
    W -- "no" --> PASS["PASS"]:::pass

    classDef err  fill:#2E3B4E,stroke:#1a2330,color:#fff;
    classDef ins  fill:#e8eef5,stroke:#7a8ca3,color:#1a1c1e;
    classDef fail fill:#e08a7b,stroke:#a8503f,color:#2b0c08;
    classDef warn fill:#f2d492,stroke:#c99a2e,color:#3a2e05;
    classDef pass fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;

GX evaluates the FAIL threshold (through mostly or the bounds). The framework reads the observed metric GX returns (for example unexpected_percent) and compares it with the WARN threshold itself. GX doesn't need to know about two thresholds.

docs.title: Configuration example
docs.text:
The YAML for the A1 source. Field names and the top-5 list are illustrative until the modelling team provides the real inventory.

source_id: uw_a1_input
domain: UW
phase: INPUT
snowflake_object: DQ_FRAMEWORK.DQ_VW_UW_A1_INPUT
timestamp_col: EVENT_TS
window: 1h
arrival_lag: 15m          # wait for late rows before checking a window
min_rows: 30
owner_team: uw-data-eng
alert_route: uw-dq-alerts

table_checks:
  - type: VOLUME
    severity: HIGH
    params: {baseline: trailing_same_hour, weeks: 4}
    warn: {min_ratio: 0.70}
    fail: {min_ratio: 0.50, max_ratio: 2.00}
  - type: FRESHNESS
    severity: HIGH
    fail: {max_lag: 2h}
  - type: DUPLICATES
    severity: MEDIUM
    params: {keys: [APPLICATION_ID]}
    fail: {max_pct: 0.001}

fields:
  - name: AVG_TICKET
    in_model: true
    importance_rank: 1
    placeholders: [-999]
    checks:
      - {type: MISSING_VALUES,   severity: HIGH,   warn: {max_pct: 0.10}, fail: {max_pct: 0.30}}
      - {type: FIELD_POPULATION, severity: MEDIUM, fail: {min_pct: 0.70}}
      - {type: ACCEPTABLE_RANGE, severity: LOW,    params: {min: 0, max: 10000, strict: true}, fail: {max_pct: 0.01}}
      - {type: TREND,            severity: MEDIUM, params: {stat: median, weeks: 4}, warn: {max_change: 0.20}, fail: {max_change: 0.35}}

  - name: EXPERIAN_HIT_STATUS
    in_model: true
    importance_rank: 2
    checks:
      - {type: NO_HIT_RATE,     severity: HIGH, params: {no_hit_values: [NO_HIT], weeks: 4}, warn: {max_increase_pp: 3}, fail: {max_increase_pp: 5}}
      - {type: ACCEPTED_VALUES, severity: MEDIUM, params: {allowed: [HIT, NO_HIT, ERROR]}, fail: {max_pct: 0.01}}

  - name: MCC
    in_rules: true
    importance_rank: 3
    checks:
      - {type: NEW_ENUMERATION, severity: MEDIUM, params: {allowed_from: reference_table}, warn: {max_new: 0}, fail: {max_pct: 0.01}}
      - {type: VALUE_LENGTH,    severity: LOW,    params: {length: 4}, fail: {max_pct: 0.01}}

docs.title: The hourly run, end to end
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant SCH as Scheduler
    participant RUN as DQ runner
    participant REG as Registry tables
    participant GX as GX Core (ephemeral)
    participant SF as Snowflake (DQ_VW view)
    participant RES as DQ_RUN / DQ_RESULT
    participant AM as Alert manager
    participant N as Email / Teams
    SCH->>RUN: trigger at 10:15 for window 09:00-10:00
    RUN->>REG: load active checks for uw_a1_input + config_version
    RUN->>RES: read trailing same-hour metrics (4 weeks)
    RUN->>RES: insert DQ_RUN (status RUNNING)
    RUN->>GX: build datasource, window query asset, expectation suite
    GX->>SF: one SQL query per check (aggregates only)
    SF-->>GX: counts, observed values
    GX-->>RUN: validation result per expectation
    RUN->>RUN: classify PASS / WARN / FAIL / INSUFFICIENT_DATA / ERROR
    RUN->>RES: write DQ_RESULT rows, close DQ_RUN
    RUN->>AM: evaluate results of this run
    AM->>RES: open / update / resolve DQ_ALERT
    alt new HIGH alert opened or resolved
        AM->>N: notify owner (one message per state change)
    end

Windowing rules:

  • Closed windows only. At 10:15 the run checks 09:00–10:00, never the hour still in progress. The arrival_lag (15 minutes) gives late rows time to land.
  • Idempotent. A run is identified by source + window + config version. Re-running a window replaces that window's results rather than duplicating them, so backfills and retries are safe.
  • Backfill. The runner accepts --from / --to to replay past windows. This is used to build the initial four weeks of trailing history quickly, instead of waiting for it.

docs.title: Onboarding a Day 2 source: config only
docs.text:
This is the modularity test from the kickoff: "if we bring in a new data source, all you should have to do is update that reference table".

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant DE as Data engineer
    participant GIT as Git + CI
    participant SF as Snowflake
    participant REG as Registry
    participant RUN as DQ runner
    DE->>GIT: add views/DQ_VW_UW_LN_INPUT.sql
    DE->>GIT: add config/sources/uw_ln.yml (fields, checks, owner)
    GIT->>GIT: CI validates the YAML and that each field exists in the view
    GIT->>SF: deploy the view (migration)
    GIT->>REG: load the new source, fields and checks
    RUN->>REG: next hourly run discovers uw_ln_input
    RUN->>SF: checks run in shadow mode (alert_enabled false)
    Note over DE,RUN: after 2 weeks of clean shadow results, flip alert_enabled in YAML

Acceptance test: onboarding LexisNexis (or any Day 2 source) involves no Python changes.

docs.title: Reporting in Phase 1
docs.text: Report Audience Contents How Weekly DQ report Team + stakeholders Per source: availability %, checks run, WARN/FAIL counts, open alerts, top recurring failures, trends for the key fields Scheduled query over DQ_RESULT / DQ_ALERT, rendered to HTML or email On-demand report Anyone (the kickoff's "generate report" button) Same as weekly, for any chosen date range Updated after the 1:1: HTML + Excel for the MVP, Power BI for production. Fixed pages: summary → main report → drill-downs (layout) GX Data Docs Engineers Expectation-level detail and history Generated by the runner, hosted internally; PII-safe

docs.title: Testing strategy
docs.text: Level What How Unit Each check builder produces the right expectation; the classifier assigns the right status pytest with GX's pandas datasource on small in-memory DataFrames; no Snowflake needed Config Every YAML file validates; every field exists in its view CI step queries information_schema.columns in the sandbox Integration End-to-end run against sandbox views Scheduled sandbox pipeline; compare results with hand-computed SQL Fault injection The framework actually catches each failure it is meant to catch A sandbox test view applies faults to a copy of the data, and the run must flag each one (table below) Injected fault Expected detection 40% of AVG_TICKET set to null MISSING_VALUES → FAIL 20% of rows set to -999 PLACEHOLDER_VALUE / FIELD_POPULATION → FAIL No-hit rate raised by 10 percentage points NO_HIT_RATE → FAIL A new MCC value inserted NEW_ENUMERATION → WARN / FAIL 80% of rows removed from the window VOLUME → FAIL No rows for 3 hours FRESHNESS → FAIL Rows duplicated DUPLICATES → FAIL AVG_TICKET turned to text VALUE_TYPE / SCHEMA → FAIL

docs.title: Sprint plan
docs.text:
Two-week sprints. Weeks are counted from project start.

Sprint Weeks Goal Deliverables Exit criteria 0: Discovery 1–2 Remove unknowns The 8 inputs listed above; ADR-04 (runtime) decided; BRD updated with A1, scope rule, no-hit check A1 path, cadence and top-5 fields confirmed in writing 1: Foundations 3–4 A platform skeleton that runs DQ_FRAMEWORK migrations; YAML schema + loader; GX runner skeleton (connection, window asset, results writer); CI pipeline; unit tests dqf run --source uw_a1_input writes a DQ_RUN in the sandbox 2: Check library 5–6 Real checks on A1, in shadow mode All Phase 1 check builders incl. custom ones; DQ_VW_UW_A1_INPUT; top-5 config; backfill of 4 weeks; hourly GitLab schedule Fault-injection suite passes; results land hourly with no notifications sent 3: Alerts & reports 7–8 People can act on results Alert manager (state, de-duplication, escalation); routing; weekly report; Data Docs; runbooks; threshold calibration from shadow data Simulated alert volume within budget; owners agree on routing 4: Go-live 9–10 Production Move runner to production runtime; expand to all model/rule fields (1b); enable HIGH alerts; heartbeat; handover Success criteria above met for 2 consecutive weeks

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
Risk Impact Mitigation A1 loads daily, not continuously Hourly checks are meaningless Confirm in sprint 0; set the source window to the real cadence Field inventory and importance ranks arrive late Scope stalls Start with BRD fields (Merch ID, Enquiry Date, Avg Ticket, Client ID); swap in the real top 5 later (config only) Too many alerts at go-live People ignore alerts Shadow mode, two-level thresholds, alert budget, and stateful de-duplication No-hit status field missing in A1 Key kickoff check can't run Derive it in the view from vendor response fields, or defer it to Day 2 per-source tables GX API changes between versions Breakage on upgrade Pin the exact GX version; upgrade deliberately with the test suite Runner fails silently False sense of safety Heartbeat alert and ERROR-as-alert (monitoring the monitor)

Next: the reference implementation shows how the runner, check builders and alert manager fit together in code.

docs.title: Phase 2: Features, scores & rule activity
docs.text: Phase 2 watches what the models see (features), what they produce (scores), and how the rules behave (hit rates and the decision mix). It catches the shifts that come before a fall in performance, months before Phase 3 can confirm one.

docs.title: Objective and success criteria
docs.text:
Detect a meaningful shift in feature distributions, score distributions or rule activity within one day, and explain it in a report stakeholders can read.

Success criterion Target (proposed) Score coverage PSI on every final score per lane, and on every component score Feature coverage CSI on the top features per model (importance-ranked, as in Phase 1) Rule coverage A hit-rate trend for every active rule Detection A shift injected into a sandbox copy is flagged in the next daily run Reporting The weekly report and the on-demand report include PSI/CSI tables and rule hit-rate trends

Rule hit-rate monitoring is the quickest win in this phase

Today the business notices "an uptick in this rule" before the team does (kickoff). A daily check of each rule's hit rate against its trailing four weeks catches exactly that signal, first. It needs only the decision section of the JSON output, not any outcome data. Recommendation: build it first in Phase 2.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: In scope Detail The new model only The kickoff explicitly excluded the legacy model. Features Raw and transformed features used by a model, starting with the top-ranked ones. Scores Per lane (MF, IDT, Credit): component scores (one per available source) and the final score; both raw (probability) and weighted. IDT and MF have up to 5 scores, Credit up to 3. Rule activity Hit rate per rule; the decision mix (for example approve / refer / decline shares). Not in scope Anything that needs outcomes, such as AUC or bad rates. That is Phase 3.

docs.title: Data source: the model service JSON output
docs.text:
Every decision produces one JSON object with header, scores, features and decision sections (kickoff). The rules engine writes it to S3 (step 5a), and it is loaded into the Snowflake history table (step 5c). Phase 2 reads that table through flattened monitoring views:

flowchart LR
    RE["uw-rules-engine-cert<br/>(writes full UW output)"]:::eng --> S3[("S3 transaction log")]:::s3
    S3 --> L["AWS2SF Trans Log<br/>Pipe Lambda"]:::eng --> H[("Snowflake history table<br/>one JSON row per decision")]:::snow
    H --> V1[("DQ_VW_UW_SCORES<br/>one row per score")]:::snow
    H --> V2[("DQ_VW_UW_FEATURES<br/>one row per feature")]:::snow
    H --> V3[("DQ_VW_UW_RULES<br/>one row per rule evaluated")]:::snow
    V1 & V2 & V3 --> M["Daily metric jobs<br/>PSI, CSI, hit rates"]:::eng

    classDef eng  fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3f12,color:#fff;
    classDef s3   fill:#54802D,stroke:#3c5d20,color:#fff;
    classDef snow fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;

The JSON schema hasn't been documented yet, so the paths below are illustrative. Getting sample payloads and a schema description is the first task of this phase.

create or replace view DQ_FRAMEWORK.DQ_VW_UW_SCORES as
select
    h.payload:header:application_id::varchar     as APPLICATION_ID,
    h.payload:header:decision_ts::timestamp_ntz  as EVENT_TS,
    s.value:lane::varchar                        as LANE,            -- MF / IDT / CREDIT
    s.value:name::varchar                        as SCORE_NAME,      -- e.g. idt_lexis_neustar, idt_final
    s.value:type::varchar                        as SCORE_TYPE,      -- COMPONENT / FINAL
    s.value:raw::float                           as RAW_SCORE,       -- probability
    s.value:weighted::float                      as WEIGHTED_SCORE
from <UW_HISTORY_DB>.<SCHEMA>.<HISTORY_TABLE> h,
     lateral flatten(input => h.payload:scores) s;

docs.title: Baselines: what "normal" means
docs.text:
Drift is always measured against something. A baseline is a frozen reference distribution for one score or feature.

Aspect Recommendation Which period The model's development / validation sample, or the first 4–8 stable weeks after the new model goes live. Modelling team approves. Bins 10 bands (as the kickoff described): score deciles from the baseline. Categorical features use their categories; rare categories are grouped into "other". Storage DQ_BASELINE (header: period, version, approver) + DQ_BASELINE_BINS (bin edges, expected share). Versioned, never overwritten. Refresh policy Frozen per model version. Re-baseline only when the model is retrained or released, through an approved config change. Reviewed quarterly. Second comparison Also compare each day with the previous 4 weeks. This catches sudden changes that a long-frozen baseline would smooth over.

Decision needed: how often is the baseline updated?

The kickoff asked "is that updated every month?". Recommendation: no. A baseline that rolls forward every month slowly absorbs drift, so gradual drift is never reported. Keep the frozen baseline for slow drift, and the trailing 4-week comparison for sudden change. That gives the benefit of both.

docs.title: Check catalog
docs.text:
Group Check How Suggested thresholds Validity (reuses Phase 1) Scores in range, not null when the source was available; feature ranges and types Phase 1 builders on the flattened views Raw scores in [0, 1]: FAIL on any value outside Score sanity A component score exists if and only if its source returned data Compare score presence with the source hit flags in the same JSON FAIL above 0.5% mismatches Score sanity The final score reconciles with its components (a weighted sum) Recompute Σ weight × component and compare it with the final score FAIL if more than 0.1% differ by more than a tolerance. Decision needed: the weights must come from the modelling team Stability PSI for each final and component score against its baseline Metric job → DQ_METRIC → GX WARN ≥ 0.10, FAIL ≥ 0.25 (common industry convention) Stability CSI for each top feature Same as PSI, per feature WARN ≥ 0.10, FAIL ≥ 0.25 Stability Summary shifts: mean, median, % of applications in the riskiest band Metric job WARN at ±10% relative to baseline Coverage Share of applications missing a component per source (for example, no TMX score) Metric job WARN at +3 points against trailing, FAIL at +5 Rule activity Hit rate per rule compared with trailing 4 weeks Metric job on DQ_VW_UW_RULES WARN at ×1.5, FAIL at ×2 (or ±X points for frequent rules) Rule activity Decision mix (approve / refer / decline shares) Metric job WARN at ±3 points, FAIL at ±5 points against trailing

How these criteria relate to the BRD's \"Dec > 10%\"

The BRD's FSI/CSI criteria were written as directional percentages. This catalog keeps the two ideas separate. PSI/CSI use index thresholds (0.10 / 0.25), because the index has no direction. Directional rules such as "mean dropped more than 10%" go under summary shifts.

docs.title: GX pattern: metrics, then expectations
docs.text:
GX has no built-in PSI or CSI expectation. Recommendation (ADR-06): compute metrics in Snowflake SQL into one long DQ_METRIC table, then let GX judge each metric. That keeps the heavy computation inside Snowflake, and keeps the judging (thresholds, WARN/FAIL, alerts) in the same framework as Phase 1.

flowchart LR
    V[("Flattened views<br/>scores, features, rules")]:::snow --> J["Metric jobs (SQL)<br/>PSI, CSI, hit rates,<br/>sanity counts"]:::eng
    B[("DQ_BASELINE<br/>+ bins")]:::cfg --> J
    J --> M[("DQ_METRIC<br/>date, target, metric, value")]:::out
    M --> G["GX runner<br/>ExpectColumnMaxToBeBetween<br/>per metric check"]:::eng
    REG[("Registry: thresholds")]:::cfg --> G
    G --> R[("DQ_RESULT")]:::out --> A["Alert manager<br/>+ reports"]:::alert

    classDef snow  fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;
    classDef eng   fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3f12,color:#fff;
    classDef cfg   fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#5e4e8a,color:#fff;
    classDef out   fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;
    classDef alert fill:#e08a7b,stroke:#a8503f,color:#2b0c08;

The PSI metric job for one score and one day, with a small floor so an empty bin can't break ln():

insert into DQ_FRAMEWORK.DQ_METRIC (metric_date, source_id, target, metric_name, metric_value, baseline_id)
with bins as (
    select bin_id, lo, hi, expected_share
    from DQ_FRAMEWORK.DQ_BASELINE_BINS
    where baseline_id = :baseline_id                 -- frozen baseline for this score
),
counts as (
    select b.bin_id, count(s.APPLICATION_ID) as n
    from bins b
    left join DQ_FRAMEWORK.DQ_VW_UW_SCORES s
      on  s.SCORE_NAME = :score_name
      and s.RAW_SCORE >= coalesce(b.lo, -1e9) and s.RAW_SCORE < coalesce(b.hi, 1e9)
      and s.EVENT_TS >= :day_start and s.EVENT_TS < :day_end
    group by b.bin_id
),
shares as (
    select b.bin_id,
           b.expected_share                                             as e,
           greatest(c.n / nullif(sum(c.n) over (), 0), 0.0001)          as a
    from bins b join counts c using (bin_id)
)
select :day, :source_id, :score_name, 'PSI', sum((a - e) * ln(a / e)), :baseline_id
from shares;

Each metric check in the registry then becomes a one-row query asset that GX checks, for example ExpectColumnMaxToBeBetween(column="METRIC_VALUE", max_value=0.25). The PSI value comes back as observed_value, so WARN classification and history work exactly as in Phase 1.

docs.title: Cadence and sample size
docs.text:
• Daily. Hourly PSI is noise: a few hundred applications spread over 10 bins can't produce a stable index.
  • Minimum sample. If a day has fewer applications than a minimum (for example 500 per score), compute on a rolling 7-day window instead and label the result so. Decision needed: confirm daily volumes per lane.
  • Reports. The weekly report adds PSI/CSI tables and rule hit-rate trends. The on-demand report produces the stakeholder FSI/PSI view the kickoff asked for.

docs.text:

docs.title: Sprint plan
docs.text:
Phase 2 starts once Phase 1 is in shadow mode and the new model's JSON output is landing in Snowflake.

Sprint Weeks Goal Deliverables Exit criteria 5: Contracts 9–10 Data access to scores, features, rules JSON schema documented; DQ_VW_UW_SCORES / FEATURES / RULES; baseline periods agreed with modelling Views return correct counts against the history table 6: Metric producers 11–12 All Phase 2 metrics computed daily DQ_BASELINE(_BINS); PSI/CSI, summary shifts, coverage, rule hit-rate and decision-mix jobs; DQ_METRIC Metrics match an independent notebook calculation 7: Judging & sanity 13–14 Metrics are checked and reported Metric checks in the registry; score-sanity checks (presence, reconciliation); report sections Injected shifts are flagged; reconciliation passes on real data 8: Shadow & go-live 15–16 Production Two weeks in shadow mode; threshold calibration; alerts on for rule hit rate and final-score PSI Alert volume within budget; modelling team signs off baselines

docs.title: Dependencies and risks
docs.text: Item Mitigation The new model must be live, with JSON output in Snowflake If it's delayed, run Phase 2 on sandbox / shadow traffic, or extend Phase 1 to Day 2 sources in the meantime The JSON schema can change between model releases The monitoring views absorb the change; CI checks the view against a sample payload Reconciliation needs the model's combination weights Request them in sprint 5; until then, check only that scores are present and in range Teams disagree about which baseline to use The modelling team owns and approves baselines (see governance) Low daily volume makes PSI noisy Rolling 7-day windows plus minimum sample rules

docs.title: Phase 3: Model & rule performance
docs.text: Phase 3 answers the question the other phases can only hint at: are the models and rules still separating good accounts from bad ones? It is the slowest signal, because an account has to age before its outcome is known. That is the "six-month lag" from the kickoff. It is also the most conclusive.

docs.title: Objective and success criteria
docs.text:
Report model and rule performance for every matured approval cohort, and alert when performance drops meaningfully below the model's development benchmark.

Success criterion Target (proposed) Labelling Every approved application in a matured cohort has an outcome label (good / bad / excluded) Model metrics AUC, Gini, KS and % bads captured, per final score and per component score, per monthly cohort Rule metrics Hit / no-hit bad rate and lift for every active rule Benchmarking Each metric shown against the development benchmark, with confidence intervals Reporting A monthly performance report, plus the on-demand report

docs.title: The performance definition
docs.text:
From the kickoff: for every approved application, if the account was later closed or terminated it is bad, otherwise it is good. The definition differs by business line (Underwriting vs Clover Capital), so it is configuration, not code:

performance_definition:
  domain: UW
  population: approved_applications
  outcome_source: <DB>.<SCHEMA>.<ACCOUNT_STATUS_TABLE>     # decision needed
  bad_when:
    status_in: [CLOSED, TERMINATED]                       # exact codes to be confirmed
    reason_not_in: [VOLUNTARY_CLOSURE]                    # decision needed (see below)
  performance_window_months: 6
  exclusions: [test_accounts, withdrawn_before_activation]
  label_version: v1

Decision needed: does every closure count as bad?

"Closed or terminated" may include merchants who simply left voluntarily, which is not a risk event. Counting those as bad would make good models look worse. Agree which closure reasons count as bad with the reviewers. The kickoff suggested asking them how they measure performance today. (inferred) The account-status codes already used by the feature store (02/03 terminated or off-boarded, 13 dormant, see Step 1) may be a usable outcome source.

docs.text:
flowchart LR

    W --> L["Month 6<br/>label assigned:<br/>bad / good / excluded"]:::lab
    L --> M["Cohort included in<br/>monthly metrics"]:::met
    W -. "early read at month 3<br/>(provisional, trend only)" .-> E["Early indicator"]:::early

    classDef m0    fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;
    classDef win   fill:#f2d492,stroke:#c99a2e,color:#3a2e05;
    classDef lab   fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#5e4e8a,color:#fff;
    classDef met   fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;
    classDef early fill:#e8eef5,stroke:#7a8ca3,color:#1a1c1e;
  • Cohorts are grouped by approval month. A cohort is matured once every application in it has had the full performance window.
  • Early reads (for example at 3 months) give a provisional trend sooner. They are always labelled provisional and never used to judge the model against its benchmark.

docs.title: Data model additions
docs.text:
Table Grain Key columns DQ_OUTCOME One row per approved application application_id, account_id, domain, cohort_month, outcome_status, outcome_reason, outcome_date, bad_flag, matured, label_version DQ_PERF_METRIC One row per cohort × target × metric cohort_month, domain, target (score or rule), metric_name, metric_value, ci_low, ci_high, n, n_bad, benchmark_value

Dependency: linking applications to accounts

Labels need a reliable join from application (in the decision JSON) to account (in the outcome source). If no such key exists, Phase 3 cannot start. Confirm it in the first weeks. This is why Phase 3 groundwork runs in parallel with Phase 1.

docs.title: Model metrics
docs.text:
Computed per final score and per component score, per lane, per matured cohort. Higher scores are assumed to mean riskier.

Metric Reads as Typical use AUC The chance a random bad scores riskier than a random good (0.5 = chance) Overall ranking power Gini 2 × AUC − 1 The figure model reports usually quote KS The largest gap between the cumulative bad and good distributions How well a cutoff separates the two % bads captured at k% Share of all bads in the riskiest k% of applications Business-facing; k is configurable (5% default, 1% for credit, per the kickoff) Bad rate by score band Bad rate in each of the 10 bands Should rise steadily from band to band (rank ordering). A band that breaks the order is a warning

Worked definitions and an example are in the kickoff notes.

# src/dqf/metrics/performance.py (sketch)
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, roc_curve


def model_metrics(y_bad: np.ndarray, score: np.ndarray, capture_pct: float = 0.05) -> dict:
    """y_bad: 1 = bad, 0 = good. score: higher = riskier."""
    auc = roc_auc_score(y_bad, score)
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_bad, score)
    top_n = max(1, int(round(len(score) * capture_pct)))
    riskiest = np.argsort(-score)[:top_n]
    return {
        "AUC": auc,
        "GINI": 2 * auc - 1,
        "KS": float(np.max(tpr - fpr)),
        f"CAPTURE_AT_{capture_pct:.0%}": y_bad[riskiest].sum() / max(1, y_bad.sum()),
    }

Only the score, the label and the cohort leave Snowflake for this calculation. No personal fields are needed.

docs.title: Rule metrics
docs.text:
For each rule, compare approved accounts where it hit with those where it didn't:

Metric Formula Healthy sign Hit bad rate bads among hits ÷ hits Clearly above the no-hit bad rate No-hit bad rate bads among non-hits ÷ non-hits Close to the portfolio bad rate Lift hit bad rate ÷ no-hit bad rate Well above 1. A lift that keeps falling means the rule is losing value Hit volume hits ÷ applications Matches Phase 2's hit-rate trend

Declined applications have no outcome

Only approved accounts have outcomes. A rule that declines an application removes it from the population, so its performance can't be measured this way (selection bias). Options, in order of ease: (1) measure rules that refer or flag without blocking; (2) measure on referred-then-approved applications; (3) a small, approved hold-out that lets some flagged applications through. Option 3 is a business and risk-policy decision. Decision needed with the reviewers.

docs.title: Statistical reliability
docs.text:
• Minimum bads. AUC and KS are unstable with few bad accounts. Recommendation: report a cohort only when it has at least ~50 bads. Otherwise pool consecutive cohorts (for example a rolling 3 months) and label it so.
  • Confidence intervals. Bootstrap each metric (ci_low, ci_high) and alert only when the interval is clearly below benchmark, not on the point estimate alone.
  • Benchmarks. Take the development benchmark from the model's documentation. The modelling team owns these values.

docs.title: GX pattern: metrics, then expectations
docs.text:
As in Phase 2 (ADR-06): compute into DQ_PERF_METRIC, then let GX judge. Typical checks:

Check Expectation on DQ_PERF_METRIC Suggested threshold Gini against benchmark ExpectColumnMinToBeBetween(column="GINI_RATIO", min_value=0.90) WARN below 95% of benchmark, FAIL below 90% KS against benchmark Same pattern WARN below 95%, FAIL below 90% Capture at k% ExpectColumnMinToBeBetween(column="CAPTURE", min_value=…) Set by modelling team Rank ordering Custom: bad rate must not fall between adjacent bands FAIL if more than one band breaks the order Rule lift ExpectColumnMinToBeBetween(column="LIFT", min_value=1.5) Per rule, set by the rule owner

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
Phase 3 has two tracks. The groundwork starts early because it has the longest lead time; the build comes after Phase 2.

Track / sprint Weeks Goal Deliverables Exit criteria Groundwork 5–14 Make labelling possible Outcome source found; application → account key confirmed; bad definition agreed (incl. closure reasons); benchmark values collected Signed-off performance definition (YAML) 9: Labelling 15–16 Outcome labels in Snowflake Labelling job; DQ_OUTCOME; backfill of historical cohorts Label counts reconcile with the business's own reporting 10: Metrics 17–18 Metrics per cohort Model + rule metrics with confidence intervals; DQ_PERF_METRIC Matches an independent notebook calculation 11: Judging & report 19–20 Checked and readable Benchmark checks in the registry; monthly report Reviewers accept the report format 12: Go-live 21–24 Production Monthly schedule; alerts on severe drops; runbook First production report delivered

Prove the pipeline on the legacy model

The new model won't have matured cohorts until about six months after it launches. Recommendation: if past decisions from the legacy model are available, build and test the labelling and metrics pipeline on those. It will then be proven and ready when the new model's first cohort matures.

docs.title: Reference implementation
docs.text:
This page shows how the Phase 1 design turns into code: the repository layout, the core modules, the CI pipeline and the tests. Phases 2 and 3 add modules to the same structure.

Reference sketch, not production code

The code shows the shape of the solution and the key patterns. It targets GX Core 1.x and Python 3.12. Pin an exact GX version in pyproject.toml, and check every API call against that version before relying on it. GX's API changed substantially between 0.x and 1.x, and some details (for example the Snowflake key-pair connection arguments) vary between releases.

docs.title: 1. Config models
docs.text:
The YAML is validated by pydantic models, both in CI and at load time. Identifiers are restricted to safe characters because they end up inside SQL.

# src/dqf/config/models.py
from enum import Enum
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator

IDENT = r"^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_$.]*$"   # identifiers only, so config can't inject SQL


class Severity(str, Enum):
    HIGH = "HIGH"
    MEDIUM = "MEDIUM"
    LOW = "LOW"


class CheckConfig(BaseModel):
    type: str
    severity: Severity = Severity.MEDIUM
    params: dict = Field(default_factory=dict)
    warn: dict | None = None
    fail: dict = Field(default_factory=dict)
    alert_enabled: bool = False          # new checks start in shadow mode


class FieldConfig(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(pattern=IDENT)
    in_model: bool = False
    in_rules: bool = False
    importance_rank: int | None = None
    is_pii: bool = False
    placeholders: list = Field(default_factory=list)
    checks: list[CheckConfig] = Field(default_factory=list)

    @field_validator("checks")
    @classmethod
    def only_monitor_used_fields(cls, checks, info):
        data = info.data
        if checks and not (data.get("in_model") or data.get("in_rules")):
            raise ValueError(f"{data.get('name')}: only fields used in a model or rule are monitored")
        return checks


class SourceConfig(BaseModel):
    source_id: str = Field(pattern=r"^[a-z0-9_]+$")
    domain: str                           # UW | RM | CLOVER
    phase: str                            # INPUT | FEATURE_SCORE | PERFORMANCE
    snowflake_object: str = Field(pattern=IDENT)
    timestamp_col: str = Field(pattern=IDENT)
    window: str = "1h"
    arrival_lag: str = "15m"
    min_rows: int = 30
    owner_team: str
    alert_route: str
    table_checks: list[CheckConfig] = Field(default_factory=list)
    fields: list[FieldConfig] = Field(default_factory=list)

The only_monitor_used_fields validator enforces the kickoff's scope rule in code: a field that isn't used in a model or rule cannot be given checks.

docs.title: 2. Check builders
docs.text:
Each check type has one builder. A builder returns a plan: the GX expectation to run, any derived columns it needs in the window query, and a warn predicate for the second threshold.

# src/dqf/engine/builders.py
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Callable
import great_expectations as gx


@dataclass
class CheckPlan:
    check_id: str
    expectation: object                       # a gx.expectations.* instance
    is_warn: Callable[[float], bool] = lambda metric: False
    derived_columns: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)   # name -> SQL expression
    probe: str = "window"                      # "window" or "freshness"
    table_level: bool = False                  # evaluated even when rows < min_rows


BUILDERS: dict[str, Callable] = {}


def builder(check_type: str):
    def register(fn):
        BUILDERS[check_type] = fn
        return fn
    return register


def _meta(spec) -> dict:
    return {"check_id": spec.check_id, "severity": spec.severity}


@builder("MISSING_VALUES")
def missing_values(spec, ctx) -> CheckPlan:
    # GX reports unexpected_percent = % null; FAIL via mostly, WARN checked by the framework
    return CheckPlan(
        check_id=spec.check_id,
        expectation=gx.expectations.ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeNull(
            column=spec.field, mostly=1 - spec.fail["max_pct"], meta=_meta(spec)),
        is_warn=lambda pct_null: spec.warn is not None and pct_null > spec.warn["max_pct"],
    )


@builder("FIELD_POPULATION")
def field_population(spec, ctx) -> CheckPlan:
    # Derived 0/1 column: populated = not null, not blank, not a placeholder.
    # Its mean is the population rate, which GX reports as observed_value.
    col = f"DQ_POP_{spec.field}"
    conditions = [f"{spec.field} is not null", f"trim({spec.field}::varchar) <> ''"]
    if spec.placeholders:   # never emit "not in (NULL)": it is NULL for every row
        literals = ", ".join(ctx.sql_literal(v) for v in spec.placeholders)
        conditions.append(f"{spec.field} not in ({literals})")
    expr = f"iff({' and '.join(conditions)}, 1, 0)"
    return CheckPlan(
        check_id=spec.check_id,
        expectation=gx.expectations.ExpectColumnMeanToBeBetween(
            column=col, min_value=spec.fail["min_pct"], meta=_meta(spec)),
        derived_columns={col: expr},
        is_warn=lambda rate: spec.warn is not None and rate < spec.warn["min_pct"],
    )


@builder("NO_HIT_RATE")
def no_hit_rate(spec, ctx) -> CheckPlan:
    # Relative to the trailing same-hour median from DQ_RESULT history
    col = f"DQ_NOHIT_{spec.field}"
    values = ", ".join(ctx.sql_literal(v) for v in spec.params["no_hit_values"])
    baseline = ctx.trailing_median(spec.check_id, weeks=spec.params.get("weeks", 4))
    if baseline is None:                              # cold start: never FAIL, only report
        fail_limit, warn_limit = 1.0, None
    else:
        fail_limit = baseline + spec.fail["max_increase_pp"] / 100
        warn_limit = baseline + spec.warn["max_increase_pp"] / 100 if spec.warn else None
    return CheckPlan(
        check_id=spec.check_id,
        expectation=gx.expectations.ExpectColumnMeanToBeBetween(
            column=col, max_value=fail_limit, meta=_meta(spec)),
        derived_columns={col: f"iff({spec.field} in ({values}), 1, 0)"},
        is_warn=lambda rate: warn_limit is not None and rate > warn_limit,
    )


@builder("ACCEPTED_VALUES")
@builder("NEW_ENUMERATION")
def accepted_values(spec, ctx) -> CheckPlan:
    allowed = spec.params.get("allowed") or ctx.reference_values(spec.field)
    return CheckPlan(
        check_id=spec.check_id,
        expectation=gx.expectations.ExpectColumnValuesToBeInSet(
            column=spec.field, value_set=allowed, mostly=1 - spec.fail.get("max_pct", 0.0),
            meta=_meta(spec)),
        is_warn=lambda pct_new: spec.warn is not None and pct_new > 0,   # any new value warns
    )


@builder("VOLUME")
def volume(spec, ctx) -> CheckPlan:
    baseline = ctx.trailing_median(spec.check_id, weeks=spec.params.get("weeks", 4))
    lo, hi = (0, None) if baseline is None else (
        baseline * spec.fail["min_ratio"], baseline * spec.fail["max_ratio"])
    return CheckPlan(
        check_id=spec.check_id,
        expectation=gx.expectations.ExpectTableRowCountToBeBetween(
            min_value=lo, max_value=hi, meta=_meta(spec)),
        is_warn=lambda n: baseline is not None and spec.warn is not None
                          and n < baseline * spec.warn["min_ratio"],
        table_level=True,
    )


@builder("FRESHNESS")
def freshness(spec, ctx) -> CheckPlan:
    # Runs on a separate probe query that returns one row: minutes since the newest record
    return CheckPlan(
        check_id=spec.check_id,
        expectation=gx.expectations.ExpectColumnMaxToBeBetween(
            column="DQ_LAG_MINUTES", max_value=ctx.minutes(spec.fail["max_lag"]), meta=_meta(spec)),
        probe="freshness",
        table_level=True,
    )

# ACCEPTABLE_RANGE, EXPECTED_FORMAT, VALUE_LENGTH, VALUE_TYPE, PLACEHOLDER_VALUE,
# DUPLICATES, SCHEMA and TREND follow the same pattern with
# ExpectColumnValuesToBeBetween / ...ToMatchRegex / ExpectColumnValueLengthsToEqual /
# ...ToBeOfType / ...ToNotBeInSet / ExpectCompoundColumnsToBeUnique /
# ExpectTableColumnsToMatchSet / ExpectColumnMedianToBeBetween.

The derived-column pattern

Rate-type checks (no-hit rate, field population) add a 0/1 indicator column to the window query and use ExpectColumnMeanToBeBetween. The mean of a 0/1 column is the rate, and GX returns it as observed_value. Every check therefore records a real measured value in DQ_RESULT, which the WARN thresholds and the trailing comparisons depend on. A custom SQL expectation would only report pass or fail.

docs.title: 3. Building the window query
docs.text:
# src/dqf/engine/query.py
from datetime import datetime


def window_query(source, plans, start: datetime, end: datetime) -> str:
    """Select only monitored columns + derived indicators, for one closed window."""
    columns = sorted({p.expectation.column for p in plans
                      if getattr(p.expectation, "column", None) and not p.derived_columns})
    derived = [f"{expr} as {name}" for p in plans for name, expr in p.derived_columns.items()]
    select_list = ",\n       ".join(columns + derived) or "1 as DQ_ROW"
    return (
        f"select {select_list}\n"
        f"from {source.snowflake_object}\n"
        f"where {source.timestamp_col} >= '{start:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S}'\n"
        f"  and {source.timestamp_col} <  '{end:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S}'"
    )


def freshness_query(source) -> str:
    return (f"select datediff('minute', max({source.timestamp_col}), current_timestamp()) "
            f"as DQ_LAG_MINUTES from {source.snowflake_object}")

docs.title: 4. The runner
docs.text:
One run covers one source and one closed window. GX runs in an ephemeral context built from the registry, so no GX state is kept on disk.

# src/dqf/engine/runner.py
import great_expectations as gx

from dqf.engine.builders import BUILDERS
from dqf.engine.classify import classify, observed_metric
from dqf.engine.query import freshness_query, window_query


def run_source(source_id: str, start, end, *, registry, results, settings):
    source = registry.load_source(source_id)
    checks = registry.load_checks(source_id)                  # active checks + config_version
    ctx = registry.run_context(source, start, end, history=results)
    plans = [BUILDERS[c.type](c, ctx) for c in checks]

    run = results.start_run(source_id, start, end, registry.config_version,
                            gx_version=gx.__version__)
    try:
        context = gx.get_context(mode="ephemeral")
        ds = context.data_sources.add_snowflake(
            name="snowflake",
            connection_string=settings.snowflake_url,          # user/account/db/schema/warehouse/role
            kwargs={"connect_args": {"private_key": settings.private_key_der}},  # verify per GX version
        )

        window_plans = [p for p in plans if p.probe == "window"]
        window = ds.add_query_asset(name=f"{source_id}_window",
                                    query=window_query(source, window_plans, start, end))
        batch = window.add_batch_definition_whole_table("window").get_batch()

        row_count = batch.validate(
            gx.expectations.ExpectTableRowCountToBeBetween(min_value=0)
        ).result["observed_value"]

        validations = [(p, batch.validate(p.expectation, result_format="SUMMARY"))
                       for p in window_plans]

        fresh_plans = [p for p in plans if p.probe == "freshness"]
        if fresh_plans:
            probe = ds.add_query_asset(name=f"{source_id}_freshness",
                                       query=freshness_query(source))
            fresh_batch = probe.add_batch_definition_whole_table("probe").get_batch()
            validations += [(p, fresh_batch.validate(p.expectation)) for p in fresh_plans]

        rows = [
            {
                "check_id": plan.check_id,
                "status": classify(plan, vr, row_count, source.min_rows),
                "metric_value": observed_metric(vr),
                "element_count": vr.result.get("element_count"),
                "unexpected_count": vr.result.get("unexpected_count"),
                "details": registry.pii_safe_details(plan.check_id, vr.result),
            }
            for plan, vr in validations
        ]
        results.write_results(run.run_id, rows)
        results.finish_run(run.run_id, status="SUCCEEDED", row_count=row_count)
        return rows
    except Exception as exc:                                    # a run that can't execute is an alert
        results.finish_run(run.run_id, status="ERROR", error=str(exc)[:2000])
        raise

One validate call per expectation

Running expectations one at a time keeps each result tied to its check and isolates failures: one bad check can't hide the others. Running them as a single ExpectationSuite is also fine and cuts round trips. In that case, map results back through the meta.check_id that every expectation carries.

docs.title: 5. Classifying results
docs.text:
# src/dqf/engine/classify.py
from enum import Enum


class Status(str, Enum):
    PASS = "PASS"
    WARN = "WARN"
    FAIL = "FAIL"
    INSUFFICIENT_DATA = "INSUFFICIENT_DATA"
    ERROR = "ERROR"


def observed_metric(vr) -> float | None:
    r = vr.result or {}
    if "unexpected_percent" in r and r["unexpected_percent"] is not None:
        return r["unexpected_percent"] / 100          # column-map checks: share of bad rows
    value = r.get("observed_value")
    return float(value) if isinstance(value, (int, float)) else None


def classify(plan, vr, row_count: int, min_rows: int) -> Status:
    if (vr.exception_info or {}).get("raised_exception"):
        return Status.ERROR
    if row_count < min_rows and not plan.table_level:
        return Status.INSUFFICIENT_DATA               # VOLUME / FRESHNESS still evaluated
    if not vr.success:
        return Status.FAIL
    metric = observed_metric(vr)
    if metric is not None and plan.is_warn(metric):
        return Status.WARN
    return Status.PASS

docs.title: 6. Alert manager
docs.text:
This component carries state, and that state is what separates useful alerting from alert storms. The full lifecycle is on the Operations page.

# src/dqf/alerts/manager.py
ESCALATE_AFTER_HOURS = {"HIGH": 4, "MEDIUM": 24, "LOW": None}
RESOLVE_AFTER_PASSES = 2                     # avoids flapping open/resolve/open


def evaluate(run_results, *, store, notifier):
    for r in run_results:
        alert = store.open_alert_for(r.check_id)          # OPEN or ESCALATED, if any
        if store.is_suppressed(r.check_id):               # maintenance window / known incident
            continue

        if r.status in ("FAIL", "ERROR") and r.alert_enabled:
            if alert is None:
                alert = store.open(r)                     # first failure -> one notification
                notifier.send("OPENED", alert, r)
            else:
                store.touch(alert, r)                     # still failing -> no new notification
                limit = ESCALATE_AFTER_HOURS[r.severity]
                if alert.state == "OPEN" and limit and alert.age_hours >= limit:
                    store.escalate(alert)
                    notifier.send("ESCALATED", alert, r)

        elif r.status == "PASS" and alert is not None:
            if store.consecutive_passes(r.check_id) >= RESOLVE_AFTER_PASSES:
                store.resolve(alert, r)
                notifier.send("RESOLVED", alert, r)

        # WARN and INSUFFICIENT_DATA never notify; they appear in reports and digests

docs.title: 7. Writing results
docs.text:
# src/dqf/results/writer.py
import json


def write_results(conn, run_id: str, rows: list[dict]) -> None:
    """Idempotent per run: re-running a window replaces its rows."""
    with conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute("delete from DQ_FRAMEWORK.DQ_RESULT where run_id = %s", (run_id,))
        cur.executemany(
            """insert into DQ_FRAMEWORK.DQ_RESULT
                 (run_id, check_id, status, metric_value, element_count, unexpected_count, details)
               select %s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s, parse_json(%s)""",
            [(run_id, r["check_id"], r["status"], r["metric_value"], r["element_count"],
              r["unexpected_count"], json.dumps(r["details"])) for r in rows],
        )

docs.title: 9. Tests
docs.text:
Unit tests use GX's pandas datasource, so they run in milliseconds without Snowflake. Fault tests make sure each check catches the failure it is meant to catch.

# tests/faults/test_missing_values.py
import pandas as pd
import great_expectations as gx

from dqf.engine.builders import BUILDERS
from dqf.engine.classify import Status, classify


def _batch(df):
    ctx = gx.get_context(mode="ephemeral")
    asset = ctx.data_sources.add_pandas("t").add_dataframe_asset("a")
    return asset.add_batch_definition_whole_dataframe("b").get_batch(
        batch_parameters={"dataframe": df})


def test_40pct_nulls_fail(spec_factory, ctx_stub):
    df = pd.DataFrame({"AVG_TICKET": [None] * 40 + [125.0] * 60})
    spec = spec_factory("MISSING_VALUES", field="AVG_TICKET",
                        warn={"max_pct": 0.10}, fail={"max_pct": 0.30})
    plan = BUILDERS["MISSING_VALUES"](spec, ctx_stub)
    vr = _batch(df).validate(plan.expectation)
    assert classify(plan, vr, row_count=100, min_rows=30) == Status.FAIL


def test_15pct_nulls_warn(spec_factory, ctx_stub):
    df = pd.DataFrame({"AVG_TICKET": [None] * 15 + [125.0] * 85})
    spec = spec_factory("MISSING_VALUES", field="AVG_TICKET",
                        warn={"max_pct": 0.10}, fail={"max_pct": 0.30})
    plan = BUILDERS["MISSING_VALUES"](spec, ctx_stub)
    vr = _batch(df).validate(plan.expectation)
    assert classify(plan, vr, row_count=100, min_rows=30) == Status.WARN


def test_quiet_hour_is_insufficient(spec_factory, ctx_stub):
    df = pd.DataFrame({"AVG_TICKET": [None] * 5 + [125.0] * 5})     # 50% null, but only 10 rows
    spec = spec_factory("MISSING_VALUES", field="AVG_TICKET", fail={"max_pct": 0.30})
    plan = BUILDERS["MISSING_VALUES"](spec, ctx_stub)
    vr = _batch(df).validate(plan.expectation)
    assert classify(plan, vr, row_count=10, min_rows=30) == Status.INSUFFICIENT_DATA

docs.title: How the framework works
docs.text:
This section explains the data quality framework in dq-framework/: how one run works, how to set it up, how to configure it, how to run it, and what each code module does. To move it to AWS, see Lift and shift to AWS.

Page Read it when you want to End-to-end flow See the whole journey, from writing a check to the alert and the report, with every service on the way One-time setup Connect it to Snowflake for the first time Configuration Change what is checked or add a business rule (dq_config.yaml), or change the settings Running it Run checks, read the results, alerts and reports, and run the tests The code, module by module Change the code, or understand where something happens

docs.title: In one paragraph
docs.text:
A YAML file (config/dq_config.yaml) lists the tables to watch, the checks to run on them, and the business rules. On a schedule (hourly or daily), the framework reads the file and turns each check into a Great Expectations (GX) expectation. GX runs these against Snowflake and returns pass or fail with the measured value. The framework then stores one row per check in a Snowflake results table and works out what changed since the last run. It emails an alert when something starts failing, recovers, or keeps failing. It also writes GX's own HTML report. The same code runs on your laptop, in a Lambda in LocalStack, and in a Lambda in AWS.

flowchart LR
    WB["<b>dq_config.yaml</b><br/>sources, checks,<br/>stability, rules"]:::cfg --> PLAN["<b>Plan</b><br/>rows → GX expectations,<br/>grouped by query"]:::code
    PLAN --> GX["<b>Great Expectations</b><br/>runs each group as one<br/>Snowflake query"]:::code
    GX <--> SF[("<b>Snowflake</b><br/>monitored tables")]:::snow
    GX --> RES["<b>Results</b><br/>PASS / WARN / FAIL / ERROR<br/>per check"]:::code
    RES --> TBL[("<b>DQ_RESULT</b><br/>history")]:::out
    TBL --> DEC{"<b>What changed</b><br/>since the last run?"}:::code
    DEC --> AL["<b>Alert</b><br/>SNS / email"]:::alert
    RES --> DOCS["<b>GX Data Docs</b><br/>HTML report"]:::out
    TBL --> APP["<b>Streamlit report</b>"]:::out

    classDef cfg fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#57498a,color:#fff;
    classDef code fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3e10,color:#fff;
    classDef snow fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;
    classDef out fill:#54802D,stroke:#3a5a1e,color:#fff;
    classDef alert fill:#a8503f,stroke:#7a3527,color:#fff;

docs.title: One run, step by step
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant T as Trigger<br/>(EventBridge, or you)
    participant H as handler / cli
    participant E as engine
    participant W as config + plan
    participant G as Great Expectations
    participant S as Snowflake
    participant A as alerts
    T->>H: {"schedule": "hourly"}
    H->>E: run("hourly")
    E->>E: the window: the previous full hour (UTC)
    E->>W: read dq_config.yaml, keep this schedule's checks
    W-->>E: groups of expectations, one query each
    loop each group
        E->>G: validate(suite, query)
        G->>S: one read-only query
        S-->>G: counts and values
        G-->>E: pass / fail and the measured value per expectation
    end
    E->>S: store one row per check, read the previous run (one transaction)
    E->>E: new failures, recoveries, reminders
    E->>A: one message, if anything changed
    E->>E: GX Data Docs for this run
  1. Trigger. In AWS, EventBridge invokes the Lambda at 20 past each hour with {"schedule": "hourly"}, and at 01:30 UTC with {"schedule": "daily"}. On a laptop, you run dqf run hourly.
  2. Window. An hourly run checks the previous full hour: a run at 10:20 checks 09:00–10:00. A daily run checks the previous full day. The 20 minutes leave time for late data to load.
  3. Plan. Only the sources with that schedule are used. Their checks become GX expectations, grouped so that each group is one Snowflake query (see Plan).
  4. Validate. GX runs each group through its built-in Snowflake data source. Only counts and measured values come back: the framework never downloads the monitored rows.
  5. Record. Each check becomes one row in DQ_RESULT. Re-running a window replaces that window's rows, so runs can be repeated safely.
  6. Decide. The framework compares this run with the previous run of the same schedule. It alerts on a check that started failing, recovered, or has been failing for another 24 hours (a reminder). A check that keeps failing does not send an email every hour.
  7. Alert and report. One email per run lists every change, explains each problem in plain words, and gives a query to see the rows. GX's HTML report is written for the run.

docs.title: Two kinds of monitoring
docs.text:
Kind Question Schedule Example Data checks Is the data valid, complete, and still arriving? hourly (or daily) AVG_TICKET empty in 57% of rows; no applications for 3 hours Drift checks (PSI / CSI) Does recent data still look like the benchmark the model was built on? daily MF_SCORE PSI 0.55 against the benchmark: a large shift

Underwriting uses both, on the A1 record. The Risk Monitoring feature store mostly uses daily checks: whether the day's load arrived, missing features, and CSI per top feature.

docs.title: Where Great Expectations is used, and where it is not
docs.text: Part Done by Connecting to Snowflake for the checks GX: context.data_sources.add_snowflake (GX's Snowflake support, through the Snowflake connector) Each check GX expectations from its gallery, e.g. ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeNull, ExpectColumnValuesToBeInSet, ExpectTableRowCountToBeBetween Business rules GX built-in expectations restricted by a row condition (when / then in the configuration, no SQL) Custom checks (e.g. the SSN / Tax ID derivation) GX custom expectations (src/dqf/expectations.py): a per-row metric with a Snowflake (SQLAlchemy) version PSI / CSI Computed in Snowflake SQL; GX ExpectColumnMaxToBeBetween judges the result against the limit The HTML report GX Data Docs Reading the configuration, scheduling, the history, alert decisions, the email The framework's own code; GX does not do these

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
There are three things to configure:

What Where Who changes it, and how often What to check, including business rules The configuration file config/dq_config.yaml Analysts and stakeholders' rules, often. Plain field conditions, no SQL, no code deploy Custom checks for logic field conditions cannot express (rare) src/dqf/expectations.py A developer, once per check How it runs Environment variables (.env locally; the Lambda's environment in AWS) Once per environment

docs.title: The configuration file
docs.text:
config/dq_config.yaml is the main configuration. It is one text file, reviewed in Git like code, with comments explaining each check. It has two sections:

  • sources: one block per table (or view) to watch, holding that table's checks and drift checks (stability).
  • rules: the business rules, written as field conditions: when a row is in scope, then what must be true of it.
sources:
  UW_A1_INPUT:                             # a short name for this table, seen this way
    table: DQF_DB.DQF.UW_A1_RECORD
    ts_column: REQUEST_TS
    schedule: hourly                       # checks the previous full hour
    checks:
      - {check_type: VOLUME, min: 1, alert: yes}
      - {field: AVG_TICKET, check_type: MISSING_VALUES, max_bad_pct: 30, alert: yes}
      - {field: SSN_TAX_ID_MATCH, check_type: ACCEPTED_VALUES, values: ['1', '0', 'Z'], max_bad_pct: 0, alert: yes}

  UW_A1_DAILY:
    table: DQF_DB.DQF.UW_A1_RECORD
    ts_column: REQUEST_TS
    schedule: daily
    row_filter: EXCLUSION_REASON is null
    stability:
      - {field: MF_SCORE, index: PSI, field_type: NUMERIC, benchmark_start: -60, benchmark_end: -30,
         active_days: 7, warn: 0.10, fail: 0.25, alert: yes}

rules:
  DECISION_MATCHES_SCORE:
    description: No auto-approval with a merchant fraud score below 400
    applies_to: UW_A1_SCORED
    when: {DECISION: AUTO_APPROVE}
    then: {MF_SCORE: {at_least: 400}}
    alert: yes

The keys are the column names in the tables below, in lower case. Writing tips:

Tip Why Quote text that looks like a number or a date: values: ['1', '0', 'Z'], ['1900-01-01'] Unquoted, YAML reads 1 as a number, which would not match a text column Quote regular expressions: regex: '^[0-9]{5}$' Braces and $ have meanings in YAML alert: yes / no (or true / false) Either works One check per line, - {...} Each change is one line in a Git diff

docs.title: Checking it
docs.text:
make validate

This checks every entry before anything runs, and lists all problems at once, each with where it is (for example sources.UW_A1_INPUT.checks[3]: unknown key(s) max_bad). It catches unknown sources, keys or check types, missing limits, regexes that do not compile, unknown rules, and row filters or rules that try to do anything but read. The Lambda runs the same validation and stops with the full list if the file is broken.

docs.title: Excel and CSV: the extra options
docs.text:
The same configuration can be kept as an Excel workbook (sheets Sources, Checks, Stability, Rules) or as a folder of CSVs (sources.csv, checks.csv, stability.csv, rules.csv). Every format is read into the same rows and validated the same way, and the tests check that all three give an identical configuration.

Use Set DQF_CONFIG_URI to YAML (the default) config/dq_config.yaml (or s3://bucket/dq_config.yaml) Excel config/dq_config.xlsx (or s3://bucket/dq_config.xlsx) CSV folder config/sheets (local only)

Converting between them:

make config-xlsx         # dq_config.yaml -> dq_config.xlsx and config/sheets/*.csv
make config-from-xlsx    # an edited dq_config.xlsx -> dq_config.yaml (YAML comments are not kept)
.venv/bin/python scripts/build_config.py SOURCE TARGET     # any format to any other

The converter validates the source first and refuses to convert a broken configuration. Keep one format as the one people edit, which is the YAML file, so the copies cannot drift apart. The Excel and CSV files in config/ are generated from it.

In the sheets, each source's checks are rows with a SOURCE column instead of being nested under the source. Everything else is the same.

docs.title: Sources: what to watch
docs.text:
One block per table or view (sources: in YAML; one row per source on the Sources sheet).

Column Meaning Example SOURCE A short name the checks refer to: the block's key in YAML UW_A1_INPUT TABLE DB.SCHEMA.TABLE DQF_DB.DQF.UW_A1_RECORD TS_COLUMN The timestamp or date column that places a row in time REQUEST_TS SCHEDULE hourly: checks the previous full hour. daily: the previous full day (UTC) hourly ROW_FILTER Optional SQL condition; only rows matching it are checked EXCLUSION_REASON is null DESCRIPTION Free text

One table can be several sources. The sample configuration has three sources, all on the single table UW_A1_RECORD:

Source Table Schedule Filter Why UW_A1_INPUT UW_A1_RECORD hourly none Input checks apply to every application UW_A1_SCORED UW_A1_RECORD hourly EXCLUSION_REASON is null Score checks apply only to applications the models scored UW_A1_DAILY UW_A1_RECORD daily EXCLUSION_REASON is null Daily volume and PSI / CSI drift

A source is "this table, seen this way, this often", not a separate table.

docs.title: Checks: what to test on each window
docs.text:
One entry per check, under its source's checks: (or one row on the Checks sheet). Each check type maps to one GX expectation.

CHECK_TYPE Fails when Needs GX expectation VOLUME Fewer than MIN (or more than MAX) rows in the window MIN or MAX ExpectTableRowCountToBeBetween FRESHNESS The newest row is more than MAX hours old MAX ExpectColumnMaxToBeBetween on a computed age MISSING_VALUES, FIELD_POPULATION More than MAX_BAD_PCT% of FIELD is empty ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeNull ACCEPTABLE_RANGE Values outside MIN–MAX MIN or MAX ExpectColumnValuesToBeBetween ACCEPTED_VALUES Values not in VALUES. With 'CY' this is a source hit rate VALUES ExpectColumnValuesToBeInSet PLACEHOLDER_VALUE Values in VALUES (e.g. -999) VALUES ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeInSet EXPECTED_FORMAT Values not matching REGEX REGEX ExpectColumnValuesToMatchRegex VALUE_LENGTH Length outside MIN–MAX MIN or MAX ExpectColumnValueLengthsToBeBetween DUPLICATE_VALUES Repeated values ExpectColumnValuesToBeUnique SOURCE_COVERAGE Rows with no partner in COMPARE_SOURCE (joined on KEY = COMPARE_KEY) COMPARE_SOURCE, KEY ExpectColumnValuesToBeInSet on a join MATCHES_SOURCE Both sides have a value and they differ (COMPARE: EXACT, TEXT, NUMERIC with TOLERANCE) COMPARE_SOURCE, KEY same LOST_IN_MAPPING The other source has a value and this one is empty COMPARE_SOURCE, KEY same

Other columns:

  • MAX_BAD_PCT: the share of rows allowed to break the check, in percent. Empty means 0. It becomes GX's mostly (mostly = 1 − MAX_BAD_PCT / 100).
  • ALERT: Yes sends alerts for this check. No still runs and stores the check, so it shows in the reports, but sends no email.

The comparison types (SOURCE_COVERAGE, MATCHES_SOURCE, LOST_IN_MAPPING) compare the payload with the raw data (or any two sources) to catch mapping errors.

docs.title: Stability: drift against a benchmark
docs.text:
One entry per score (PSI) or feature (CSI), under a daily source's stability: (or one row on the Stability sheet).

Column Meaning Default SOURCE, FIELD What to compare INDEX PSI (a score) or CSI (a feature). The calculation is the same FIELD_TYPE NUMERIC: binned at the benchmark's quantiles. CATEGORICAL: the benchmark's most common values, plus OTHER BINS Number of bins. Missing values always get their own bin 10 BENCHMARK_START, BENCHMARK_END Fixed dates (2026-01-01), or days relative to the run (-60, -30) ACTIVE_DAYS The recent period compared with the benchmark 7 WARN, FAIL Limits. WARN shows in the reports; FAIL alerts 0.10, 0.25

The index is Σ (recent share − benchmark share) × ln(recent share ÷ benchmark share). It is computed inside Snowflake, so no rows are downloaded.

docs.title: Pointing it at the real tables
docs.text:
Use Sources Typical checks Underwriting input The A1 record table, hourly Missing values, source hit rates ('CY'), SSN_TAX_ID_MATCH, volume, freshness Underwriting output The same table, hourly, ROW_FILTER = scored population Scores 300–900, decision consistent with score Payload against raw data Both tables, hourly SOURCE_COVERAGE, MATCHES_SOURCE, LOST_IN_MAPPING using the input mapping spreadsheet Risk Monitoring feature store One daily source per model's feature view (TS_COLUMN = LOADDT) VOLUME (merchants per day), FRESHNESS, MISSING_VALUES per feature, and a stability entry per top feature and per score

Remember to grant SELECT on each new table to DQF_ROLE.

docs.title: Business rules
docs.text:
Business rules are written as field conditions, not SQL, so they can be stated by the people who own them. Each rule says when a row is in scope, and then what must be true of it:

rules:
  DECISION_MATCHES_SCORE:
    description: No auto-approval with a merchant fraud score below 400
    applies_to: UW_A1_SCORED
    when: {DECISION: AUTO_APPROVE}
    then: {MF_SCORE: {at_least: 400}}
    alert: yes

  MINIMUM_DATA_FOR_MODEL:
    description: A model with the Experian component is used only when Experian returned data
    applies_to: UW_A1_SCORED
    when: {MF_MODEL_USED: [SS_MF_100, SS_MF_101]}
    then:
      BUREAU_INQUIRY_STATUS: CY
      BIZID_INQUIRY_STATUS: CY
    alert: yes

  SCORES_IN_RANGE:
    description: Scores lie between 300 and 900
    applies_to: UW_A1_SCORED
    then:
      MF_SCORE: {between: [300, 900]}
      IT_SCORE: {between: [300, 900]}
      CR_SCORE: {between: [300, 900]}
    alert: yes

docs.title: The keys of a rule
docs.text: Key Meaning description The rule in a sentence. Shown in the alert email and in GX's Data Docs applies_to The source, or a list of sources, the rule checks. It runs on each source's schedule, window and row_filter when Which rows the rule is about. Leave it out for every row. Several fields: all must match. A list of field groups: any group then What must be true of those rows. Several fields: each must hold check Instead of then: a named custom check written by a developer (see below) max_bad_pct The share of in-scope rows allowed to break the rule, in percent (default 0) alert yes sends an email when the rule starts failing, recovers, or keeps failing

docs.title: The words
How a rule runs
docs.text:
Nothing is written in SQL. Each then field becomes a built-in Great Expectations expectation, and when becomes its row condition (GX 1.x, "Restrict an Expectation to specific rows"). GX then generates the SQL and runs it inside Snowflake:

Rule Great Expectations when: {DECISION: AUTO_APPROVE} row_condition = Column("DECISION") == "AUTO_APPROVE" then: {MF_SCORE: {at_least: 400}} ExpectColumnValuesToBeBetween(column="MF_SCORE", min_value=400, row_condition=…) then: {BUREAU_INQUIRY_STATUS: CY} ExpectColumnValuesToBeInSet(column="BUREAU_INQUIRY_STATUS", value_set=["CY"], …) then: {CODE: {matches: …}} ExpectColumnValuesToMatchRegex(…) then: {A: {equals_field: B}} ExpectColumnPairValuesToBeEqual(column_A="A", column_B="B", …)

A rule with several then fields is still one result: it fails if any field fails, and the alert says which. It reports the share of the in-scope rows that break it, for example: "No auto-approval with a merchant fraud score below 400: broken in 66.7% of rows where DECISION is AUTO_APPROVE (2 of 3 rows). Required: MF_SCORE must be at least 400." The alert also gives a query to list those rows in Snowsight, generated from the rule.

make validate checks every rule and says where any problem is (rules.DECISION_MATCHES_SCORE.when.DECISION: unknown condition 'abov').

docs.title: Custom checks (developers)
docs.text:
A few rules compare values in ways field conditions cannot. For example, SSN_TAX_ID_MATCH must be 1 when SSN and Tax ID are equal, 0 when they differ, and Z when either is empty. A developer writes such a check once, as a custom GX expectation in src/dqf/expectations.py, and the rule uses it by name:

  SSN_TAX_ID_MATCH_DERIVED:
    description: SSN_TAX_ID_MATCH follows the documented derivation
    applies_to: UW_A1_INPUT
    check: ssn_tax_id_match_follows_derivation
    alert: yes

A custom check is a GX multicolumn map expectation: a per-row yes/no metric with a SQLAlchemy version (what runs on Snowflake) and a pandas version (for tests), as GX's custom expectation guides describe. It therefore gets mostly, percentages, row conditions (when) and Data Docs like a built-in. To add one, write the metric and the expectation and register it in CHECKS with a sentence for the alerts and a condition for the "see the rows" query. It is code, so it needs a code deploy; using it is configuration.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: All settings are environment variables. Locally they come from .env; in AWS, from the Lambda's environment, which the CloudFormation template fills in.

docs.title: Snowflake login
docs.text:
Setting Meaning SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT, _USER, _ROLE, _WAREHOUSE, _DATABASE, _SCHEMA The login SNOWFLAKE_AUTH keypair (what the Lambda uses), password, or externalbrowser (your own SSO, laptop only) SNOWFLAKE_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH, _PASSPHRASE The key file, and its passphrase if encrypted DQF_SNOWFLAKE_SECRET_ID AWS and LocalStack. When set, the whole login is read from this Secrets Manager secret instead

The secret is JSON:

{"account": "ORG-ACCOUNT", "user": "DQF_SVC", "role": "DQF_ROLE", "warehouse": "DQF_WH",
 "database": "DQF_DB", "schema": "DQF", "auth": "keypair",
 "private_key": "-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----\n...\n-----END PRIVATE KEY-----"}

docs.title: The framework
docs.text: Setting Meaning Default DQF_CONFIG_URI The configuration: a .yaml or .xlsx path or s3://bucket/key, or a CSV folder config/dq_config.yaml DQF_RESULT_TABLE The results table, DB.SCHEMA.TABLE DQ_RESULT DQF_REMIND_HOURS Repeat an alert for a check still failing after this many hours. 0 = never 24 DQF_DATA_DOCS GX's HTML report: a folder, s3://bucket/prefix, or empty for none empty DQF_REPORT_URL The Streamlit report's address. Every alert links to it. Empty = no link empty

docs.title: Alert settings
docs.text:
Setting Meaning DQF_ALERT_CHANNELS Any of sns, email, log, comma separated. AWS: sns,log. Laptop: log,email DQF_SNS_TOPIC_ARN The SNS topic (set by the template) DQF_SMTP_HOST, _PORT, _USER, _PASSWORD, DQF_EMAIL_FROM, DQF_EMAIL_TO Direct email. Local inbox: localhost, 1025. Gmail: smtp.gmail.com, 587, your address and an app password DQF_LOCAL_ALERT_CHANNELS, DQF_LOCAL_SCHEDULES Only for the Lambda in LocalStack

In AWS, email goes through SNS: the template subscribes an address to the topic, and SNS sends the email. SMTP is only for running on a laptop or in LocalStack.

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.text:
This page follows the framework from start to finish:

  1. Someone writes a data quality check in the configuration file.
  2. Great Expectations runs it against Snowflake.
  3. The result lands in a Snowflake table.
  4. An alert reaches someone's inbox.
  5. The team opens the report.

It names every service involved and says where each piece of code is hosted and runs.

The checks, including the business rules, are written in one YAML file, config/dq_config.yaml. An Excel workbook or a folder of CSVs can be used instead; see Configuration formats. Everything after the reading step is the same whichever format is used.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C["<b>1. Checks file</b><br/>dq_config.yaml<br/>(or Excel / CSV)<br/><i>in S3</i>"]:::cfg --> L["<b>2. Lambda</b><br/>reads the checks,<br/>builds GX expectations<br/><i>AWS, every hour / day</i>"]:::aws
    L -- "3. GX runs the checks" --> T[("<b>Snowflake tables</b><br/>monitored data")]:::snow
    T -- "counts only" --> L
    L -- "4. stores results" --> R[("<b>DQ_RESULT</b><br/><i>Snowflake</i>")]:::out
    L -- "5. if something changed" --> S["<b>SNS</b><br/>email alert"]:::alert
    R -- "6. reads" --> ST["<b>Streamlit report</b><br/><i>in Snowflake</i>"]:::out
    S -. "link" .-> ST

    classDef cfg fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#57498a,color:#fff;
    classDef aws fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3e10,color:#fff;
    classDef alert fill:#a8503f,stroke:#7a3527,color:#fff;
    classDef snow fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;
    classDef out fill:#54802D,stroke:#3a5a1e,color:#fff;
  1. The checks file. You describe each check in a file, not in code: which table, which column, what counts as bad, how much bad is allowed, and whether to alert. Business rules, such as "no auto-approval with a score below 400", are written in the same file as plain field conditions (when DECISION is AUTO_APPROVE, then MF_SCORE at least 400), with no SQL. The file is config/dq_config.yaml, reviewed in Git like code; an Excel workbook or CSVs are optional alternatives. make validate checks every entry first. The deployment copies the file to an S3 bucket, where the Lambda reads it at every run. A change to the checks therefore needs no code release.
  2. The Lambda. EventBridge starts it at 20 past every hour, and at 01:30 UTC every day. It works out the window to check (the previous full hour or day), reads the checks file, and turns each row into a Great Expectations expectation, such as "AVG_TICKET is not empty in at least 70% of rows". It groups the expectations so that each table needs as few queries as possible. The Lambda's container image holds the framework, Great Expectations and the Snowflake connector.
  3. Great Expectations runs the checks in Snowflake. It logs in as the service user DQF_SVC, using the key from Secrets Manager. It compiles every expectation into SQL that runs inside Snowflake on the warehouse DQF_WH, then judges each count against its limit: pass, warn, fail, or error. Only numbers come back, never the monitored rows.
  4. The results are stored. Each check becomes one row in the Snowflake table DQ_RESULT: what was checked, the window, the status, the measured value, and the limit. Re-running a window replaces its rows. The table is the history that everything else reads, and anyone with access can query it in Snowsight.
  5. An alert, only when something changed. The run compares itself with the previous one. If a check started failing, recovered, or is still failing a day later, one email goes out through SNS to the subscribed addresses. For each problem, it says what is wrong in plain words, the measured value and the limit, and gives a query to see the affected rows. An unchanged problem does not send an email every hour.
  6. The report. A Streamlit app hosted in Snowflake shows the results table: what needs attention, the status of every field, and each check's history. It is separate from the Lambda, so it is always available. The alert email links to it.
