docs.title: handler.py
docs.text:
The AWS Lambda entry point (dqf.handler.handler). EventBridge calls it with an event:

Event Does {"schedule": "hourly"} / {"schedule": "daily"} One scheduled run + "window_end": "2026-10-17 10:00" Check the window ending then (UTC), for a manual re-run + "send_alerts": false Store results, send nothing {"action": "test_alert"} Send a test message through the alert channels, nothing else

It returns the run's counts (checks, passed, failed, alerts sent, report location). It keeps the engine between calls while the Lambda container is warm, and imports GX lazily, because GX takes seconds to import and Lambda allows 10 seconds for start-up.

docs.title: cli.py and __main__.py
docs.text: The dqf command (python -m dqf works too). It reads .env, then calls the same engine as the Lambda: run, backfill, validate, init, check-connection, describe-table, test-alert, show. It prints one line per check.

docs.title: settings.py
docs.text: Reads every setting from environment variables into one Settings object. The Snowflake login comes from Secrets Manager when DQF_SNOWFLAKE_SECRET_ID is set (AWS and LocalStack), otherwise from the SNOWFLAKE_* variables (a laptop). The rest of the code never reads the environment directly, so it behaves the same everywhere.

docs.title: engine.py
docs.text:
One run from start to finish. Engine.run(schedule, end):

  1. Works out the window (plan.windows).
  2. Loads the configuration (YAML, Excel or CSV) and keeps the sources with this schedule.
  3. For each group from plan.plan, builds a GX ExpectationSuite, adds the group's query as a GX query asset on the Snowflake data source, and runs batch.validate(suite). A group that breaks (bad SQL, missing column) marks its checks ERROR and the run continues.
  4. Turns GX's results into rows: PASS, WARN (PSI / CSI between the warn and fail limits), FAIL, or ERROR (GX could not evaluate it). GX is told not to fetch example values (partial_unexpected_count: 0), and any it returns are dropped. Only the counts in SAFE_KEYS are kept.
  5. Adds a plain-language explanation and a "see the rows" query to each row (explain.py).
  6. Stores the rows and reads the previous run (snowflake.record).
  7. decide() picks the new failures, recoveries and reminders. Only checks with ALERT = Yes count, and WARN never alerts by itself.
  8. Builds the GX report (datadocs.py) and sends one alert (alerts.py) if anything changed.

Engine.backfill(schedule, periods) runs past windows, oldest first, without alerts. It reuses one GX context and one Snowflake data source.

The GX context is ephemeral (in memory): no GX project folder, and the Snowflake login is never written to disk.

docs.title: workbook.py
docs.text:
Reads the configuration from a path or s3://: - YAML (.yaml, .yml), the main format; - an Excel workbook (.xlsx); - a folder of CSVs.

Every format is turned into the same rows (yaml_rows() for YAML, _rows() for sheets), and then one function, _build(), validates everything before anything runs. It reports all problems at once, each with where it is (sources.UW_A1_INPUT.checks[3], or Checks row 5). Among them: - an unknown key, source or rule; - a missing limit, a bad regex or a non-numeric value; - a row filter or rule containing anything but reading (;, --, drop, insert, … are refused).

It returns a Config: - sources, checks and stability rows, each with a stable CHECK_ID such as UW_A1_INPUT|AVG_TICKET|MISSING_VALUES. Alerts use the ID to tell "still failing" from "new". - rules: each business rule, checked and read into a rules.Rule (its when blocks and then parts). It also adds one check row per rule and source the rule applies_to, with the ID SOURCE||RULE_NAME, so rules are planned, stored and alerted on like any other check.

docs.title: plan.py
docs.text:
Turns configuration rows into GX expectations (BUILDERS: one per check type; rules.build for business rules) and groups them by the query they run on, so each group needs only one Snowflake query:

Group Query Checks in it Named in the GX report Window The source's rows in the window All standard checks and the business rules hourly.UW_A1_INPUT.checks Freshness Hours since the newest row of the whole table FRESHNESS hourly.UW_A1_INPUT.freshness Comparison The window joined to the other source; one 0/1 flag column per check SOURCE_COVERAGE, MATCHES_SOURCE, LOST_IN_MAPPING hourly.A.compared_with_B Stability PSI / CSI computed in SQL, one row One PSI or CSI daily.UW_A1_DAILY.drift_MF_SCORE

It also holds windows() (previous full hour or day), criteria_text() (the limit in words) and metric_name().

docs.title: sql.py
docs.text: The Snowflake SQL behind the groups: window_query, freshness_query, compare_query and stability_query (binning at benchmark quantiles or top categories, a missing-value bin, and a small floor on empty bins so the logarithm is defined). Every query is read-only and starts with SELECT, as GX requires. When a period has no rows, NO_ROWS (999999) makes the check fail instead of passing silently.

docs.title: rules.py
docs.text:
The rule vocabulary: the words of when and then (is, in, at_least, between, present, matches, equals_field, …). - parse_rule() reads and checks a rule. It is plain Python, so validation needs no GX. - build() turns each then field into a built-in GX expectation, with the when blocks as its row condition (Column("DECISION") == "AUTO_APPROVE"; blocks joined with & and |). A rule using check: becomes that custom expectation. - text() writes the rule in words, for the criteria and the alert. - breaks_sql() writes the condition for the alert's "see the rows" query. GX writes the SQL that actually runs.

The engine (engine.combine()) merges the parts of a rule into one result: it fails if any part fails and reports the worst part. The current rules, all in dq_config.yaml:

Rule Checks SSN_TAX_ID_MATCH_DERIVED SSN_TAX_ID_MATCH follows the documented derivation (1, 0, Z) SCORES_IN_RANGE MF, IT and CR scores are between 300 and 900 MINIMUM_DATA_FOR_MODEL A model with the Experian component is used only when the bureau and BizID returned data DECISION_MATCHES_SCORE No auto-approval with a merchant fraud score below 400

See Business rules to add one.

docs.title: expectations.py
docs.text: Custom GX expectations for logic that field conditions cannot express, written by a developer and used by rules by name (check: …). Each is built the GX way: a MulticolumnMapMetricProvider with a per-row condition for SQLAlchemy (Snowflake) and pandas (tests), and a MulticolumnMapExpectation that uses it, so it gets mostly, percentages and row conditions for free. CHECKS registers each one with a sentence for the alerts and a condition for the "see the rows" query. Today it has one: ssn_tax_id_match_follows_derivation.

docs.title: snowflake.py
docs.text:
Everything that talks to Snowflake:

  • Login: key pair (the service user), password, or browser SSO (laptop only). Every session runs in UTC.
  • add_gx_source: registers GX's built-in Snowflake data source (context.data_sources.add_snowflake) with that login. GX runs all the check queries through it.
  • column_names_without_rows: GX 1.24 learns a query asset's column names by running the query unchanged, which returns the window's rows. This makes it run select * from (…) limit 0 instead: the same names, no rows.
  • The results table: ensure_result_table creates it. record stores one run in one transaction: it reads the previous run's statuses and when each failing check started failing, deletes any earlier rows for the same window, and inserts the new rows.
  • read_results, whoami, describe: read-only helpers for the CLI and tests.

It writes to no table except the results table.

docs.title: How it connects to Snowflake
docs.text:
There are two connection paths. Both use the Snowflake Python connector underneath, and each does a different job:

Job Connection Code The checks: every expectation, business rule and PSI / CSI GX's built-in Snowflake data source, context.data_sources.add_snowflake(...). GX goes through SQLAlchemy and snowflake-sqlalchemy, which use the connector add_gx_source() The results table: create it; read the previous run; delete and insert this run The Snowflake Python connector directly, snowflake.connector.connect(...) connect(), ensure_result_table(), record() dqf check-connection, describe-table, show, the Lambda's check action The connector directly whoami(), describe(), read_results() The Streamlit report The connector on a laptop; the app's own Snowpark session in Streamlit in Snowflake app/streamlit_app.py

Why two paths:

  • The checks go through GX. That is the point of using GX: it compiles each expectation to SQL that runs inside Snowflake, so only counts and measured values come back, never the rows.
  • The results go through the connector. GX validates data but does not write tables. Storing a run also needs one transaction: read the previous statuses, delete any earlier rows for the window, insert the new ones. That is simpler and safer with the connector.
flowchart LR
    LOGIN["<b>One login</b><br/>settings.py:<br/>Secrets Manager or .env"]:::cfg --> GXS["<b>GX Snowflake data source</b><br/>SQLAlchemy +<br/>snowflake-sqlalchemy"]:::code
    LOGIN --> CONN["<b>snowflake.connector</b>"]:::code
    GXS -- "check queries<br/>(read-only)" --> SF[("<b>Snowflake</b>")]:::snow
    CONN -- "results table<br/>(one transaction per run)" --> SF

    classDef cfg fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#57498a,color:#fff;
    classDef code fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3e10,color:#fff;
    classDef snow fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;

One login for both:

  • settings.py builds a single login dictionary: from Secrets Manager when DQF_SNOWFLAKE_SECRET_ID is set (AWS, LocalStack), otherwise from .env.
  • Key pair (the DQF_SVC service user) is the default. Password and browser single sign-on (laptop only) also work.
  • The private key is loaded once. GX gets it as base64 text and the connector as raw bytes, because each library expects a different format.
  • Both paths set the same session options: TIMEZONE = UTC, and platform_detection_timeout_seconds = 0. The second skips a cloud-metadata probe that costs about 2 seconds at every login.

Connections per run:

  • The checks: the GX data source is created once per Engine and reused for every check group. It is also reused across a backfill and across invocations while the Lambda container stays warm. Each group is one query on it.
  • The results table: the connector opens one short connection to store a run, then closes it. One more short connection creates the results table the first time.

docs.title: explain.py
docs.text: For each result, explain() writes a sentence a person can act on, e.g. "BUREAU_INQUIRY_STATUS has a value other than 'CY' in 75.0% of rows (24 of 32 rows); at most 10% allowed. For a source status field this means the source did not return data for those applications." investigate_sql() writes a Snowflake query that shows the rows (or, for drift, the two periods side by side). These go into the alert, not the results table.

docs.title: alerts.py
docs.text:
Builds the message and sends it.

  • subject(), body() (plain text, for SNS and the log) and body_html() (for email) build the message: new problems, still failing, recovered, and everything else not passing.
  • report_link() builds the link to the Streamlit report from DQF_REPORT_URL. It adds ?schedule=…&window=… so the report opens on this run. A Snowsight address is linked as it is, because its route after # would lose the parameters.
  • Channels: sns (publish to the topic; SNS emails the subscribers), email (SMTP, HTML and text), log (print). A channel that fails is logged and does not stop the others.

docs.title: datadocs.py
docs.text: GX's own HTML report. After each validation the engine hands the result to a second GX context that only stores results and renders pages. For a folder target it builds in place. For an s3:// target (Lambda), GX 1.x has no S3 store, so it builds in /tmp: it first downloads the last 7 days of results, so the index shows recent history, then uploads the new pages. If the report fails, the run is not affected.

docs.title: Outside src/
docs.text: File Does app/streamlit_app.py The report on the results table. Does not import dqf, so it runs as one file in Streamlit in Snowflake. Opens on the run named by ?schedule=&window= scripts/publish_report.py make report-publish: uploads the app to a stage and creates or updates the Streamlit in Snowflake app DQ_REPORT; prints its address scripts/local.py LocalStack: build the Lambda folder, store the login in Secrets Manager, deploy the template, invoke, read SNS messages and logs. Talks only to localhost:4566 scripts/build_config.py Converts the configuration between YAML, Excel and a CSV folder (make config-xlsx, make config-from-xlsx); refuses a configuration with problems scripts/make_snowflake_key.sh The service user's key pair infra/cloudformation.yaml Every AWS resource. See What gets created infra/deploy.sh Build and push the image, deploy the stack, upload the configuration Dockerfile The Lambda image: AWS's Python 3.12 Lambda base, the pinned requirements, dqf, dq_config.yaml (a fallback)

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
There are three ways to run the framework. All three run the same code against the same real Snowflake account.

Where How it is started What it is for Your laptop dqf command (make run-hourly, …) Developing, trying configuration changes, backfills Lambda in LocalStack make local-invoke Testing the AWS packaging and wiring (S3, Secrets Manager, SNS) before AWS Lambda in AWS EventBridge, every hour and every day Production. See Lift and shift to AWS

docs.title: On your laptop
docs.text:
make run-hourly      # dqf run hourly: the previous full hour
make run-daily       # dqf run daily: yesterday; volume and PSI / CSI
make backfill        # 24 hourly and 7 daily runs of history, without alerts
make show            # a summary of the results table
make test-alert      # a test message through the alert channels in .env

The dqf command has more options:

Command Does dqf run hourly --end "2026-10-17 10:00" Check the window ending then (UTC), e.g. to re-run a past hour dqf run hourly --no-alerts Store results but send nothing dqf backfill hourly 48 --end "2026-10-17 00:00" 48 past hourly windows, oldest first, no alerts dqf describe-table DB.SCHEMA.TABLE A table's columns and row count, to help write the checks dqf check-connection, dqf validate, dqf init Log in; check the configuration; create the results table dqf -v … Verbose log

A run prints one line per check:

hourly window 2026-10-17 09:00 to 2026-10-17 10:00 UTC   run 3f9c2a1b7d4e
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
FAIL  UW_A1_INPUT      AVG_TICKET               MISSING_VALUES   56.7% bad rows   at most 30% bad rows
ok    UW_A1_INPUT      (table)                  VOLUME           30 rows          min 1
...
Great Expectations report: /home/…/dq-framework/build/data_docs/site/index.html
23 checks: 22 passed, 0 warnings, 1 failed, 0 errors.

docs.title: In LocalStack (AWS on your laptop)
docs.text:
LocalStack runs fake AWS services in Docker. The stack deployed there uses the same CloudFormation template as AWS, with Target=localstack.

make local-up            # start LocalStack 4.9 and the mail inbox (http://localhost:8025)
make local-deploy        # build the Lambda folder, put the login in Secrets Manager, deploy, upload dq_config.yaml
make local-test-alert    # the Lambda sends a test alert through SNS and email
make local-invoke        # the Lambda runs the hourly checks
make local-daily         # the Lambda runs the daily checks
make local-alerts        # what the Lambda published to SNS
make local-logs          # the Lambda's log
make local-docs          # the URL of the GX report the Lambda wrote to S3
make local-down          # stop it
After you change Run Code in src/dqf/ make local-build (the folder is mounted; no redeploy) dq_config.yaml (checks, business rules) make local-deploy (uploads it to S3 again) requirements.txt or the template make local-deploy

LocalStack is pinned to 4.9, the last open-source community release: no account or token, and the Apache 2.0 licence allows work use. It has no ECR, so the Lambda runs from a mounted folder instead of the container image AWS uses. The image is tested separately (make image).

docs.title: 1. The results table
docs.text:
DQF_DB.DQF.DQ_RESULT: one row per check per run.

Column Meaning RUN_ID, RUN_TS, SCHEDULE, WINDOW_START, WINDOW_END Which run, and which window it checked CHECK_ID A stable name: SOURCE|FIELD|TYPE, e.g. UW_A1_INPUT|AVG_TICKET|MISSING_VALUES SOURCE, TABLE_NAME, FIELD_NAME, CHECK_TYPE, RULE_NAME, CRITERIA What was checked, and the limit STATUS PASS, WARN (drift between the warn and fail limits), FAIL, or ERROR (could not run) METRIC, OBSERVED_VALUE What was measured: bad_pct, row_count, hours_since_last, rows_returned, stability_index ELEMENT_COUNT, UNEXPECTED_COUNT Rows checked, rows breaking the check ALERT_FLAG, DETAILS Whether it alerts; GX's numbers (or the error) as JSON

Only counts are stored, never example values, because the data includes personal information.

docs.title: 2. The alert email
docs.text:
When Example subject A check starts failing, or can no longer run [DQ hourly] 1 new problem in UW_A1_INPUT A failing check passes again [DQ hourly] 1 recovered in UW_A1_INPUT A check is still failing after another DQF_REMIND_HOURS [DQ hourly] 1 still failing in UW_A1_INPUT

Nothing is sent when nothing changed. A WARN never alerts by itself. Each problem in the email says:

  • what is wrong, in plain words: "AVG_TICKET is empty in 56.7% of rows (17 of 30 rows); at most 30% allowed."
  • the measured value, the limit, and the table;
  • a query to see the rows, ready to paste into Snowsight.

The email also lists everything else that is not passing. It has an Open the data quality report button, which links to the Streamlit report (DQF_REPORT_URL), and it links to the GX report.

docs.title: 3. Great Expectations' report (Data Docs)
docs.text:
GX's standard HTML report: an index of runs, and one page per group of checks, with each expectation, its result and the measured value.

Where it ran How to view it Laptop make docs, then http://localhost:8777/index.html (or open build/data_docs/site/index.html) LocalStack make local-docs prints the URL AWS aws s3 sync s3://<bucket>/data_docs/site ./site, then open site/index.html

Example values are removed from the report, as from the results table.

docs.title: 4. The Streamlit report
docs.text:
make app        # http://localhost:8501

It reads only the results table and shows what needs attention now, the status of each field, and the history of any one check. It is not part of the Lambda. It is a separate web app that keeps running and reads whatever the latest runs wrote.

The alert's link opens it on the run the email is about: http://localhost:8501?schedule=hourly&window=2026-10-17 12:00. To host it for the team, publish it to Streamlit in Snowflake (make report-publish). See Hosting the report.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Command What it checks Needs make test Reading the configuration in every format, business rules, planning, SQL, alert decisions and messages, the Lambda handler, the image contents Nothing make test-snowflake Every planted problem in the sample table is caught by the right check, and nothing else fails .env, the sample table re-run recently DQF_LOCALSTACK_TESTS=1 .venv/bin/python -m pytest -m localstack The deployed stack in LocalStack make local-up and make local-deploy

make test-snowflake writes only to DQF_TEST_RESULT_TABLE, never to the real results table.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix Snowflake login settings missing: … Fill in .env (or the secret, in AWS / LocalStack) 404 Not Found at login SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT is the bare locator; use ORGNAME-ACCOUNTNAME JWT token is invalid The public key in Snowflake does not match the private key: re-run the alter user line A check shows ERROR It could not run: a wrong column or table, or no SELECT grant. The error is in DETAILS and in the email No email arrives DQF_SMTP_HOST=localhost sends to the local inbox (http://localhost:8025), not to your mailbox. For Gmail use port 587 and an app password LocalStack is not running make local-up docker build fails on docker-credential-desktop.exe ~/.docker/config.json names a Windows credential helper WSL cannot run: build with a temporary DOCKER_CONFIG folder, or start Docker Desktop with WSL integration Lambda times out at login in AWS No network path from its subnets to Snowflake: see Network

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text: What you do once, on a laptop, before the first run. All commands run in dq-framework/.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: Tool Why Python 3.12 and uv The framework, its tests and the report A Snowflake account, as ACCOUNTADMIN (or a role that can create users and roles) To create the service user and the sample table Docker (WSL integration on Windows) Only for LocalStack and for building the AWS image

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
make setup        # creates .venv with the package, the Streamlit report and the tests
make test         # unit tests: no Snowflake, no AWS needed

docs.title: 2. A key pair for the service user
docs.text:
scripts/make_snowflake_key.sh

This writes keys/dqf_svc_key.p8 (the private key, which never leaves your machine or Secrets Manager) and prints the public key. keys/ is git-ignored.

docs.title: 3. Snowflake objects: sql/01_setup.sql
docs.text:
Open the file in Snowsight, paste the public key into the alter user DQF_SVC line, and run all of it as ACCOUNTADMIN. It creates:

Object Purpose DQF_DB database, DQF_DB.DQF schema Where the sample table and the results table live DQF_WH warehouse (X-Small, auto-suspend) Runs the check queries DQF_ROLE role SELECT on the tables it checks, CREATE TABLE in DQF_DB.DQF (for the results table) DQF_SVC user, TYPE = SERVICE Logs in with the key, no password, no MFA prompt. What the Lambda uses

It also grants DQF_ROLE to you, so you can look at the results in Snowsight.

Monitoring other tables

For each real table the framework must check, grant SELECT on it to DQF_ROLE (and USAGE on its database and schema). That is the only access it needs to the monitored data.

docs.title: 4. The sample table: sql/02_sample_table.sql
docs.text:
This creates one table, DQF_DB.DQF.UW_A1_RECORD: 60 days of made-up Underwriting A1 records, 30 applications an hour, with problems planted in known hours and drift in the last 7 days. The sample table section lists them.

"Hour N" counts back from when the SQL ran, so re-run it shortly before a demo or a test.

docs.title: 5. .env
docs.text:
cp .env.example .env

Fill in at least:

Setting Value SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT Snowsight: your name (bottom left) > Account > Copy account identifier, in the form ORGNAME-ACCOUNTNAME (e.g. BGFREGI-JI18204). The bare locator alone does not work outside us-west-2 SNOWFLAKE_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH The absolute path the key script printed DQF_EMAIL_TO Who gets the alerts DQF_SMTP_* Where the email goes: see Configuration

.env is git-ignored and is never copied into the Lambda image. In AWS the same values come from the Lambda's environment and Secrets Manager.

docs.title: 6. Check it
docs.text:
make check        # logs in; prints the account, DQF_SVC, DQF_ROLE, DQF_WH
make validate     # reads config/dq_config.yaml, lists any problems
make init         # creates the results table DQF_DB.DQF.DQ_RESULT

If make check fails, see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Feature Risk Monitoring — feature store pipeline
docs.text:
This section documents the Risk Monitoring (RM) Feature Store pipeline — a Snowflake-based pipeline that turns daily merchant transaction aggregations into a large library of time-series features used by the risk-monitoring models (attrition, sales, fraud, credit).

Sources

This is derived from a walkthrough recording of the feature store pipeline, the "Risk Monitoring – Feature Stores" diagram, and the "Feature Store Backfill" instructions email. Where something is an interpretation rather than stated in those sources, it is marked (inferred). Illustrative example values (merchants, feature numbers, sample data) are marked (illustrative).

This is a different system from Underwriting

The Underwriting Decisioning service is a real-time, synchronous scoring service on AWS. This pipeline is a batch, Snowflake-native feature-engineering pipeline. They share terminology ("primitive vs composite") and both live under Risk/Merchant Solutions, but they are separate systems with separate code and data.

docs.title: The pipeline in one picture
docs.text:
Everything inside the dotted boundary is the feature store pipeline. It is a three-step process (the yellow boxes). Black cylinders are upstream inputs, purple cylinders are config tables, and blue/teal cylinders are pipeline tables / outputs.

flowchart LR
    %% ---- upstream inputs ----
    DA[("Daily Aggregations<br/>CR_AGG_RMI_INFO<br/>(+ _EXPOSURE)")]:::up
    PV[("Profile Variables<br/>DSLR_RISK")]:::up

    %% ---- config tables ----
    TAD[("Transaction Array<br/>Definitions")]:::cfg
    FD[("Feature<br/>Definitions")]:::cfg
    NC[("Naming<br/>Conventions")]:::cfg
    MFM[("Model Feature<br/>Mapping")]:::cfg

    %% ---- steps ----
    S1["<b>Step 1</b><br/>Update Arrays"]:::step
    S2["<b>Step 2</b><br/>Compute Features"]:::step
    S3["<b>Step 3</b><br/>Registration &<br/>Governance"]:::step

    %% ---- pipeline tables / outputs ----
    TA[("Transaction Arrays<br/>TRXN_ARRAYS")]:::out
    FS[("Canonical Feature Store<br/>OFFLINE_FEATURE_STORE")]:::out
    FIN[("Feature ID → Name<br/>FEATURE_NAMES")]:::out
    FSV[("Model-specific<br/>Feature Store Views")]:::out
    CL[("Feature Store<br/>Change Log")]:::out

    DA --> S1
    PV --> S1
    TAD --> S1
    S1 --> TA

    TA --> S2
    FD --> S2
    NC --> S2
    S2 --> FS
    S2 --> FIN

    FS --> S3
    MFM --> S3
    S3 --> FSV
    S3 --> CL

    classDef up   fill:#2b2b2b,stroke:#000,color:#fff;
    classDef cfg  fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#5e4e8a,color:#fff;
    classDef step fill:#f2d492,stroke:#c99a2e,color:#3a2e05;
    classDef out  fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;

docs.title: The three steps
docs.text:
Step Input Output In one line 1 — Update Arrays Daily Aggregations + Profile Variables, driven by Transaction Array Definitions Transaction Arrays (TRXN_ARRAYS) Build/extend per-merchant rolling arrays of daily & monthly activity. 2 — Compute Features Transaction Arrays, driven by Feature Definitions + Naming Conventions Canonical feature store (OFFLINE_FEATURE_STORE) + Feature Names Run calculations over the arrays to produce the full feature library. 3 — Registration & Governance Canonical feature store, driven by Model Feature Mapping Model-specific feature store views + Change Log Pivot each model's selected features into wide, inference-ready views.

The code lives in the Feature Store GitLab repo. Running the pipeline over a set of merchant / observation-date pairs is called a backfill — see the Backfill runbook.

docs.title: The scale problem (why this is hard)
docs.text:
• ~3 million merchants, features generated every day.
  • The daily aggregation source holds ~5,000 variables per merchant per day.
  • The pipeline maintains ~821 arrays per merchant (per the array-definitions table).
  • A training-sample request from the modelling team was on the order of ~300,000 features — each of which must be generated for every merchant. "It's a big scaling problem."

This is why the canonical feature store is stored long (one row per feature), the arrays cap at a 366-day lookback, and the backfill runs as a server-side, fire-and-forget Snowflake procedure.

docs.title: Key tables at a glance
docs.text:
Table Type Role CR_AGG_RMI_INFO Upstream Daily aggregated transaction data — base (one row per merchant per day). CR_AGG_RMI_INFO_EXPOSURE Upstream Same, but only transactions where Fiserv owns the risk (exposure). DSLR_RISK Upstream Profile variables — merchant snapshots (status, install date, region, …). Transaction Array Definitions Config Which attributes to collect into which arrays (source, source_group, cadence). TRXN_ARRAYS Pipeline output One row per merchant; the rolling daily/monthly arrays. Feature Definitions Config The calculation for every feature (atomic & composite). Naming Conventions Config Abbreviations used to build short, algorithmic feature names. FEATURE_NAMES Pipeline output Feature ID → generated feature name mapping. OFFLINE_FEATURE_STORE Pipeline output The canonical feature store (long format). Model Feature Mapping Config Model name → the features it needs. Feature Store Views Pipeline output Wide, per-model, inference-ready views.

Most pipeline/config tables live in the AP_SBX_GBSRISK_AUTO.FEATURE_ENG schema (inferred to be the sandbox schema used in the walkthrough); the upstream sources live under GBS_PROD_CRANALYTICS.CRAGGR and the DSLR risk schema.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Step 1: Update Arrays — the arrays and how they roll.
  • Step 2: Compute Features — atomic vs composite features, naming.
  • Step 3: Registration & Governance — model-specific views.
  • Backfill runbook — how to run, monitor and restart a backfill.

docs.title: Backfill runbook
docs.text:
Running the feature store pipeline over a set of merchant / observation-date pairs is called a backfill. This page is the operational guide: how to kick one off, monitor it, and restart it after a failure. It consolidates the walkthrough and the "Feature Store Backfill" instructions email.

Read this before you deploy anything

The DDL deploy drops and recreates everything (a clean slate), including FEATURE_BACKFILL_COHORT and your in-flight progress. Deploy first, insert the cohort second. Never deploy in the middle of a run to "apply a fix" without understanding that it wipes progress — see Restart on failure.

docs.title: What a backfill request looks like
docs.text:
The RM developers hand you a table of merchant_id + obs_date combinations (e.g. AP_SBX_GBSRISK.RMDEV.MERCHANT_BASE_OBS_DATE_LIST_2). Notes:

  • The same date (e.g. Oct 1) appears many times; dates are otherwise scattered. A merchant may appear once or dozens of times.
  • For each merchant/observation-date, the pipeline generates the full feature set for that merchant on that specific day.

Do a little analysis first

Before running, eyeball the cohort: how many merchants, how many observation dates, and the distribution. It sets expectations for runtime (a large backfill can run for days).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Clone the Feature Store GitLab repo; use branch cr_agg_rmi_info-as-input.
  • Place the Snowflake private key file in C:\Users\<LAN ID>\.snowflake.
  • Note the PRIVATE_KEY_PASSPHRASE — you'll be prompted when you run any notebook.
  • You'll need DBA privilege on the warehouse to abort queries during recovery.

Repo layout

The project mirrors the underwriting-models repo: same GitLab CI/CD pipeline, .infra, data, notebooks, source. The infrastructure here is pure DDL (no AWS component) — it operates inside the FEATURE_ENG schema.

docs.title: Running a backfill — step by step
docs.text:
Order matters

Steps 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6. In particular, DDL deploy (step 1) comes before the cohort insert (step 2), because the deploy wipes the cohort table.

docs.title: 1. Create a clean slate (deploy the DDL) — do this FIRST
docs.text:
The first DDL script drops everything in the FEATURE_ENG schema and recreates it from scratch. Deploy by either:

  • Running the notebook notebooks/deploy_ddl.ipynb, or
  • Pushing to a non-main branch so the GitLab CI/CD runner executes the DDL scripts.

docs.title: 2. Insert the cohort into FEATURE_BACKFILL_COHORT
docs.text:
Pick a run_id (e.g. big_sample_2) and insert the merchant/observation-date pairs. INSERT INTO adds rows; unspecified columns default to null — the other columns don't matter much.

insert into AP_SBX_GBSRISK_AUTO.FEATURE_ENG.FEATURE_BACKFILL_COHORT (run_id, mrch_no, feature_date)
select
    'big_sample_2' as run_id,
    merchant_id    as mrch_no,      -- source merchant_id → target mrch_no
    obs_date       as feature_date  -- source obs_date    → target feature_date
from AP_SBX_GBSRISK.RMDEV.MERCHANT_BASE_OBS_DATE_LIST_2;

docs.title: 3. Terminate long-window features
docs.text:
Because these samples use a 366-day (12-month) lookback, any feature whose window needs more than 12 months of monthly history can't be computed — the arrays won't hold that history. Terminating them tells the engine not to waste computation on features it can't produce.

Why this is needed

Monthly arrays can hold up to 36 months, but the backfill only builds a 12-month lookback. A feature asking for a >12-month monthly window would have no data → a wasted (and wrong) computation.

-- (a) Terminate ATOMIC features whose monthly time window exceeds 12 months,
--     except consecutive-streak calcs (which only use a max window).
UPDATE feature_definitions
SET termination_dt = '2023-01-01'
WHERE calculation NOT LIKE '%consecutive%'
  AND inp_col1 LIKE '%_mly'
  AND array_max(transform(split(time_window1, '-'), v -> try_to_number(v::varchar))) > 12;

-- (b) Terminate COMPOSITE features that depend on a now-terminated upstream feature.
--     RUN THIS ONE TWICE — there are two layers of composites.
UPDATE feature_definitions fd
SET fd.termination_dt = '2023-01-01'
WHERE ((fd.inp_type1 = 'feature' AND fd.inp_col1 IN (
          SELECT feature_id::VARCHAR FROM feature_definitions WHERE termination_dt IS NOT NULL))
    OR (fd.inp_type2 = 'feature' AND fd.inp_col2 IN (
          SELECT feature_id::VARCHAR FROM feature_definitions WHERE termination_dt IS NOT NULL)))
  AND fd.termination_dt IS NULL;

Run statement (b) twice

Composites can depend on other composites (two layers). The first pass terminates composites built on atomic features; the second pass catches composites built on those composites.

docs.title: 4. Check the orchestrator parameters
docs.text:
Open notebooks/backfill_orchestrator.ipynb and confirm:

Parameter Value Notes RUN_TYPE 'procedure' Use procedure, not local — see below. run_id 'big_sample_2' Must match the run_id you inserted in step 2. lookback_days 366 Agreed one-year lookback; leave as-is. platform None Leave default. subplatform None Leave default. step2_merchant_shard_fanout 1 Leave default. max_stage_retries 2 Failed steps auto-retry this many more times.

RUN_TYPE = procedure, not local

local runs the whole thing inside your notebook — which must stay alive for 4–5 days straight. procedure launches a server-side Snowflake stored procedure: fire-and-forget. You can close your laptop.

docs.title: 5. Run the notebook (fire-and-forget)
docs.text: Running the notebook kicks off the server-side procedure (for RUN_TYPE = local it instead calls backfill_orchestrator_main in-process). The notebook itself returns quickly; the real work continues on the server.

docs.title: 6. Back up the outputs when it completes
docs.text:
When the run finishes, back up these tables with a run-specific suffix (e.g. _BS2 for "Big Sample 2"):

  • TRXN_ARRAYS
  • FEATURE_DEFINITIONS
  • FEATURE_NAMES
  • OFFLINE_FEATURE_STORE
flowchart TB
    A["1 - Deploy DDL<br/>(clean slate) FIRST"]:::s --> B["2 - Insert cohort<br/>into FEATURE_BACKFILL_COHORT"]:::s
    B --> C["3 - Terminate >12-month features<br/>(atomic; composites x2)"]:::s
    C --> D["4 - Check orchestrator params<br/>(RUN_TYPE=procedure, run_id, ...)"]:::s
    D --> E["5 - Run notebook<br/>(fire-and-forget → SF procedure)"]:::s
    E --> F["6 - Back up TRXN_ARRAYS, FEATURE_DEFINITIONS,<br/>FEATURE_NAMES, OFFLINE_FEATURE_STORE (_BS2)"]:::s
    classDef s fill:#f2d492,stroke:#c99a2e,color:#3a2e05;

docs.title: Monitoring the backfill
docs.text:
Because the run is fire-and-forget, no error pops up in the notebook. Watch these instead:

Table What it tells you FEATURE_BACKFILL_PROGRESS Primary monitor. Every Step 1 / Step 2 execution with a STATUS of SUCCESS / FAILED / RUNNING. Order by started_ts desc for the latest activity on top. PROCEDURE_LOG Lower-level, job-specific detail — use when a step is stuck. TRXN_ARRAYS Watch arrays build up per merchant as a liveness signal. 
select * from AP_SBX_GBSRISK_AUTO.FEATURE_ENG.FEATURE_BACKFILL_PROGRESS
order by started_ts desc;

Auto-retry

A failed Step 2 is automatically retried up to max_stage_retries (2) more times before it's considered failed.

docs.title: Step 1 — decide if it's actually dead
docs.text:
• A step that has failed 3 times in a row is dead.
  • It can also be dead silently: no new activity for a long time in FEATURE_BACKFILL_PROGRESS or PROCEDURE_LOG, or a step stuck in RUNNING.

docs.title: Step 2 — diagnose
docs.text:
• If you see a FAILED status, read the ERROR_MESSAGE column and troubleshoot (Copilot helps).
  • A silent death (no FAILED) is harder — the usual culprits are a warehouse issue or a session timeout.

docs.title: Step 3 — kill orphaned queries
docs.text:
A failure doesn't guarantee everything stopped — child queries can be orphaned and keep running. Abort everything on the warehouse:

ALTER WAREHOUSE MSDESCI_EXT_HEAVY ABORT ALL QUERIES;

This affects teammates

This kills all queries on that warehouse, not just yours. Give your team a heads-up first.

docs.title: Step 4 — fix, then redeploy carefully
docs.text:
Fix the underlying issue. Then be very careful deploying the fix:

Do NOT lose your progress

A default deploy creates a clean slate and wipes the run so far. Make sure however you apply the fix does not re-run the full DDL drop against your in-flight cohort/progress.

docs.title: Step 5 — resume
docs.text:
Re-run the same notebook with the same run_id. The orchestrator is smart enough to read FEATURE_BACKFILL_PROGRESS and resume where it left off — so keeping the same run_id is essential.

flowchart TB
    A{"Dead?<br/>(3 fails in a row, no new activity,<br/>or stuck in RUNNING)"} -- "No" --> W["Keep monitoring"]:::ok
    A -- "Yes" --> B{"FAILED status?"}
    B -- "Yes" --> C["Read ERROR_MESSAGE → troubleshoot"]:::warn
    B -- "No (silent)" --> D["Suspect warehouse issue /<br/>session timeout"]:::warn
    C --> E["ABORT ALL QUERIES<br/>on MSDESCI_EXT_HEAVY"]:::warn
    D --> E
    E --> F["Fix the issue"]:::warn
    F --> G["Redeploy fix WITHOUT<br/>wiping progress"]:::danger
    G --> H["Re-run same notebook,<br/>SAME run_id → auto-resumes"]:::ok

    classDef ok     fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;
    classDef warn   fill:#f2d492,stroke:#c99a2e,color:#3a2e05;
    classDef danger fill:#e08a7b,stroke:#a8503f,color:#2b0c08;

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text:
Thing Value Repo / branch Feature Store / cr_agg_rmi_info-as-input Orchestrator notebook notebooks/backfill_orchestrator.ipynb DDL deploy notebook notebooks/deploy_ddl.ipynb Cohort table AP_SBX_GBSRISK_AUTO.FEATURE_ENG.FEATURE_BACKFILL_COHORT Progress monitor AP_SBX_GBSRISK_AUTO.FEATURE_ENG.FEATURE_BACKFILL_PROGRESS Low-level log AP_SBX_GBSRISK_AUTO.FEATURE_ENG.PROCEDURE_LOG Warehouse MSDESCI_EXT_HEAVY Lookback 366 days (12 months) Tables to back up on finish TRXN_ARRAYS, FEATURE_DEFINITIONS, FEATURE_NAMES, OFFLINE_FEATURE_STORE

Where this is inferred

The step sequence, parameters, SQL and recovery procedure come directly from the walkthrough and the backfill email. Schema prefixes (AP_SBX_GBSRISK_AUTO.FEATURE_ENG) are taken from the email's examples; confirm the exact database/schema for your environment (sandbox vs. prod) before running.

docs.title: Step 1 — Update Arrays
docs.text:
Step 1 builds and maintains the Transaction Arrays: per-merchant, rolling caches of daily and monthly activity. These arrays are the raw material every feature in Step 2 is calculated on.

flowchart LR
    DA[("Daily Aggregations<br/>CR_AGG_RMI_INFO (base)<br/>CR_AGG_RMI_INFO_EXPOSURE")]:::up
    PV[("Profile Variables<br/>DSLR_RISK")]:::up
    TAD[("Transaction Array<br/>Definitions<br/>(821 arrays)")]:::cfg
    S1["<b>Step 1</b><br/>Update Arrays"]:::step
    TA[("Transaction Arrays<br/>TRXN_ARRAYS<br/>(1 row / merchant)")]:::out

    DA --> S1
    PV --> S1
    TAD -. "which attrs → which arrays" .-> S1
    S1 --> TA

    classDef up   fill:#2b2b2b,stroke:#000,color:#fff;
    classDef cfg  fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#5e4e8a,color:#fff;
    classDef step fill:#f2d492,stroke:#c99a2e,color:#3a2e05;
    classDef out  fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;

docs.title: 1. Daily Aggregations (the main input)
docs.text:
Table CR_AGG_RMI_INFO (referred to as "CRAG RMI info"), in GBS_PROD_CRANALYTICS.CRAGGR.

This is not transaction-level data

It is already aggregated to one record per merchant per load date. For a given merchant on a given loaddt there is a single row holding totals/counts like gross sales amount, chargeback amount, chargeback count, etc. There are on the order of ~5,000 such variables per merchant per day (different ways of slicing every transaction — card-present, swiped, keyed, high value, same card, possibly-foreign card, government card, same-bin, …). The feature store only uses a subset of them.

Base vs. Exposure — two twin tables:

Table What it holds CR_AGG_RMI_INFO The base table — all transactions. CR_AGG_RMI_INFO_EXPOSURE The exposure table — same schema, but only transactions where Fiserv owns the risk.

Both are considered "daily aggregations". Which one an array pulls from is chosen per-array via the source_group column in the definitions table (see below).

-- illustrative: inspect one merchant for one day (filters are required or the query is very slow)
select mrch_no, platform, loaddt, dly_grs_sls_amt, dly_cr_opn_tot_disp_chgbk_amt
from GBS_PROD_CRANALYTICS.CRAGGR.CR_AGG_RMI_INFO
where loaddt = '2026-08-01'
  and merch_group_lvl = 'Outlet'
  and mrch_no = '<merchant id>'
order by loaddt, platform;

-- the exposure twin is identical except for the table name:
--   ...CRAGGR.CR_AGG_RMI_INFO_EXPOSURE

See all available columns

Because there are thousands of columns, inspect the schema row-wise instead of scrolling: select * from information_schema.columns where table_name = 'CR_AGG_RMI_INFO';

docs.title: 2. Profile Variables
docs.text:
Table DSLR_RISK ("DSLR risk data"). One record per merchant per load date, holding snapshot / inherent attributes that don't change day to day:

  • Risk monitoring channel group names (e.g. region such as Canada).
  • Account status — e.g. 13 ≈ dormant for some time; 02 / 03 ≈ terminated / off-boarded.
  • First post date — the merchant's first-ever transaction.
  • Install date — the actual boarding date.
  • Onboarding declarations such as stated annual volume and average ticket, region, etc.

These flow through to the front of the TRXN_ARRAYS row as profile columns.

docs.title: 3. Config: Transaction Array Definitions
docs.text:
The purple config table that tells the Step 1 algorithm which attributes to collect into which arrays. In the walkthrough it had 821 rows → 821 arrays maintained per merchant.

Column Meaning array_name The root array name (e.g. gross_sales_amount). source Which column from the daily-aggregation table to pull (used in a select against RMI info). source_group base or exposure — which of the twin tables to read from. cadence daily or monthly — whether to maintain a daily array, a monthly array, or both.

docs.title: Output: the Transaction Arrays table (TRXN_ARRAYS)
docs.text:
The blue output table. Its defining characteristic:

One row per merchant — for all time

There is no merchant-date grain here. Each merchant has exactly one row that is updated over time. The row starts with profile variables (from DSLR_RISK), followed by the arrays.

docs.title: Daily arrays (*_dly)
docs.text:
• Each element = one day, going back in time. The first element is the latest entry.
  • Capped at a 366-day lookback. Once full, the oldest element drops off as a new day is appended — so you only ever have up to one year of daily history.
  • The day_snapshot column tells you which date the first element corresponds to; count backwards from there.

docs.title: Monthly arrays (*_moy / "MOY")
docs.text:
• Each element = one full elapsed month, starting with the latest completed month.
  • Built by rolling up a full month of daily data once the month has elapsed. (Example: on Oct 2, to append September you roll up all of September per merchant and append it.)
  • Monthly arrays can go back up to 36 months. (Note: Step 2 only uses up to 12 months for the 366-day-lookback samples — see the backfill runbook.)
  • The month_snapshot column tells you which month the first element corresponds to; count backwards.
Reading an array (illustrative):
  account_status_moy = [ <Apr-2025>, <Mar-2025>, <Feb-2025>, <Jan-2025>, ... ]
                          ^ first element = month_snapshot
  gross_sales_amount_dly = [ <today-1>, <today-2>, <today-3>, ... up to 366 ]
                             ^ first element = day_snapshot

Sanity check: array count matches the definitions

The number of arrays in TRXN_ARRAYS equals the number of rows in the array-definitions table (821 in the walkthrough). If they diverge, a definition didn't materialise.

docs.title: Special case: the account-status monthly array (population pruning)
docs.text:
The account_status monthly array does double duty — besides being a feature input, it maintains the merchant population in TRXN_ARRAYS:

  • Inactive signals are statuses 02, 03, 13 (and blanks).
  • If a merchant has 13 consecutive months of inactive statuses or blanks, the merchant is pruned (completely removed) from TRXN_ARRAYS.

This keeps the table from growing without bound as merchants churn.

flowchart TB
    A["New month elapses"] --> B{"Last 13 months all<br/>inactive (02/03/13) or blank?"}
    B -- "Yes" --> C["Prune merchant<br/>(remove row from TRXN_ARRAYS)"]
    B -- "No"  --> D["Keep merchant;<br/>append this month to arrays"]
    classDef n fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;
    class A,C,D n;

docs.title: How Step 1 builds an array (summary)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant D as Transaction Array Definitions
    participant R as RMI daily agg (base / exposure)
    participant L as Step 1 algorithm
    participant T as TRXN_ARRAYS
    L->>D: read the 821 array definitions
    loop for each array definition
        L->>R: select <source> from <source_group> table
        alt cadence = daily
            L->>T: prepend today's value to <array>_dly (drop oldest if > 366)
        else cadence = monthly (month just elapsed)
            L->>R: roll up the full month
            L->>T: prepend the month's value to <array>_moy
        end
    end
    Note over L,T: also evaluates account_status_moy → prune merchants<br/>with 13 consecutive inactive/blank months

docs.title: Worked example: one merchant through Step 1 (illustrative)
docs.text: Follow merchant 22553150012 on load date 2026-10-01. (All numbers here are illustrative; we reuse this same merchant in Step 2 and Step 3.)

docs.title: Appending a daily value
docs.text:
One array definition says: pull DLY_GRS_SLS_AMT from the base table into a daily array.

Definition column Value array_name gross_sales_amount source DLY_GRS_SLS_AMT source_group base cadence daily

On 2026-10-01 the daily-aggregation row for this merchant has DLY_GRS_SLS_AMT = 400. Step 1 prepends it (newest first) and drops the oldest element if the array now exceeds 366:

before (day_snapshot = 2026-09-30):  gross_sales_amount_dly = [120, 0, 300, 50, ... ]   (len 366)
append today's value 400 →
after  (day_snapshot = 2026-10-01):  gross_sales_amount_dly = [400, 120, 0, 300, 50, ... ]  (oldest dropped, len 366)

The exposure twin is a separate array fed from CR_AGG_RMI_INFO_EXPOSURE (a definition with source_group = exposure). On the same day its value might be 260 → gross_sales_amount_exp_dly gets 260 prepended. Base and exposure never mix within one array.

docs.title: Rolling up a monthly value
docs.text:
Because it is now October, September 2026 has fully elapsed. For any array with cadence = monthly, Step 1 rolls up the whole month and prepends one element:

roll up all of Sep-2026 daily gross sales → 8,250
before (month_snapshot = 2026-08):  gross_sales_amount_moy = [7,900, 6,540, ... ]
after  (month_snapshot = 2026-09):  gross_sales_amount_moy = [8,250, 7,900, 6,540, ... ]

docs.title: Population check (pruning)
docs.text:
Suppose this merchant's account_status_moy reads [13, 13, '', 02, 13, 13, 13, '', 13, 02, 13, 13, 13] — 13 consecutive inactive/blank months. Step 1 would prune the merchant: its entire row is removed from TRXN_ARRAYS. (Our example merchant is active, so it stays.)

Next: Step 2 — Compute Features.

docs.title: Step 2 — Compute Features
docs.text:
Step 2 takes the Transaction Arrays and runs a large library of calculations over them to produce the canonical feature store. It is driven by two config tables: Feature Definitions (what to calculate) and Naming Conventions (how to name the results).

flowchart LR
    TA[("Transaction Arrays<br/>TRXN_ARRAYS")]:::out
    FD[("Feature<br/>Definitions")]:::cfg
    NC[("Naming<br/>Conventions")]:::cfg
    S2["<b>Step 2</b><br/>Compute Features"]:::step
    FS[("Canonical Feature Store<br/>OFFLINE_FEATURE_STORE")]:::out
    FIN[("Feature ID → Name<br/>FEATURE_NAMES")]:::out

    TA --> S2
    FD -. "the calculation per feature" .-> S2
    NC -. "abbreviations for names" .-> S2
    S2 --> FS
    S2 --> FIN

    classDef cfg  fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#5e4e8a,color:#fff;
    classDef step fill:#f2d492,stroke:#c99a2e,color:#3a2e05;
    classDef out  fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;

Scale

A training-sample request was ~300,000 features, each generated for every merchant (~3M) for every day requested. The canonical store is therefore stored long (one row per feature), not wide.

docs.title: Config: Feature Definitions
docs.text:
Every feature is one row. The key columns:

Column Meaning feature_id Unique ID for the feature. calculation The operation to perform (e.g. percent, count, average, percent_compare, max_consecutive_monotonic, ratio, …). inp_col1 First input — usually an array name; for composites, a feature ID. inp_type1 array or feature — tells the engine whether the input is an array or another feature. inp_col2 / inp_type2 A second input, for calculations that compare/combine two inputs. time_window1 The window (see time windows). operator A comparison used by the calculation (e.g. greater_than, less_than). threshold The value compared against (e.g. 0).

docs.title: Two kinds of features
docs.text:
The pipeline reuses the model world's primitive vs composite idea (here the walkthrough also called them atomic vs composite):

Kind Operates on How to read it Atomic (primitive) the arrays Self-contained — the row tells you the whole calculation. Composite other features You must look at the upstream feature IDs to know what it means.

docs.title: Time windows
docs.text:
• A plain window (e.g. 7) means the most recent N elements (last 7 days).
  • A hyphenated window (e.g. 15-28) is an offset from today — "from 15 to 28 days ago", not starting from the most recent element.

docs.title: Worked examples (illustrative feature IDs)
docs.text:
Atomic — percent (feature #11)

calculation = percent, inp_col1 = activity_dly, inp_type1 = array, time_window1 = 7, operator = greater_than, threshold = 0 → "the percent of the activity daily array over the last 7 days that was greater than zero."

Atomic — average over an offset window (feature #1132)

calculation = average, input = card-present sales count with exposure (..._cnt_..._exp), time_window1 = 15-28, operator = greater_than, threshold = 0 → "the average daily count of card-present sales (exposure) over the window 15–28 days ago, where the count was greater than zero." (EXP in the name = exposure.)

Atomic — percent_compare across two arrays (feature #1387, window 10)

Compares two arrays over the same window: → "the percent of times over this 10-day period where the declined auth amount was greater than the approved auth amount." The window is sliced over both arrays simultaneously.

Atomic — max_consecutive_monotonic (feature #116053)

calculation = max_consecutive_monotonic, input = refund counts, time_window1 = 365, operator = less_than → "the longest streak of consecutive decreases in refund counts over the last 365 days." (less_than ⇒ a decreasing streak. For the series [.. , a, b, c, ..] it finds the longest run where each element is smaller than the previous.)

Composite — ratio of two features (feature #139648)

calculation = ratio, inp_type1 = feature, inp_col1 = 227, inp_col2 = 243. Upstream: feature 227 = count of (approved auth amount > 0) over 7 days; feature 243 = same count over the 8–14 day window. → "the ratio of (approved-auth-count, last 7d) to (approved-auth-count, 8–14d ago)." e.g. 1 vs 2 ⇒ 0.5. You can't tell what a composite means without resolving its upstream features.

-- illustrative: resolve a composite by pulling the feature and its two inputs together
select * from feature_definitions
where feature_id in (139648, 227, 243);

docs.title: Config: Naming Conventions
docs.text:
Feature names are generated algorithmically by concatenating the array name + calculation + window + operator + threshold. Raw, that produces very long names (e.g. count_approved_auth_amount_7D_greater_than_0_...). The Naming Conventions table maps each verbose term → a short abbreviation so the generated names stay manageable.

  • For composite features, the generated name injects the upstream feature names (converting those inner tokens to camelCase) inside the outer snake_case name — so names can still get long.
  • The abbreviations help a lot, but some names remain long by nature.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: Step 2 produces two tables:

docs.title: 1. Feature ID → Name mapping (FEATURE_NAMES)
docs.text: Maps each feature_id to its generated name. Join it to the definitions (or to the feature store) to make either human-readable.

docs.title: 2. The canonical feature store (OFFLINE_FEATURE_STORE)
docs.text:
This is "the feature store" everyone refers to. It is stored long:

Grain & shape

  • Unique key = merchant_id + feature_date + feature_id.
  • One row per feature per merchant per feature date (values live in a single value column).
  • Not model-friendly as-is — ML training wants features as columns. It cannot be pivoted wide for all features: ~275,000 columns would collapse Snowflake. Widening only happens per-model in Step 3 after feature selection.

Sentinel value -999

A value of -999 means "not sensible / not computable" (e.g. a ratio with a zero denominator). These appear often — the data is fairly sparse. Treat -999 as a null-like default, not a real measurement.

-- illustrative: make the long store readable by joining names on
select s.merchant_id, s.feature_date, s.feature_id, n.feature_name, s.value
from offline_feature_store s
join feature_names n using (feature_id)
where s.merchant_id = '<merchant id>'
  and s.feature_date = '2026-10-01';

docs.title: Worked example: from arrays to feature rows
docs.text: Let's compute real values for merchant 22553150012 on feature_date 2026-10-01, using the arrays built in Step 1. All numbers are illustrative — the point is the arithmetic, not the values.

docs.title: The input arrays (one merchant's TRXN_ARRAYS row)
docs.text:
day_snapshot = 2026-10-01, so element 0 = Oct 1 (1 day back), element 1 = Sep 30, … The | marks the day-7 / day-8 boundary just to make the windows easy to see:

                              last 7 days          8–14 days ago
activity_dly            = [ 3, 0, 5, 2, 0, 4, 1 | 0, 0, 6, 2, 3, 0, 1 | ... up to 366 ]
approved_auth_amt_dly   = [120, 0,300,50, 0,200,80 | 0, 0,400,90,150, 0,60 | ... ]
declined_auth_amt_dly   = [ 40,10, 0,90, 0, 20,100 | 0, 5, 0, ...                 ]

card_present_sales_cnt_exp_dly   (the 15–28-days-ago slice) = [ 2,0,3,1,0,0,4,2,1,0,5,0,2,3 ]
refund_cnt_dly          (oldest → newest, one 365-day run)  = [ 5, 3, 4, 2, 1, 6, 2 ]

The engine computes atomic features first (they only need arrays), then composite features (which read other features). Here's each feature type worked out against the arrays above.

docs.title: Atomic #11 — percent of activity_dly > 0 over last 7 days
docs.text:
Window = indices 0–6 → [3, 0, 5, 2, 0, 4, 1]. Values > 0: 3, 5, 2, 4, 1 → 5 of 7.

value = 5 / 7 = 0.714

docs.title: Atomic #243 — count of approved_auth_amt_dly > 0 over the 8–14-day window
docs.text: Hyphenated window 8-14 = an offset → indices 7–13 → [0, 0, 400, 90, 150, 0, 60]. Values > 0: 400, 90, 150, 60 → 4.

docs.title: Composite #139648 — ratio of feature 227 ÷ feature 243
docs.text:
A composite reads the two feature values just computed, not the arrays:

value = #227 / #243 = 5 / 4 = 1.25

This is why composites are unreadable alone

Row 139648 only says ratio, feature, 227, 243. You must resolve 227 and 243 to know it means "approved-auth-count last-7d vs 8–14d-ago."

docs.title: Atomic #1387 — percent_compare: declined > approved over last 10 days
docs.text:
Slice both arrays over indices 0–9 and compare element-by-element:

idx approved declined declined > approved? 0 120 40 no 1 0 10 yes 2 300 0 no 3 50 90 yes 4 0 0 no 5 200 20 no 6 80 100 yes 7 0 0 no 8 0 5 yes 9 400 0 no

4 of 10 → value = 0.40.

docs.title: Atomic #1132 — average of card_present_sales_cnt_exp_dly over 15–28 days ago, where > 0
docs.text:
Slice = [2,0,3,1,0,0,4,2,1,0,5,0,2,3]. Keep only > 0: 2,3,1,4,2,1,5,2,3 (nine values, sum = 23).

value = 23 / 9 = 2.56

Interpretation of operator/threshold here

> 0 acts as a filter (average only the days that had activity), (inferred) from the phrasing in the walkthrough. If instead it averaged over all 14 days, it'd be 23/14 = 1.64 — confirm the exact semantics with the team.

docs.title: Atomic #116053 — max_consecutive_monotonic (decreasing) of refund_cnt_dly over 365 days
docs.text:
operator = less_than ⇒ find the longest run where each value is lower than the previous. On [5, 3, 4, 2, 1, 6, 2]:

5 → 3   decrease  (run: 5,3)
3 → 4   increase  (reset)
4 → 2   decrease
2 → 1   decrease  (run: 4,2,1)  ← longest
1 → 6   increase  (reset)
6 → 2   decrease  (run: 6,2)

Longest decreasing run = 3 points (4, 2, 1) → value = 3.

docs.title: The result: rows written to OFFLINE_FEATURE_STORE (long)
docs.text:
Each computed value becomes one row keyed by merchant + date + feature:

merchant_id feature_date feature_id value 22553150012 2026-10-01 11 0.714 22553150012 2026-10-01 227 5 22553150012 2026-10-01 243 4 22553150012 2026-10-01 139648 1.25 22553150012 2026-10-01 1387 0.40 22553150012 2026-10-01 1132 2.56 22553150012 2026-10-01 116053 3

When a value is -999

If feature 243 had been 0, the ratio #139648 would divide by zero → the engine writes the sentinel -999 instead of a number. With sparse data these show up a lot.

docs.title: Naming: how FEATURE_NAMES labels those rows
docs.text:
The name generator concatenates calculation + input + window + operator + threshold, applying the Naming Conventions abbreviations:

Raw term Abbreviation count cnt percent pct percent_compare pctCmp approved_auth_amount apprvAuthAmt greater_than gt 7 day / 8-14 day 7d / 8-14d feature_id generated name value 11 pct_activity_7d_gt0 0.714 227 cnt_apprvAuthAmt_7d_gt0 5 243 cnt_apprvAuthAmt_8-14d_gt0 4 1387 pctCmp_declAuthAmt_gt_apprvAuthAmt_10d 0.40 139648 ratio_cntApprvAuthAmt7dGt0_to_cntApprvAuthAmt8to14dGt0 1.25

Notice the composite name (139648) injects the two upstream names — converting those inner tokens to camelCase while the whole thing stays snake_case. That's why composite names get long.

docs.title: The whole Step-2 flow for this merchant
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["TRXN_ARRAYS row<br/>(merchant 22553150012)"]:::out
    subgraph CALC["Step 2 — per feature"]
        direction TB
        W["slice array(s)<br/>by time window"] --> OP["apply calculation<br/>(+ operator/threshold)"]
    end
    FD[("Feature Definitions")]:::cfg
    NC[("Naming Conventions")]:::cfg
    S[("OFFLINE_FEATURE_STORE<br/>7 rows for 2026-10-01")]:::out
    N[("FEATURE_NAMES<br/>id → pct_activity_7d_gt0, ...")]:::out

    A --> W
    FD -. "what to compute" .-> OP
    OP --> S
    NC -. "how to name" .-> N
    S -. "composites read<br/>prior feature values" .-> OP

    classDef cfg fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#5e4e8a,color:#fff;
    classDef out fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;

docs.title: Training vs. inference (why "long" is intentional)
docs.text:
• Training: the modelling team reads the canonical long store directly (a subset of features) and reshapes it themselves — because the exact feature set isn't known until after feature selection.
  • Inference: once a model's feature list is fixed, Step 3 pivots just those features into a wide, pretty view.
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant T as TRXN_ARRAYS
    participant D as Feature Definitions
    participant E as Step 2 engine
    participant N as FEATURE_NAMES
    participant S as OFFLINE_FEATURE_STORE
    E->>D: read feature definitions
    loop for each feature (atomic first, then composite)
        alt atomic
            E->>T: slice array(s) by time window → apply calculation
        else composite
            E->>S: read upstream feature values → combine (e.g. ratio)
        end
        E->>S: write (merchant_id, feature_date, feature_id, value)
    end
    E->>N: write feature_id → generated name

Next: Step 3 — Registration & Governance.

docs.title: Step 3 — Feature Store Registration & Governance
docs.text:
Step 3 turns the big, hard-to-read canonical feature store into wide, inference-ready views, one per model. It is the simplest step.

flowchart LR
    FS[("Canonical Feature Store<br/>OFFLINE_FEATURE_STORE")]:::out
    MFM[("Model Feature<br/>Mapping")]:::cfg
    S3["<b>Step 3</b><br/>Registration &<br/>Governance"]:::step
    FSV[("Model-specific<br/>Feature Store Views")]:::out
    CL[("Feature Store<br/>Change Log")]:::out

    FS --> S3
    MFM -. "model → its features" .-> S3
    S3 --> FSV
    S3 --> CL

    classDef cfg  fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#5e4e8a,color:#fff;
    classDef step fill:#f2d492,stroke:#c99a2e,color:#3a2e05;
    classDef out  fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;

docs.title: Config: Model Feature Mapping
docs.text:
A very simple config table: it maps a model name → the features that model needs. Models seen in the walkthrough include attrition, sales, fraud, credit.

Column Meaning model_name The model the row belongs to (e.g. fraud). feature_id A feature that model requires.

Conceptually this is a row-level mask over the canonical store: "for model X, keep only these features." Once the modelling team has finished feature selection, you simply update this table and re-run Step 3 — no feature recomputation needed.

docs.title: 1. Model-specific feature store views
docs.text:
For each model, Step 3 pivots the selected features out wide into a view that looks like what an ML pipeline expects — one column per feature, rather than the long format of the canonical store.

Why wide is possible here but not in Step 2

The canonical store can't be pivoted wide for all ~275,000 features (Snowflake would collapse). A model only needs on the order of ~100 features, so that subset pivots cleanly into a readable view.

docs.title: 2. Feature Store Change Log
docs.text: A log table (top-right of the architecture diagram) recording changes to the registered feature store (exact contents not detailed in the source — inferred to support governance/versioning).

docs.title: Snowflake feature store governance
docs.text:
Step 3 registers these views using Snowflake's built-in feature store governance tooling. That gives you version IDs for the offline store — you can select which version to view, and it controls which columns you see. This is the "registration & governance" part of the step's name.

flowchart TB
    A["Modelling team finishes<br/>feature selection"] --> B["Update Model Feature Mapping<br/>(model → feature_id list)"]
    B --> C["Run Step 3"]
    C --> D["Pivot each model's features wide"]
    D --> E["Registered, versioned<br/>model-specific views"]
    classDef n fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;
    class A,B,C,D,E n;

docs.title: Worked example: long → wide
docs.text:
Continuing merchant 22553150012 from Step 2. Suppose the fraud model, after feature selection, needs just three features: 11, 227, 1387. The modelling team updates Model Feature Mapping:

model_name feature_id fraud 11 fraud 227 fraud 1387

Step 3 reads the long canonical store rows for those feature IDs…

merchant_id feature_date feature_id value 22553150012 2026-10-01 11 0.714 22553150012 2026-10-01 227 5 22553150012 2026-10-01 1387 0.40

…joins FEATURE_NAMES, and pivots them wide into the fraud model's view — one column per feature, one row per merchant/date, exactly what an ML pipeline expects:

merchant_id feature_date pct_activity_7d_gt0 cnt_apprvAuthAmt_7d_gt0 pctCmp_declAuthAmt_gt_apprvAuthAmt_10d 22553150012 2026-10-01 0.714 5 0.40

The sales, attrition and credit models get their own views from their own rows in Model Feature Mapping — each a different, usually overlapping, subset of the same canonical store.

flowchart LR
    LONG[("OFFLINE_FEATURE_STORE (long)<br/>id 11=0.714, 227=5, 1387=0.40, ...")]:::out
    MFM[("Model Feature Mapping<br/>fraud → {11, 227, 1387}")]:::cfg
    S3["Step 3: filter to fraud's<br/>features, then pivot wide"]:::step
    VIEW[("fraud feature view (wide)<br/>1 row: 0.714 | 5 | 0.40")]:::out
    LONG --> S3
    MFM -. "which features" .-> S3
    S3 --> VIEW
    classDef cfg  fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#5e4e8a,color:#fff;
    classDef step fill:#f2d492,stroke:#c99a2e,color:#3a2e05;
    classDef out  fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;

docs.title: Training vs. inference (recap)
docs.text:
Use case Reads from Shape Why Training canonical OFFLINE_FEATURE_STORE (subset) long The feature set isn't known until after feature selection. Inference the Step 3 model-specific view wide The feature set is fixed, so it can be pivoted into a clean view.

Status at time of walkthrough

The presenter could not show a live example here because the views table was empty at the time — Step 3 output is produced on demand once a model's feature list is registered.

Next: the Backfill runbook — how to actually run the pipeline.

docs.title: Monitoring kickoff: overview
docs.text:
This section explains a kickoff meeting in which a manager hands an engineer a new project: build proactive monitoring for the risk models. It is based on an audio transcript of the meeting and a photo of the whiteboard drawn during it.

Sources and labels

  • The recording: an automatic speech-to-text transcript. It has many mis-heard words. Where I've corrected one (for example "my tricks" → TMX), the correction is listed in Transcript corrections.
  • The whiteboard photo: handwritten and partly faded. Where a word is hard to read, my reading is marked (inferred).
  • The meeting leads directly to the BRD described in Data Quality Monitoring. The last page of this section compares the two.

docs.title: The meeting in one paragraph
docs.text: The team has historically done a poor job of monitoring its models. Today the business notices a problem first ("I saw an uptick in this rule, can you look into it?"), and the team reacts. The manager wants this reversed: detect problems ourselves, early. The plan is to monitor three layers: the input data, the features and scores, and the model and rule performance. The engineer is asked to own the project end to end: write the business requirements, have them reviewed, then design and build the solution over roughly 4–6 months. It must be modular, so the same build works for Underwriting, Risk Monitoring and Clover Capital.

docs.title: The three layers, and how fast each one warns you
docs.text:
The core idea of the meeting is that each layer gives a warning at a different speed:

flowchart LR
    I["<b>1. Input data</b><br/>Is the raw data present and valid?<br/><i>fastest signal: hours</i>"]:::fast
    F["<b>2. Features & scores</b><br/>Has what the model sees or outputs shifted?<br/><i>next level: days</i>"]:::mid
    P["<b>3. Model & rule performance</b><br/>Are decisions still good?<br/><i>slowest: about 6 months</i>"]:::slow
    I --> F --> P

    classDef fast fill:#7fc1c6,stroke:#3f8389,color:#0c2b2d;
    classDef mid  fill:#f2d492,stroke:#c99a2e,color:#3a2e05;
    classDef slow fill:#e08a7b,stroke:#a8503f,color:#2b0c08;
Layer What it answers Why it is slow or fast Input data "Did a data source break or change?" Checks run as soon as data arrives. The quickest sign something is wrong. Features & scores "Is the model seeing or producing something unusual?" Needs enough applications to compare distributions. Model & rule performance "Are our decisions actually separating good from bad?" You only learn an account was bad when it is closed or terminated, often months after approval.

docs.title: Who does what
docs.text: Role Responsibility Manager (speaker, unnamed) Sets the vision and business requirements; reviews the draft. Engineer (being briefed) Owns end to end: requirements → review → architecture → implementation. Two reviewers Review the requirements. One is Jack; the other name is garbled in the transcript. They are also the people to ask how performance is reported today.

docs.title: The plan, as described
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Draft business<br/>requirements (BRD)"] --> B["Review with manager<br/>and two reviewers"]
    B --> C["Architect the<br/>solution"]
    C --> D["Implement"]
    D --> E["Quick wins first:<br/>top 5 fields per source"]
    A -. "can start now,<br/>model fields are known" .-> E

Phase 1 (input monitoring) can start before the new model is deployed, because the fields the model and rules use are already known.

docs.text: After the BRD was written, a 1:1 with the manager set the next steps: send the templates, raise a Jira ticket, and build end to end on a stand-in table. See After the BRD.
