docs.title: From kickoff to BRD
docs.text: The BRD is the engineer's first deliverable from this meeting. This page checks it against what the manager asked for. It also notes what the meeting reveals about the Underwriting service documented elsewhere on this site.

docs.title: Coverage: what the meeting asked for vs the BRD draft
docs.text:
Statuses: Covered · Partly · Missing · Later BRD (planned for a later part of the series).

# Asked for in the meeting BRD draft status Notes 1 Be proactive; monitor three layers Covered Executive summary and problem statement match closely; the BRD series follows the three layers. 2 Reusable across UW, Risk Monitoring, Clover Capital Covered Stated as a single modular architecture. 3 Day 1 monitors the A1 dataset; per-source datasets on Day 2 Missing The BRD has a placeholder Snowflake path. Naming A1 as the first target would make Phase 1 concrete. 4 Only fields used in the model or rules Missing An important scope limit (TMX: about 50 of 2,000 fields). Worth stating explicitly. 5 Quick win: top 5 fields per source first Missing A natural Phase 1a. 6 Alert on a rise in "no hit" responses (e.g. Experian) Partly No check type fits exactly. A "no hit" is a response status, not a null value, so Missing Values won't catch it. Needs a rate check on the no-hit flag. 7 Detect new enumerations Partly The Accepted Values check type covers it once each field's allowed values are listed. 8 Drift in application fields (avg ticket, annual sales) Conflict See below. 9 Alerts: when, who, what volume Partly Frequency is set (hourly). Recipients and expected volume are not. 10 A "generate report" button for stakeholders, including FSI/PSI Partly The BRD has a scheduled weekly report. The on-demand report isn't mentioned. 11 PSI with 10 score bands; decide how often the baseline is refreshed Partly Benchmark is "Date". Band count and refresh cadence are open. 12 Component scores and final score; raw and weighted versions Partly The Feature_Scores tab lists FICO, Phone Health, IDT Score, etc., but doesn't separate component from final, or raw from weighted. 13 Read features, scores and rules from the model service JSON output Missing The BRD refers to generic "Snowflake paths". The meeting names one consistent source. 14 A reference table (table, field, check) so a new source needs only new rows Partly The spreadsheet is effectively this table. The BRD could say so outright. 15 Performance definition: closed / terminated = bad Later BRD Planned "Model Performance Monitoring" part. 16 AUC, Gini, KS, % bads captured at a configurable cutoff Later BRD Same. 17 Rule hit / no-hit bad rates Later BRD Planned "Rule Monitoring" part.

docs.title: The one real conflict: drift on input data
docs.text:
• The meeting: the whiteboard lists drift analysis directly under the input data sources, and the manager gives average ticket and annual sales as examples.
  • The BRD: Part 1 says input monitoring involves no comparison between a benchmark population and the active population. Drift is moved to feature & score monitoring.

Both are defensible. Average ticket and annual sales are raw inputs and model features, so drift on them could live in either layer. But the BRD should either include input drift, or say clearly that it was moved to Part 2 and why, so the manager doesn't think it was dropped.

docs.title: Questions the meeting already answers
docs.text:
Several items in the BRD review notes are settled, or nearly, by what the manager said:

Review note What the meeting says #1 Blocking or after-the-fact Monitoring reads the model service's JSON output, which exists only after a decision. So it is after-the-fact monitoring. BO-01's "before being consumed by models" should be reworded. #5 Availability checks The "no hit" rate is exactly this kind of check: data that silently stops arriving. Tool choice (implementation guide) The manager names Great Expectations, which tips the choice toward Option A. #4 FSI/CSI criteria The manager describes PSI as 10 score bands, baseline % vs new %: an index, not a directional percentage.

docs.title: What the meeting reveals about the Underwriting service
docs.text:
The whiteboard's onboarding flow is the Underwriting decisioning service seen from the business side. It fills in a few gaps:

From the meeting Matches on this site MRD (formerly Diligence) sends the application by API The "External service (MRD, RASI, …)" at step 1. Model service output: JSON with header, scores, features, decision The "Full UW output structure" the rules engine writes to S3 at step 5a, then loaded into the Snowflake history table. This is the data the monitoring platform should read. Component scores, one per available source The primitive Lambdas, e.g. idt-lexis-neustar-cert. Final score = linear combination of the components The lane aggregate Lambdas (idt-aggregate-cert, …). New detail: the aggregate is a weighted sum, with weights depending on which sources were available (inferred). Up to 5 scores for IDT, up to 3 for credit IDT has 4 sources + 1 final = 5; Credit has 2 sources + 1 final = 3. This matches the state machine exactly (inferred). MF would also be 5. Raw score (probability) and a weighted score Not yet documented on the UW pages.

docs.title: Suggested additions to the BRD
docs.text:
1. Name A1 as the Day 1 data source and describe the Day 2 per-source datasets.
  2. Add the scope rule: only fields used in the model or rules, starting with the top 5 per source.
  3. Add a "no hit rate" check type (a rate of a response status, compared over time).
  4. Resolve the input drift conflict above.
  5. Name the model service JSON output (through the Snowflake history table) as the source for features, scores and rules.
  6. Add an on-demand report requirement alongside the weekly schedule.
  7. List alert recipients and an expected alert volume per day.
  8. In the Feature_Scores tab, separate component vs final scores and raw vs weighted.

docs.title: What was discussed
docs.text: The meeting, organised by topic rather than in the order things were said. Quotes are paraphrased from the transcript and lightly cleaned up.

docs.title: 1. Why this project exists
docs.text:
• Monitoring has historically been weak. Problems reach the team only when the business notices a rule behaving oddly: "Hey, I saw an uptick in this rule. Can you look into it?"
  • The business only sees rules. Stakeholders don't get the model scores or features today, so a problem upstream is invisible until it changes a rule outcome.
  • The goal is to be proactive, both internally and externally: find data problems quickly, and tell the business before they notice.
  • The manager calls this "a vision since day one" that the team never got to.

docs.title: 2. Input data (layer 1)
docs.text:
What to monitor first. For the initial release the input is the A1 dataset: a consolidated set of fields the team has needed in the past, chosen because it's easy to deploy. Later, in the "native deployment" (Day 2), each data source gets its own dataset: LexisNexis, GNF response, application, and so on.

The tool. The manager specifically mentions Great Expectations.

What should trigger an alert. Examples given:

Trigger Example Why it matters Rise in "no hit" responses More applicants come back from Experian with no record A broken integration (for example, badly formatted names sent to the bureau) or a population change. Either way the model loses an input. Drift in application fields Average ticket or annual sales shifts over time The applicants look different from before. New enumerations A categorical field gets a value never seen before The model may handle an unknown category badly and produce an unexpected value. Population change The mix of applicants changes The model was built on a different population.

Scope: only the fields that matter. Monitor only fields used in the model or in rules. TMX alone sends about 2,000 fields and the model uses about 50. Two consequences:

  • Phase 1 can start now, even before the new model is deployed, because the used fields are already known.
  • Quick win: start with the five most important fields per data source, rather than all of them (around 250).

docs.title: 3. Alerts
docs.text:
The manager lists three open questions (circled on the board):

  • When to alert?
  • Who to alert?
  • What volume of alerts to expect? Too many and they get ignored.

Alerts go to the team (internal). The team then tells stakeholders when something matters: "I noticed you had an increase here; that's something we should keep an eye on."

docs.title: 4. Features & scores (layer 2)
docs.text:
Features are either raw fields or transformations of them. This applies to the new model only, not the legacy one.

How an application gets scored. This is the centre of the whiteboard (redrawn here):

  1. An onboarding application comes into MRD (previously called Diligence), the platform for decisioning and managing applications.
  2. It lands in a table, calls third-party data, and comes back into MRD.
  3. MRD sends an API request to the model service.
  4. The model service retrieves the model, works out which features it needs and calculates them, scores, then runs the rules to reach a decision.
  5. It returns one JSON object per application: a header, the scores, the features and the decision. The manager calls this "a really rich data set".

Scores are plural. There are three model suites: identity theft, merchant fraud and credit risk, so at minimum three scores. Within each suite:

  • The service checks what data it has: LexisNexis, the bureau, the application, TMX.
  • For each available source it produces a component score.
  • The final score is a linear combination (a weighted sum) of the component scores.
  • Identity theft can have up to five scores; credit up to three.
  • Each score comes as a raw score (a probability) and a weighted version.

Stability measures. For features, a Feature Stability Index (FSI/CSI). For scores, a Population Stability Index (PSI): split scores into 10 bands and compare the share of the baseline population in each band with the share of the new population. The manager is "not the biggest fan" of these indices, but they exist and stakeholders expect them in reports. Open questions: how often is the baseline updated (monthly?), and should the team watch drift or changes in values? The engineer is asked to recommend what's best.

The PSI calculation is worked through on the Feature & score monitoring page.

docs.title: 5. Reporting
docs.text: There is a formal report to stakeholders, and the manager wants this system to produce it. The picture is a "generate report" button that outputs things like FSI and PSI on demand. This is separate from the internal alerts.

docs.title: 6. Model & rule performance (layer 3)
docs.text:
This layer needs a feedback loop: outcomes for accounts that were approved.

The performance definition. For every approved application, check whether the account was later closed or terminated. Those are bad. Accounts that were not closed or terminated are good. This definition has to be coded up, and other data will be needed to support it. Outcomes take time to appear, which is the "six-month lag".

Model metrics named on the board:

Metric What it measures How to read it AUC The chance that a randomly chosen bad account gets a riskier score than a randomly chosen good one. 0.5 = no better than chance; 1.0 = perfect. Gini The same information rescaled: Gini = 2 × AUC − 1. 0 = no better than chance; 1 = perfect. AUC 0.75 → Gini 0.50. KS The biggest gap, at any score cutoff, between the share of all bads flagged and the share of all goods flagged. KS 0.40 means at the best cutoff you flag 40 percentage points more of the bads than of the goods. % bads captured at 5% Take the riskiest 5% of applicants by score. What share of all bads are in that group? Higher is better. A random model captures about 5%.

Worked example (illustrative): 10,000 approved accounts, of which 200 turned bad. Sort by risk score and take the riskiest 5%, which is 500 accounts. If 60 of the 200 bads are among them, the model captures 30% of bads in 5% of the population, six times better than random. The manager wants the 5% to be configurable: credit might use 1% instead.

docs.title: Rule performance
docs.text:
For each rule, compare the accounts where it fired (hit) with those where it didn't (no hit):

Rule R (illustrative) Accounts Bad (closed / terminated) Good Bad rate Hit 400 40 360 10.0% No hit 9,600 160 9,440 1.7%

Accounts that hit this rule go bad about six times as often as those that don't, so the rule is doing its job. If the two bad rates converge over time, the rule is losing value.

A catch with declined applications (my addition)

Outcomes only exist for approved accounts. A rule that declines an application leaves no outcome to measure, so this table works best for rules that flag or refer without fully blocking. It is worth raising with the reviewers when asking how they measure rule performance today.

The manager suggests asking the two reviewers how they currently report on performance, and expects this layer to take the next four to six months.

docs.title: 7. Build it once, reuse it everywhere
docs.text:
• The model service's JSON output has the same structure across all three solutions, so features, scores and rules can always be read from it. "That's fantastic."
  • Different per solution: the definition of bad (Underwriting vs Clover Capital), and the input data.
  • Configure, don't code. Keep a reference table listing, for each data source, which table, which fields, and which checks. Adding a data source should mean updating that table and nothing else. The manager points to Austin's feature store as the example of doing this well.
  • "Think: what happens if I swap out a data source? How will that break everything here?" Because "we're never going to be static as a company".

docs.title: 8. What Clover Capital is
docs.text: Clover Capital offers credit to merchants. It starts from the merchants already covered by risk monitoring: the team decides whether to pre-approve / pre-qualify a merchant for an offer. When a merchant then applies, the application goes through underwriting, with a different set of underwriting models from the ones documented on this site.

docs.title: Transcript corrections
docs.text:
The speech-to-text made a number of mistakes. These are my readings:

In the transcript Most likely meant "my tricks" (2,000 fields) TMX (ThreatMetrix) "no hit responses from experience" from Experian (the bureau) "new animations" new enumerations (unseen category values) "Clown Capital" Clover Capital "CFI or a feature stability index" CSI / FSI "fields in model or intervals" fields in model or in rules (as on the board) "a six month black" a six-month lag "write articles" raw attributes (inferred) "bad termite", "a battery" bad / terminated, bad rate (inferred) "what's monitoring" risk monitoring (inferred) "Shira's", "Shirafsi" a reviewer's name; unclear

The bracket labels this group "descriptive". ‒ raw / ‒ transformations / ‒ Scores Features come in two kinds: raw fields and transformations of them. Then there are the scores. → FSI, → PSI The two stability measures for this layer: Feature Stability Index (also called CSI) and Population Stability Index. docs.title: C. Alerting questions (circled, top right)
docs.text:
When to alert? Who to alert to? Volume of alerts

These are open design questions the manager wants answered. Alerts are internal (to the team), and the number of alerts matters: too many and people stop reading them.

docs.title: D. The onboarding flow (centre)
docs.text:
This is the clearest part of the board. It shows how an application becomes a decision:

flowchart LR

    MRD <--> TP["3rd Party Data<br/>(bureau, LN, TMX, ...)"]:::ext

docs.text:
Circles for IDT (identity theft) and MF (merchant fraud). Under IDT: "What data?", branching into the sources, each labelled "if yes", and joining into Final score:

docs.title: After the BRD: overview
docs.text:
This section covers a 1:1 with the manager held the day after the BRD walkthrough. The meeting answers the question "the BRD is written, what happens now?" It turns the proposal into concrete next steps: who to email, what ticket to raise, which table to build on, what the reports must look like, and how the hourly alerts get sent.

Source and labels

This section is based on an automatic speech-to-text transcript, which garbles names and table names. Spellings I'm unsure of are marked (spelling uncertain). Anything I've worked out rather than heard is marked (inferred). See Transcript corrections.

docs.title: The meeting in one paragraph
docs.text:
The team has a lot of model deployments in the next ~45 days, and deployments remain the priority for the next couple of weeks. Monitoring continues in parallel. On monitoring, the manager wants three things now:

  1. Socialise the BRD. Send the two templates to everyone and raise a Jira ticket so the modelling team fills them in for the new Underwriting models.
  2. Don't wait for them. Build the whole thing end to end on a stand-in table that already refreshes every 15 minutes.
  3. Make it real. Turn the filled-in Excel template into running checks. Produce clean, fixed-layout reports, and send hourly email alerts from AWS (Lambda + SNS).

The first review is on Friday, 12:30–1:00 pm.

Updated by the Implementation Support Document

The model team's implementation document for UW US V2 gives the go-live dates (A1: 15 October 2026, A2: January 2027), names the Day 1 Snowflake tables, and links a field mapping sheet the comparison checks need. See Implementation Support Document.

Updated by a stakeholder email

An email from Michelle Davis sets the first focus (the A2 input, from January; A1 today) and adds two requirements: compare raw data with the payload, and alert when a dataset gets no activity. See Requirements update.

Updated by a later check-in

A follow-up conversation changed how to ask for the templates, added a test plan for the alerting, and set a target: fully automated in about three weeks. See Check-in: templates, test plan & timeline.

docs.title: Deployment context
docs.text:
The first part of the 1:1 was about deployments. It explains why monitoring is "in parallel" rather than the main job for now.

  • Upcoming work in ~45 days: the lift-and-shift model, a new EWS solution, new models, and GNF. The manager is worried about becoming a bottleneck.
  • Primitive models: you have already deployed, merged and tested them, including checking the outputs on AWS. The composite models come next (RN is finishing other work first).
  • Learning goal: shadow Amok and Austin on every deployment. The aim is to deploy with RN alone if both are out, "not day one, but pretty soon". Long term, everyone should deploy and support both real-time and batch.
  • Branching, as the manager understands it (confirm with Amok):
flowchart LR
    DEV["Developer<br/>feature work"] -- "merge request" --> STG["<b>staging</b><br/>(treated as the feature branch;<br/>stays here through cert)"]
    STG -- "deployment team adds CI/CD<br/>changes, merges at prod" --> MAIN["<b>main</b><br/>(production only)"]

Developers merge into staging. The deployment team handles staging → main, adding what CI/CD needs before the merge. While a model is in cert, it stays in staging; main is only touched for production.

docs.title: Resend the templates
docs.text:
The first message assumed too much. The reader got a link and had to work out which sheet to fill and how. Fix three things:

Problem Fix A link to a workbook, with no titles Two separate files, each named for what it is No instruction One sentence: for each table you want tracked, fill in both files No date Ask for an ETA

Suggested file names:

  • Template to be filled - Input data monitoring.xlsx
  • Template to be filled - Feature, rule and score monitoring.xlsx

Add a short "How to fill this in" note at the top of each file, with one example row. The reader has seen the template once, in a meeting.

docs.title: Test plan while you wait
docs.text:
The goal is to prove that every part works: template → check → result → email. The values themselves don't matter yet.

Rule Why One check of each type Proves the parser and the SQL for every check type in the template. One field per type is enough A few columns only "Take a few columns, take a shot at it." You don't need to know which columns matter yet Tight criteria An alert should fire rarely. A loose threshold on a 15-minute table can send hundreds of emails Force one failure on purpose Set one threshold you know will be breached, once, to see the email arrive. Then tighten it again Stateful alerts Email when an alert opens or resolves, not every hour it stays open (alert lifecycle) Send to yourself first Subscribe only your own address until the alerts behave

A starting set, one row per check type. Columns are placeholders until you've picked them:

Check type Example column (inferred) Tight criterion for testing Missing Values An ID that is always filled Fail if > 50% missing Field Population A usually-filled field Fail if < 10% populated Acceptable Range An amount Fail if any value is outside a very wide range Accepted Values Final status Fail on a value outside the known list Expected Format A date or timestamp Fail if > 20% don't match Duplicate Values Application ID + status timestamp Fail if > 5% duplicated Value Length An ID Fail if the length is outside a wide band Data Type A numeric field Fail if > 20% aren't numeric Placeholder Value An amount Fail if > 50% are -999 Freshness / volume Last-updated timestamp Fail if no rows changed in 3 hours

The step-by-step build for this is on POC: getting started.

The manager offered to help set the first thresholds. Bring this table, with the real column names filled in, to the next catch-up.

docs.text:

Week Monitoring work Done when 1 Templates resent with an ETA. Columns chosen. Simple report view A test alert email arrives from AWS on a schedule 3 Template is plug and play. Real UW templates loaded if they have arrived A new filled-in template runs with no code change

Check-ins run through all three weeks: every other day, 10 minutes is enough. Bring what moved, what is blocked, and one question.

Leave

The day off on Monday 19 October stands, and the manager offered an extra day if you want it. It falls inside week 2, so plan the Lambda work around it.

docs.title: Who will use it
docs.text:
The manager gave the reason for the deadline: in a few weeks there may be "a real use case". Compliance, model risk management (MRM) and the teams handling partner-bank reporting will ask for these reports in a standard, templated form.

This shapes the report design:

  • Templated: the same layout for every model and table, so a reviewer learns it once.
  • Clean: a summary first, detail on request (the fixed pages).
  • Repeatable: the same template always gives the same checks. That is what "plug and play" buys.

docs.title: The framework: design and status
docs.text:
The data quality framework is built from scratch in the dq-framework/ folder. It serves both Underwriting (hourly data checks on the A1 record) and feature and score monitoring, including the Risk Monitoring feature store (daily PSI / CSI drift). It runs as an AWS Lambda; during development, the AWS side runs on your machine in LocalStack, and Snowflake is always the real account.

This page summarises the design and the status. For the details, see DQ Framework: How It Works (setup, configuration, running, each module) and Lift & Shift to AWS.

docs.title: What runs where
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph AWS["AWS (production) / LocalStack (development)"]
        EB["<b>EventBridge</b><br/>hourly at :20<br/>daily at 01:30"]:::aws --> L["<b>Lambda: dqf</b><br/>Python + Great Expectations"]:::aws
        S3[("<b>S3</b><br/>dq_config.yaml")]:::cfg -. "checks + rules" .-> L
        SM[("<b>Secrets Manager</b><br/>Snowflake login")]:::cfg -. "key pair" .-> L
        L --> SNS["<b>SNS topic</b>"]:::alert --> MAIL["Email subscribers"]:::alert
    end
    L -- "Snowflake connector:<br/>read-only queries,<br/>only counts come back" --> SF[("<b>Snowflake</b><br/>monitored tables")]:::snow
    L -- "one row per check" --> RES[("<b>DQ_RESULT</b><br/>Snowflake")]:::out
    RES --> APP["<b>Report</b><br/>Streamlit"]:::out

    classDef aws fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3e10,color:#fff;
    classDef cfg fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#57498a,color:#fff;
    classDef alert fill:#a8503f,stroke:#7a3527,color:#fff;
    classDef snow fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;
    classDef out fill:#54802D,stroke:#3a5a1e,color:#fff;
Piece Production (AWS) Development (your machine) Lambda Container image from ECR LocalStack Lambda, code folder mounted (LocalStack's free edition has no ECR) Schedules EventBridge rules, hourly and daily The same rules, off by default; invoked by hand Configuration (dq_config.yaml) S3 bucket created by the stack The same, in LocalStack's S3 Snowflake login Secrets Manager The same, in LocalStack's Secrets Manager, filled from .env Alerts SNS topic, email subscribers LocalStack's SNS (readable from a queue) and email to a local inbox Snowflake The real account The real account Infrastructure infra/cloudformation.yaml, Target=aws The same template, Target=localstack

One template and one code package serve both. Only Target changes, so what is tested locally is what goes to AWS.

docs.title: Why LocalStack 4.9
docs.text:
Option Outcome LocalStack, current release (2026.10) Refuses to start without an account token. Its free plan is for non-commercial use only LocalStack 4.9, the last open-source community release Starts without an account; Apache 2.0 licence, so work use is allowed; has Lambda, S3, SNS, SQS, Secrets Manager, EventBridge and CloudFormation. Chosen What 4.9 lacks ECR, so container-image Lambdas. Locally the Lambda runs from a mounted folder; in AWS it is an image

The image is needed in AWS anyway: the dependencies (Great Expectations, the Snowflake connector, pandas, pyarrow) are about 490 MB installed, above Lambda's 250 MB limit for zip packages.

docs.title: Two schedules, two kinds of check
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    W["<b>dq_config.yaml</b>"]:::cfg --> SRC["<b>Sources</b><br/>table, timestamp column,<br/>schedule, row filter"]:::cfg
    SRC --> H["<b>hourly</b> sources<br/>the previous full hour"]:::run
    SRC --> D["<b>daily</b> sources<br/>the previous full day"]:::run
    H --> CH["<b>Checks</b><br/>missing, range, values, format,<br/>duplicates, length, placeholders,<br/>volume, freshness, business rules,<br/>comparison with a source"]:::chk
    D --> CH
    D --> ST["<b>Stability</b><br/>PSI for scores, CSI for features:<br/>the last N days against a benchmark"]:::chk

    classDef cfg fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#57498a,color:#fff;
    classDef run fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3e10,color:#fff;
    classDef chk fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;
Use Source schedule Typical checks Underwriting input (A1 record) hourly Missing and invalid values, data-source hit rates ('CY'), the SSN_TAX_ID_MATCH derivation, no-activity Underwriting output hourly, with ROW_FILTER = scored population Scores 300–900, decision consistent with score, model used consistent with available data Payload against raw data hourly SOURCE_COVERAGE, MATCHES_SOURCE, LOST_IN_MAPPING Score and feature drift daily PSI per score, CSI per feature, against a benchmark period Risk Monitoring feature store daily, on each model's feature view Merchants per day, today's load arrived, missing features, CSI per top feature

PSI / CSI. Numeric fields are cut into bins at the benchmark's quantiles; categorical fields use the benchmark's most common values plus "other"; missing values get their own bin. The index is Σ (active share − benchmark share) × ln(active share ÷ benchmark share). It is computed in Snowflake, and Great Expectations judges it against the limits: WARN at 0.10 (shown in the report), FAIL at 0.25 (alerts). The SQL was checked against an independent numpy calculation and gives the same numbers.

docs.title: Great Expectations' own report (Data Docs)
docs.text: Every run also writes GX's standard HTML report: an index of runs, and a page per group of checks showing each expectation, its result and the measured value. On a laptop it goes to build/data_docs/site/index.html (make docs serves it at http://localhost:8777/index.html); the Lambda writes it to the stack's S3 bucket under data_docs/ (make local-docs prints the LocalStack URL). Example bad values are removed, so no customer data ends up in the report: only counts.

docs.title: The sample table
docs.text: sql/02_sample_table.sql creates one table, DQF_DB.DQF.UW_A1_RECORD, shaped like the A1 record in the Implementation Support Document: application fields, the inquiry status of each data source, model features, exclusions, and the model output. It holds 60 days of made-up data, so the drift checks have a benchmark period. Problems are planted in known hours (missing values, a wrong SSN_TAX_ID_MATCH, an Experian outage, duplicates, three silent hours, scores out of range) and drift in the last week (score, ticket size, channel mix). make test-snowflake checks that each one is caught by the right check and by nothing else.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
Part Status Code, configuration reader (YAML, Excel, CSV), business rules, check planning, alert logic Unit-tested PSI / CSI calculation Checked against numpy The CloudFormation template on LocalStack Deployed and run: the Lambda sent a test alert through SNS and by email The AWS container image Built and invoked locally Your Snowflake account Run (2026-10-17): key-pair login; hourly (23 checks) and daily (8 checks, PSI / CSI) runs; 12 of 14 planted-problem tests passed, the 2 misses were a sample-data bug, since fixed The Lambda in LocalStack against your Snowflake Run: secret from Secrets Manager, configuration from S3, results in Snowflake, alert through SNS and email GX's own HTML report (Data Docs) Run: written locally and, from the Lambda in LocalStack, to S3 A real AWS deployment Not done. No AWS access yet; infra/deploy.sh with the same template. Plan: Lift & Shift to AWS

The earlier dq-poc code, which POC: getting started describes, is replaced by this framework.

docs.title: Implementation Support Document: UW US V2
docs.text:
The Model Implementation Support Document for the Underwriting US V2 release, the two field mapping spreadsheets it links to, and the Merchant Underwriting Workflow slide describe the new models end to end: where the data comes from, what the model service does with it, what it returns, and how the release must be tested and signed off.

This page summarises them and draws out what they mean for data quality monitoring.

Source and labels

Based on photos of the documents (a draft dated 9-7-2026, 28 pages, marked Fiserv Restricted) and of the spreadsheets and slide. Some sections are still templates with placeholders. Anything worked out rather than stated is marked (inferred). Keep this site internal.

docs.title: In one paragraph
docs.text: Version 2.0 releases three model suites (Merchant Fraud, Identity Theft, Credit Risk) and a new framework on AWS and Snowflake. MRD collects the application and every third-party and internal source, then calls the model service. The model service checks eligibility, builds features, scores component models per data source, combines them into score-of-scores models, calibrates to a 300–900 score, generates reason codes, applies the rules and returns a decision. Day 1 (15 October 2026) runs on the existing A1 record with 56 added input fields and 11 new output fields; Day 2 (January 2027) moves to the A2 record carrying the full response from each source. The document ends with testing and release sign-off requirements, which include monitoring and alerting being operational.

docs.text:
To make Day 1 easier to deploy, the new models use the existing A1 input record, with 56 fields added. They are listed in AWS_US_INPUT_MAPPING_NEW_UW_MODEL_DEVELOPMENT_V6.xlsx, tab Main, rows 377–432.

One field is derived: SSN_TAX_ID_MATCH, from the first principal's application data.

SSN Tax ID SSN_TAX_ID_MATCH Present Present, identical "1" Present Present, different "0" Missing or missing "Z"

docs.title: Day 1: the A1 output record and the display
docs.text:
• Output fields: AWS_US_OUTPUT_MAPPING_NEW_UW_MODEL_DEVELOPMENT_V1.xlsx.
  • An extra display of auto-approval reason codes and actions, one line per control group: Policy and Business, AML (KYC principal), AML (KYC secondary), AML (KYB), with "Passed" or "Not passed" and the negative reasons (for example 22A LexisNexis consumer verification, 32A Neustar phone not linked to the business, 33A EWS bank account not verified). On Day 1 the codes alone, without descriptions, are enough.
  • Client routing: US_UW_Model_Routing.xlsx.

docs.text: The API call will carry the full payload response from each source plus a header record. The layout is in New Model Service Output Structure V0.1.xlsx (Decision Science SharePoint, Data Layouts and Dictionaries).

docs.text:
Input mapping (AWS_US_INPUT_MAPPING_NEW_UW_MODEL_DEVELOPMENT, tabs Main and Audit Log): one row per model field, with where its value comes from.

Group Controls G0 Policy and business G1 AML (KYC principal) G2 AML (KYC secondary principals) G3 AML (KYB) G4 Negative and restricted: GNF G5 Negative and restricted: other G6 Identity theft G7 Fraud G8 Credit G9 Bespoke for SMS / banking partners

The output column is headed "Actimize Derived Field Name". Actimize is presumably the platform these fields were first derived in (inferred).

docs.title: Who is scored
docs.text:
• Excluded: additional outlets, and WISO. The A1 model is not called for them; a separate framework decides them. On Day 2 the team may move all auto-decisions into the A1 framework.
  • The score choices are configurable.

docs.title: Segmentation, components and score of scores
docs.text:
• No segmentation: one model per suite (Merchant Fraud, Identity Theft, Credit Risk).
  • Component models (CS_…) score one data source each, but only when that source has enough data:
Source Minimum data needed to score Application and GNF None Experian and BizID bureau inquiry status = CY and BizID inquiry status = CY LexisNexis / Neustar CLN inquiry status = CY and NEU inquiry status = CY ThreatMetrix request ID present and not ZZ, and request result = success
  • Score-of-scores models (SS_…) combine the component scores that are available. Component scores are calibrated before they are combined.

docs.title: Calibration and alignment
docs.text:
Parameter Value Base score 600 Base odds 20 PDO (points to double the odds) 20 Score range 300 to 900 Higher score means Lower risk

Each component model has alignment parameters, a multiplier and an additive factor, configurable through a platform list and expected to change about once a year. The defaults are multiplier 1 and additive 0, and the aligned score is truncated. This is the MODEL_ALIGNMENT lookup table that Aryan's change to the MF Aggregate Lambda reads from S3.

docs.title: What it means for data quality monitoring
docs.text: Finding What it changes Day 1 went live on 15 October 2026, on the A1 record Monitoring is now needed for live data, not only for January. The A1 tables are the first real target The A1 output Snowflake table and a Full response Snowflake table exist from Day 1 The first real tables to point the template at. The full-response table is most likely the raw data Michelle wants compared with the payload (inferred) The input mapping spreadsheet lists model field, source, raw field name and raw file This is the mapping sheet the comparison checks (MATCHES_SOURCE, LOST_IN_MAPPING) need. Its rows translate almost directly into template rows 56 new A1 input fields (rows 377–432) The first fields to put under input checks: they are new, so most likely to arrive empty or mis-mapped SSN_TAX_ID_MATCH has three valid values An ACCEPTED_VALUES check ('1','0','Z'), and a business rule that recomputes it from SSN and Tax ID Minimum data criteria per source (CY statuses, ThreatMetrix request result) A hit rate per source: the share of applications where each source had enough data to be scored. A drop is the "provider stopped returning data" signal Exclusions (additional outlets, WISO) are not scored by A1 Checks on scored data must leave them out, or volume and missing-value checks will mis-fire Scores are 300–900, higher is lower risk The existing FINAL_SCORE_IN_RANGE rule matches. The same range applies to component and aligned scores Alignment defaults are multiplier 1, additive 0 A check on MODEL_ALIGNMENT: values present for every model, client and channel in use, and within sensible bounds Reason-code groups G0–G9 Output monitoring (Phase 2): how often each group fires, per hour or day Experian bureau will be replaced by Equifax Expect volume and missing-value changes on bureau fields; plan the switch in the template Release readiness requires monitoring and alerting to be operational The DQ framework is part of what the release is signed off on, not an extra Test types include null, malformed, duplicate and mapping cases The same check types run in production by the DQ framework; its results can serve as evidence

docs.title: Building the MVP, end to end
docs.text: The manager's ask: "take in the input as a data frame, those parameters, and create a report", then send hourly alerts from AWS. This page breaks that into parts you can build and demo, starting with the stand-in table.

docs.title: Step 1: load and reshape
docs.text:
The BRD template is a wide grid: one row per variable, three columns per check type (Check?, Criteria, Alert?). Code works better with a long list, with one row per (variable, check):

Template (wide) → Check specs (long) Variable Missing Values Criteria Alert? … Variable Check type Criteria Alert Avg Ticket Yes > 30% Yes Avg Ticket MISSING_VALUES > 30% Yes Avg Ticket Avg Ticket ACCEPTABLE_RANGE (<=$0 >=$10000) No

Rows where Check? is No are dropped.

docs.title: Step 2: validate the template ("cross-validation")
docs.text:
The manager asked you to "make sure everything is covered". Validate the template before running anything, and send the problems back to whoever filled it in:

Validation Example problem caught The table (Snowflake path) exists and you can read it Typo in the path; missing grant Every variable exists as a column in that table AVG_TCKET instead of AVG_TICKET The check type is a known one "Missing" instead of "Missing Values" The criteria can be parsed (Step 3) >= 30 with no % on a percentage check The criteria fit the column type A numeric range on a text column Check? = Yes has criteria; Alert? = Yes has Check? = Yes Alert switched on for a check that doesn't run No duplicate (variable, check) rows The same check entered twice with different thresholds Coverage "50 fields identified, 12 have no checks" (this goes on the summary page)

The validation result is itself a deliverable. It is what the summary page reports as "what we started with".

docs.title: Step 3: parse the criteria
docs.text:
The criteria are free text, written by people. The manager called out the hard parts: "less than equal, greater than equal, single quotes, double quotes". Define a small, strict grammar, and reject anything outside it with a clear message (rather than guessing).

Written in template Means Parsed to > 30% FAIL if more than 30% of rows {op: ">", value: 0.30, unit: "pct"} < 70% FAIL if less than 70% {op: "<", value: 0.70, unit: "pct"} (<=0 >=15) FAIL if a value is ≤ 0 or ≥ 15 (outside the allowed range) {fail_le: 0, fail_ge: 15} (<=$0 >=$10000) Same, with currency symbols {fail_le: 0, fail_ge: 10000} ('01','02','03') or ("01","02","03") Allowed values. Quotes keep 01 as text, not the number 1 {allowed: ["01","02","03"]} ≠ 8 char / = 8 Length must be 8 {length: 8} ^\d{8}$ Must match this pattern {regex: "^\\d{8}$"} 
import re

NUM = r"\$?(-?[\d,]+(?:\.\d+)?)"

def parse_criteria(check_type: str, text: str) -> dict:
    t = text.strip().replace("≤", "<=").replace("≥", ">=")
    if check_type in {"MISSING_VALUES", "FIELD_POPULATION", "PLACEHOLDER", "DUPLICATE_VALUES"}:
        m = re.fullmatch(r"(<=|>=|<|>)\s*" + NUM + r"\s*(%?)", t)
        if not m:
            raise ValueError(f"{check_type}: expected e.g. '> 30%', got {text!r}")
        op, num, pct = m.groups()
        value = float(num.replace(",", ""))
        return {"op": op, "value": value / 100 if pct else value, "unit": "pct" if pct else "abs"}
    if check_type == "ACCEPTABLE_RANGE":
        bounds = dict(re.findall(r"(<=|>=)\s*" + NUM, t))   # {'<=': '0', '>=': '10000'}
        if not bounds:
            raise ValueError(f"ACCEPTABLE_RANGE: expected e.g. '(<=0 >=15)', got {text!r}")
        return {"fail_le": _num(bounds.get("<=")), "fail_ge": _num(bounds.get(">="))}
    if check_type == "ACCEPTED_VALUES":
        # 'A' or "A" quoted items; fall back to bare comma-separated tokens
        items = re.findall(r"'([^']*)'|\"([^\"]*)\"", t)
        values = [a or b for a, b in items] or [v.strip() for v in t.strip("()").split(",")]
        return {"allowed": values}
    if check_type == "VALUE_LENGTH":
        m = re.search(r"\d+", t)
        return {"length": int(m.group())}
    if check_type == "EXPECTED_FORMAT":
        re.compile(t)                                       # fail now if the regex is invalid
        return {"regex": t}
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown check type {check_type!r}")

def _num(s):
    return None if s is None else float(s.replace(",", ""))

Unit-test the parser with every string in the real templates

Each new template will contain new ways of writing the same thing. Keep a test file of (input text → expected spec) pairs. Add every surprise to it. This is the most fragile part of the pipeline.

docs.title: Step 4–5: run and evaluate
docs.text:
Each check becomes one aggregate expression. All checks on one table run as one query per window, so the cost stays low:

-- generated for the stand-in table, window 09:00–10:00
select
    count(*)                                                     as n_rows,
    avg(iff(AVG_TICKET is null, 1, 0))                           as AVG_TICKET__MISSING_VALUES,
    avg(iff(AVG_TICKET <= 0 or AVG_TICKET >= 10000, 1, 0))       as AVG_TICKET__ACCEPTABLE_RANGE,
    avg(iff(FINAL_STATUS not in ('01','02','03','13'), 1, 0))    as FINAL_STATUS__ACCEPTED_VALUES
from <DATABASE>.<SCHEMA>.<STAND_IN_TABLE>
where LAST_UPDATED_TS >= '2026-10-09 09:00' and LAST_UPDATED_TS < '2026-10-09 10:00';

Comparing each measured value with its parsed criteria gives PASS / FAIL (add WARN later). Every result is appended to a results table, so the reports and the trend history read from one place. The blueprint runs the same logic through Great Expectations. The parser output feeds either engine.

docs.title: Page 2: Main report
docs.text:
One row per field, one column per check type. Healthy cells are plain; only WARN and FAIL are coloured; failing fields sort to the top; a filter offers "show only issues". A 50–60 field table scrolls but stays readable.

 Field          Missing   Population   Range     Accepted   Format   Duplicates   Length   Placeholder

Decision for you: fields as rows (shown above) or check types as rows. The manager said either is fine. Recommendation: fields as rows. People ask about a field ("is AVG_TICKET OK?") more often than about a check type, and it fits the template's layout.

docs.title: Page 3+: Drill-downs
docs.text:
Open only when someone clicks:

  • Field history: the measured value per hour for the last 7–30 days, with the threshold line. It shows whether a failure is new or chronic.
  • Sample bad values: a few example rows that failed (masking any PII).
  • Check details: the template row, the parsed criteria, the SQL that ran, the alert state.

docs.title: The second report: features, rules and scores
docs.text:
Same three-page structure, different content on page 2:

Page 2 section Shows Score stability PSI per final and component score, benchmark vs active (how PSI works) Feature stability CSI for the top features Rule activity Hit rate per rule against its normal level Decision mix Share approved / declined / manual review

On the stand-in table there are no model scores. Demo this report with the final status mix and one or two numeric fields treated as "scores", so the layout is ready when the real 5c output arrives.

docs.title: Choosing the output format
docs.text:
Format Good for Drawbacks Excel Quick to produce from pandas; easy to email; people can filter Not interactive across pages; files pile up HTML (what you have now) One file or one URL; can link pages and colour cells; easy to view Needs hosting for a shared URL; you write the layout yourself Power BI What the team already uses for most reporting; drill-through between pages is built in; scheduled refresh; access control Needs a workspace and a refresh connection to Snowflake; less control from code

Recommendation: keep the data and the presentation separate. The run writes results to a Snowflake table; each format just reads it.

  1. For Friday: generate HTML (refining what you have) and an Excel export from the same results data frame. This is the fastest way to show the fixed pages.
  2. For production: a Power BI report on the results table, with pages that match the fixed layout. This fits how the team already works and gives drill-through for free.

docs.title: Hourly alerting on AWS
docs.text:
The manager's direction: a Lambda that connects to Snowflake, runs the checks, and sends the alert through SNS, every hour.

flowchart LR
    EB["EventBridge Scheduler<br/>cron: 20 * * * ? *"]:::aws --> LMB["DQ check Lambda<br/>(container image)"]:::lambda
    SM["Secrets Manager<br/>service account key"]:::aws --> LMB
    LMB -- "SQL (read window)" --> SF[("Snowflake<br/>monitored table")]:::snow
    LMB -- "write results +<br/>alert state" --> RES[("DQ_RESULT /<br/>DQ_ALERT")]:::snow
    LMB -- "only on a new FAIL<br/>with Alert = Yes" --> SNS["SNS topic<br/>dq-alerts-uw"]:::aws
    SNS --> MAIL["Email subscribers<br/>(team list)"]
    CW["CloudWatch alarm<br/>errors / missed runs"]:::aws -.-> SNS

    classDef aws fill:#C93C92,stroke:#8f2a68,color:#fff;
    classDef lambda fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3e10,color:#fff;
    classDef snow fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant EB as EventBridge (hourly, 20 past)
    participant L as DQ check Lambda
    participant SEC as Secrets Manager
    participant SF as Snowflake
    participant SNS as SNS topic
    EB->>L: invoke (window = previous full hour)
    L->>SEC: get service account key
    L->>SF: load check specs (from template / registry)
    L->>SF: run one aggregate query per table
    SF-->>L: measured values
    L->>L: compare with criteria → PASS / FAIL
    L->>SF: append results, read open alerts
    alt new FAIL with Alert = Yes
        L->>SNS: publish alert message
        SNS-->>SNS: deliver email to subscribers
    else still failing (already alerted)
        L->>L: no new email (stateful)
    end
Topic What to know "Constantly alive" A Lambda isn't a server that stays on. EventBridge Scheduler starts it every hour; it runs for seconds and stops. "Always on" means: the schedule is enabled, and a CloudWatch alarm tells you if a run fails or doesn't happen. Reuse what exists The manager said there already is a Lambda that sends emails. Only its trigger changes: for this use case, it fires when a table-level threshold is breached. Options: (a) your check Lambda publishes to SNS and the existing email path subscribes, or (b) your Lambda publishes straight to an SNS email subscription. Austin owns it (check-in): ask him whether to reuse it or build a new one. Either is fine. Connecting AWS → Snowflake The UW service already does this: the AWS2SF Trans Log Pipe Lambda writes to Snowflake. Copy its pattern (connector library, secret handling, network path) rather than inventing a new one. Package size GX + the Snowflake connector + pandas exceed the 250 MB zip limit. Deploy the Lambda as a container image (up to 10 GB). Time limit Lambda stops at 15 minutes. One aggregate query per table finishes in seconds. Keep it that way: don't pull rows into Python. Don't spam While testing, keep the criteria tight so alerts are rare (test plan). Email only when an alert opens, escalates or resolves, not every hour it is still failing (alert lifecycle). Keep the open alerts in a Snowflake table. SNS email is plain text Fine for alerts. Put the link to the report in the message. If you need formatted HTML emails, use SES instead. Subscriptions Each SNS email subscriber must click a confirmation link once. Subscribe a team distribution list, not individuals. 
# handler.py: sketch of the hourly check Lambda
import json, os, boto3
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from dq import load_specs, run_checks, open_new_alerts, write_results, snowflake_conn

sns = boto3.client("sns")

def handler(event, context):
    end = datetime.now(timezone.utc).replace(minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)
    start = end - timedelta(hours=1)
    with snowflake_conn(secret_id=os.environ["SF_SECRET_ID"]) as conn:
        specs = load_specs(conn)                       # parsed template rows
        results = run_checks(conn, specs, start, end)  # one query per table
        write_results(conn, results)
        new_alerts = open_new_alerts(conn, results)    # FAIL + Alert=Yes + not already open
    for a in new_alerts:
        sns.publish(
            TopicArn=os.environ["ALERT_TOPIC_ARN"],
            Subject=f"[DQ][{a.severity}] {a.table} · {a.field} · {a.check_type}"[:100],
            Message=a.render_text(),                   # what, since when, threshold, report link
        )
    return {"window": f"{start:%H:%M}–{end:%H:%M}", "checks": len(results), "alerts": len(new_alerts)}

docs.title: Access and approvals
docs.text:
"Do you need to get some approvals? Do you need to have some pipes or connectors built?" Find out early; this is where schedules slip.

Need Why Ask Snowflake service account (key-pair) "If you want to automate and schedule jobs, you need a service account." Your personal login can't run unattended Snowflake / platform admins Role with read on the monitored tables and write on a DQ results schema Lambda reads the data and stores results Platform admins A small warehouse for the checks Cost tracking; doesn't compete with analysts Platform admins AWS account and IAM role for the Lambda Where it runs; permissions for Secrets Manager, SNS, CloudWatch Cloud / DevOps (Amok, Austin know the UW setup) Network path from Lambda to Snowflake A Lambda in a VPC needs NAT or PrivateLink to reach Snowflake. Snowflake may need the egress IPs on its network policy Cloud team + Snowflake admins. Check how AWS2SF does it Secrets Manager secret for the key Never put keys in code or environment variables Cloud team SNS topic + team email list Alert delivery Cloud team; manager decides recipients

No approvals needed to start

Everything up to and including the reports runs from your machine with your own sandbox access. Only the hourly AWS schedule needs the service account and approvals. Request them now, build the rest while you wait.

docs.title: Excel template vs YAML config
docs.text:
The blueprint keeps check definitions as YAML in Git. The manager's direction is that the Excel template is the input. The two fit together:

flowchart LR
    X["Excel template<br/>(stakeholders fill in)"]:::cfg -- "MVP: read directly<br/>as a data frame" --> RUN["Checks run"]
    X -- "later: convert + validate<br/>(script)" --> Y["YAML in Git<br/>(reviewed by MR)"]:::cfg
    Y -- "CI loads" --> REG[("Registry tables<br/>in Snowflake")]:::snow --> RUN

    classDef cfg fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#57498a,color:#fff;
    classDef snow fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;
  • MVP (now): read the Excel template directly. It's what the manager asked for and what stakeholders know.
  • Production (later): keep Excel as the intake form, but convert it into the reviewed config (YAML in Git → registry tables). The Lambda then reads the registry, never a file on someone's laptop. This keeps an audit trail of who changed a threshold and when.

docs.title: Build order to Friday
docs.text:
Target after the check-in

The check-in set the wider target: fully automated in about three weeks, tested with one check of each type. The steps below still apply; steps 8–9 move into weeks 1–2.

# Step Done when 1 Confirm the stand-in table's path; pick ~10 variables You can select them in Snowflake 2 Draft the template rows yourself (don't wait for the manager's version) 10 variables × several check types 3 Loader + validator + parser, with unit tests All template rows parse or give a clear error 4 Query generator + evaluation for one window Results data frame with PASS / FAIL 5 Loop over the last 7 days hourly; store the results History for trends and the summary page 6 Page 1 + page 2 in HTML; Excel export The fixed views to show on Friday 7 One drill-down (field history) Click-through works for one field 8 Lambda + SNS prototype in a sandbox account, if access allows A test email arrives 9 List of approvals requested and their status Ready to discuss on Friday

docs.title: POC: getting started
docs.text:
Replaced by the framework

The dq-poc code this page describes has been replaced by the data quality framework in dq-framework/, built from scratch for Underwriting and the Risk Monitoring feature store, with LocalStack for development. See The framework: design and status. The explanations below (check types, comparison with the raw data, no-activity checks) still apply.

This page describes the working proof of concept for data quality monitoring on the Underwriting (UW) models. Rules written in an Excel template are checked with Great Expectations (GX) on Snowflake data once an hour, by an AWS Lambda. Results go to a Snowflake table, changes raise an alert, and a Streamlit report shows the history.

The code is in the dq-poc/ folder next to this docs site. Its README.md is the reference for commands and settings; this page explains how it works.

Status

The code is built and unit-tested. It connects with the Snowflake Python connector. Alerts go by email: through SNS in AWS, or straight through an SMTP server from a laptop. It has not yet run against the real Snowflake account, a real SNS topic or a real mail server: that is the next step, once credentials are in place. The shipped rules template points at the one sample table built by sql/e2e_test_data.sql.

docs.title: How it follows the UW flow
docs.text:
The business described the flow before the model service is called (Requirements update). The POC monitors the three places where that flow leaves data in Snowflake.

flowchart TB
    ON["Onboarding system"] --> MRD["<b>MRD</b><br/>pulls third-party data and look-ups,<br/>maps everything into the API structure"]:::up
    MRD -- "API call with the payload" --> SVC["<b>Model service</b><br/>ALB, Lambda, Step Functions,<br/>models and rules"]:::svc
    SVC -- "decision" --> MRD

    MRD -. "stores" .-> RAW[("<b>Raw data</b><br/>as collected")]:::raw
    SVC -. "saves" .-> PAY[("<b>Input payload</b><br/>A1 today, A2 from January")]:::pay
    SVC -. "5a, 5b, 5c" .-> OUT[("<b>Output, 5c</b>")]:::out

    RAW --> DQ["<b>DQ Lambda</b><br/>hourly"]:::dq
    PAY --> DQ
    OUT --> DQ
    DQ --> RES[("DQ_POC_RESULT")]:::dq
    DQ --> MAIL["Email alert"]:::dq

    classDef up fill:#7C69B2,stroke:#57498a,color:#fff;
    classDef svc fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3e10,color:#fff;
    classDef raw fill:#8a6d1c,stroke:#5e4a12,color:#fff;
    classDef pay fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;
    classDef out fill:#54802D,stroke:#3a5a1e,color:#fff;
    classDef dq fill:#a8503f,stroke:#7a3527,color:#fff;
Question Answer Which data is checked? The payload as the models received it, the raw data MRD stored, and the output When does a check run? Afterwards, once an hour, on the last hour of data. It is not in the request path Does it block a bad request? No. The request is still scored. The check reports that quality dropped Why look at the raw data too? A payload can look valid and still be wrong. Only a comparison with the raw data shows a mapping error

docs.title: Which tables
docs.text:
Several tables mean more template rows, not more code. The example template uses these names as placeholders; the real table names are still to be confirmed.

Example table Stands for Checked with A1_INPUT_PAYLOAD The payload sent to the model service Field checks, activity checks, comparison with the raw tables MRD_RAW_APPLICATION The application as MRD received it Volume, and "did every application reach the payload?" MRD_RAW_EXPERIAN, MRD_RAW_LEXISNEXIS, MRD_RAW_TMX What each provider returned Volume. They are the source side of the comparisons UW_OUTPUT_5C The decision Field checks and business rules

If the payload is stored as JSON

GX checks columns. If a table keeps the payload in one JSON (VARIANT) column, create a view that turns the monitored fields into columns, and put the view name in the template.

docs.title: The three kinds of check
docs.text: Kind Question Check types Field checks Is the data in this table valid? Missing values, range, accepted values, format, duplicates, length, placeholders, business rules Activity Is data still arriving? VOLUME, FRESHNESS Compared with source Does the payload hold what the raw data says? SOURCE_COVERAGE, MATCHES_SOURCE, LOST_IN_MAPPING

docs.title: Field checks
docs.text:
Each check type is a standard expectation from the GX Expectation Gallery. The limit comes from the template row.

Check type GX expectation Limit from the template Missing Values, Field Population ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeNull MAX_BAD_PCT Acceptable Range ExpectColumnValuesToBeBetween MIN, MAX, MAX_BAD_PCT Accepted Values ExpectColumnValuesToBeInSet VALUES, MAX_BAD_PCT Expected Format ExpectColumnValuesToMatchRegex REGEX, MAX_BAD_PCT Duplicate Values ExpectColumnValuesToBeUnique MAX_BAD_PCT Value Length ExpectColumnValueLengthsToBeBetween MIN, MAX, MAX_BAD_PCT Placeholder Value ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeInSet VALUES, MAX_BAD_PCT

MAX_BAD_PCT is the one rule to remember: the share of rows allowed to break the rule. GX calls the opposite mostly, the share that must pass. Confirm in the gallery that each expectation supports Snowflake before relying on it.

docs.title: Activity checks
docs.text:
These answer "is data still arriving?". The business asked for this after the A1 dataset received no applications and nobody was told.

Check type Looks at Fails when Good for VOLUME The rows in this hour The count is below MIN or above MAX A source that should send something every hour FRESHNESS The newest row in the whole table It is older than MAX hours "Tell me when nothing arrives", with quiet hours allowed 
flowchart LR
    subgraph T["Applications per hour"]
        direction LR
        H1["82"] --- H2["77"] --- H3["0"]:::bad --- H4["0"]:::bad --- H5["0"]:::bad --- H6["0"]:::bad --- H7["91"]
    end
    H3 -. "VOLUME fails<br/>in the first empty hour" .-> V["Hourly volume"]:::chk
    H5 -. "FRESHNESS fails<br/>once the silence exceeds 3 hours" .-> F["Freshness, limit 3 h"]:::chk

    classDef bad fill:#a8503f,stroke:#7a3527,color:#fff;
    classDef chk fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3e10,color:#fff;

Use VOLUME where an empty hour is always wrong. Use FRESHNESS where quiet hours are normal (nights, weekends): set MAX to the longest silence that is still acceptable.

A check that keeps failing is repeated as a reminder every 24 hours (configurable), so an outage that lasts days is not forgotten after the first email.

docs.title: Compared with source
docs.text:
This compares two copies of the same application's information: the raw data MRD collected, and the payload MRD built from it. The mapping between them is where mistakes have happened before.

Take one application, with made-up values:

Information Raw data Payload Result Check that catches it Requested amount 50,000 50,000 Same ZIP code 07302 7302 Different MATCHES_SOURCE Channel WEB POS Different MATCHES_SOURCE TMX score 41 (empty) Lost LOST_IN_MAPPING The whole application (no record) present No partner SOURCE_COVERAGE 
flowchart LR
    PAY[("One hour of<br/>the payload")]:::pay --> J{"Join on the<br/>application key"}
    RAW[("Raw table")]:::raw --> J
    J --> C1["<b>SOURCE_COVERAGE</b><br/>no partner on the other side"]:::chk
    J --> C2["<b>MATCHES_SOURCE</b><br/>both have a value,<br/>the values differ"]:::chk
    J --> C3["<b>LOST_IN_MAPPING</b><br/>raw has a value,<br/>payload is empty"]:::chk
    C1 --> R[("Share of bad rows<br/>per check")]:::out
    C2 --> R
    C3 --> R

    classDef raw fill:#8a6d1c,stroke:#5e4a12,color:#fff;
    classDef pay fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;
    classDef chk fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3e10,color:#fff;
    classDef out fill:#54802D,stroke:#3a5a1e,color:#fff;
Check type A row is bad when Catches SOURCE_COVERAGE It has no partner in the other table Data that never made it across. Swap the two tables to check the other direction MATCHES_SOURCE Both sides have a value and they differ A value in the wrong field, a changed code, a lost leading zero LOST_IN_MAPPING The raw side has a value and the payload is empty A field dropped by the mapping

The three never count the same row twice, so each number has one meaning. MATCHES_SOURCE compares in one of three ways: EXACT, TEXT (ignores case and surrounding spaces) or NUMERIC (with a tolerance).

Why it matters. A payload check alone cannot tell these apart:

What happened Missing-values check on the payload LOST_IN_MAPPING Who fixes it The provider sent no score Fails Passes (the raw data is empty too) The provider, or nobody The provider sent a score and the mapping dropped it Fails Fails MRD The mapping wrote a valid but wrong value Passes n/a: MATCHES_SOURCE fails MRD

The unit tests check the SQL behind each of the three. Their behaviour on real data is checked on the first Snowflake run.

Three things decide whether this works on real data

  • A shared key. Both sides must carry the same application identifier.
  • Timing. If the raw data lands later than the payload, the newest hour shows false gaps.
  • Intended transformations. If MRD converts a value on purpose, the comparison must know.

These are open questions for the MRD team (list).

docs.title: Business rules
docs.text:
A business rule is a check the gallery cannot express, such as a condition across several columns or a lookup in a reference table. There are three ways to get an expectation, in the order to try them:

Way When Example in the code 1. Gallery expectation, as is A standard check on one field Every field check above 2. A preset of a gallery expectation A fixed rule that deserves a name "The final score is between 300 and 900" 3. Custom SQL (UnexpectedRowsExpectation) Nothing in the gallery fits "An approved application has a final score"

For custom SQL, the query selects the rows that break the rule, and the check passes when it returns none. The template picks a rule by name (CHECK_TYPE = BUSINESS_RULE, RULE_NAME = …). The SQL lives in src/dq_poc/business_rules.py, where it is reviewed. Nobody types SQL into Excel.

Comparing with a source table does not need custom SQL: use the three check types above.

docs.title: The template
docs.text:
One row is one check. The stakeholder template is wide (one row per field); a reshape step turns it into this long form (template to checks).

Column Meaning TABLE, TS_COLUMN The table, and the timestamp column used to pick the hour FIELD Column to check. Empty for table-level checks CHECK_TYPE One of the check types above MIN, MAX, VALUES, REGEX, MAX_BAD_PCT The limits RULE_NAME For a business rule SOURCE_TABLE, SOURCE_FIELD, KEY, COMPARE, TOLERANCE For a comparison with a source table ALERT Yes sends an alert when the check starts failing

Example rows, one of each kind:

TABLE FIELD CHECK_TYPE Limits SOURCE_TABLE KEY ALERT A1_INPUT_PAYLOAD ZIP EXPECTED_FORMAT REGEX ^[0-9]{5}$, MAX_BAD_PCT 25 Yes A1_INPUT_PAYLOAD FRESHNESS MAX 3 (hours) Yes A1_INPUT_PAYLOAD ZIP MATCHES_SOURCE COMPARE TEXT, MAX_BAD_PCT 1 MRD_RAW_APPLICATION APPLICATION_ID Yes A1_INPUT_PAYLOAD TMX_SCORE LOST_IN_MAPPING MAX_BAD_PCT 2 MRD_RAW_TMX APPLICATION_ID Yes UW_OUTPUT_5C BUSINESS_RULE RULE_NAME APPROVED_HAS_FINAL_SCORE Yes

The template is read on every run, and the GX expectations are built from it in memory. Changing a limit, a field or a table needs no code change. A template with a problem stops the run and lists every problem with its row number, before any check runs.

Steps What happens Where in src/dq_poc/ 1–2 The schedule starts the Lambda, which picks the previous full hour lambda_handler.py, runner.py 3–4 The Lambda gets the Snowflake login settings.py 5–7 The Lambda reads and validates the template template.py 8 Checks become expectations, grouped so each table is read as few times as possible expectations.py, sql.py 9–11 GX runs each group. Only counts come back. A broken check becomes ERROR and the rest continue runner.py, store.py 12–14 The Lambda compares with the previous run and stores the results store.py 15–17 One message is sent only if something changed or a reminder is due alerts.py 18 The run ends with one log line runner.py 19–20 People read the results table through the report. This never touches GX or the Lambda app/streamlit_app.py

If a step fails, the place to look is:

Fails at Likely cause Look in 3–4 Missing secret or permission Lambda logs in CloudWatch 5–7 Template missing in S3, or a problem in a row Lambda logs: the error lists the rows 9–10 No network path to Snowflake, wrong table or column name Lambda logs. A bad check is stored as ERROR with the message in DETAILS 14 No write access to the results table Lambda logs 15–16 Email subscription not confirmed SNS console

docs.title: Results and alerts
docs.text:
Results. One row per check per window, in one flat table. Re-running a window replaces its rows. The main columns are the window, the check, STATUS (PASS, FAIL, ERROR), the observed number and what it means (METRIC: share of bad rows, row count, or hours since the newest row), and the limit as text. Only counts are stored, never example values: UW data includes personal data.

Alerts. One message per run, for checks with ALERT = Yes:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Passing
    Passing --> Failing: check fails, email NEW FAILURE
    Failing --> Failing: still failing, quiet
    Failing --> Failing: every 24 hours, email STILL FAILING
    Failing --> Passing: check passes, email RECOVERED

docs.title: Before AWS: run it from your machine
docs.text:
The same code and the same image run on a laptop, against the real Snowflake account, before anything is deployed.

flowchart LR
    ENV[".env<br/>Snowflake login,<br/>results table, SNS topic"]:::cfg --> CLI["<b>dq-poc</b><br/>command line"]:::dev
    ENV --> IMG["<b>The Lambda image</b><br/>run by the emulator<br/>inside the AWS base image"]:::dev

    IMG --> SF

app/streamlit_app.py reads only the results table. The same file runs on a laptop and inside Streamlit in Snowflake, where it needs no hosting and uses Snowflake's own access control.

Page Shows Summary Checks run, passed, failed. Counts by table and by kind of check. What needs attention Status by field For one table: a grid of field by check History of one check The observed number hour by hour, with the limit, and every past result

These are the three fixed pages the manager asked for (the reports). A Snowsight dashboard on the same table is a fallback if Streamlit is not enabled.

docs.title: What you will demo
docs.text:
A 10-minute story:

  1. "Here are the rules." The Excel template: one row per check, three kinds of check.
  2. "Here is the run." One run on the real tables, with the observed number beside each limit.
  3. "Here is the alert." The email for the check that just started failing.
  4. "Here is the history." The report: summary, grid, and the trend for one check.
  5. "Here is the comparison with the raw data." The share of applications where payload and raw data disagree, per field. A mapping error shows here even when every payload check passes.
  6. "Here is the no-activity alert." The freshness check on the A1 dataset, and the reminder that repeats while it stays empty.

Then change one limit in the template, run again, and show the result change with no code change.

docs.title: Requirements update: upstream flow, reconciliation & no-activity alerts
docs.text:
An email from Michelle Davis (Sunday 11 October, to you and Srayasee Chakraborty) sets the first focus for monitoring and adds two requirements the plan did not cover. It also explains the upstream flow and what A1 and A2 are.

Source and labels

This page is based on a photo of the email. Anything worked out rather than stated in the email is marked (inferred). Your reply to the email (Monday 12 October) is not included here.

docs.title: The email in one paragraph
docs.text: Monitoring should first focus on the input into the Model Service. That input is the A2 payload, sent through an API call starting in the January timeframe, and it will be saved into Snowflake. Because there have been mapping issues before, the team wants to compare the raw data with the payload that reaches the API. They also want an alert on the absence of activity: the A1 analytic dataset received no applications from 10 October, and nobody was told.

docs.title: What it confirms, changes and adds
docs.text: Point Effect on the plan Confirms Start with input monitoring Same as Phase 1 of the blueprint Confirms The input payload is saved into Snowflake The working assumption is right. Checks still run after the data lands Confirms MRD is the system that calls the model service Already on the architecture diagram as an external service Changes A1 is the API structure today. A2 replaces it in the January timeframe The new UW payload is A2 and does not exist yet. A1 is what can be monitored now Changes There are two kinds of input data in Snowflake: MRD's raw data and the payload The "one request table per source" assumption is refined, see below Adds Compare raw data with the payload New capability: reconciliation. Not in the blueprint or the POC Adds Alert on no activity In the blueprint as Freshness, but left out of the POC. See no-activity alerts

docs.title: A1 and A2

A1 A2 What it is The API structure MRD sends today The API structure for the new models When Live now. The Implementation Support Document adds that an A1 output Snowflake table and a full response Snowflake table exist from Day 1. The full-response table is most likely the raw data this email refers to (inferred), and the document's input mapping spreadsheet (model field, source, raw field) is the mapping sheet the comparison needs.

Two timelines to reconcile

The manager said Underwriting is "the first one that's going to go live this year". This email says the A2 input arrives through the API "starting in Jan timeframe". Both can be true (for example, a deployment this year and live traffic in January), but confirm it. It decides when real A2 data exists to test on.
