# Data Written by Monitoring When 1 A1 analytic dataset Exists today (layout to be confirmed) Input checks, and the no-activity alert Now. It is real and has a real, recent problem 2 Raw data MRD Reconciliation against the payload Once the tables and the key are known 3 A2 input payload Model service Input checks, reconciliation, no-activity alert From the January timeframe 4 Output, 5c Model service Feature, score and rule monitoring Phase 2, unchanged

Earlier pages assumed the payload is stored as one table per source. The email does not say how either data set is laid out. A better reading (inferred): the raw data may be split by source (it is what MRD pulled from each provider), and the payload is one aggregated structure. Both layouts work with the POC: a table is a set of template rows.

docs.title: New requirement 1: compare raw data with the payload
docs.text:
"Could we build a capability to compare data across sources: the raw data to our input payload?"

This is reconciliation: for the same application, does the payload hold what the raw data says?

docs.title: What is compared with what
docs.text:
There are two copies of each application's information, both in Snowflake.

Copy 1: the raw data Copy 2: the payload What it is Everything MRD gathered, as it was gathered The same information, rearranged into the layout the model service expects It includes The application from the onboarding system, what each third-party provider returned, MRD's internal look-ups One record per application with the fields the models use (A1 today, A2 from January) Written by MRD The model service saves what it received Used by Nobody downstream: it is the record of what was collected The models. This is what gets scored

MRD builds copy 2 from copy 1. That step is the mapping, and it is where mistakes have happened before. Comparing the copies checks that nothing was lost or changed on the way.

An example, with made-up values, for one application APP-123:

Information Raw data Payload Result Requested amount 50,000 50,000 Same ZIP code 07302 7302 Different: the leading zero was lost Channel WEB POS Different: the wrong value was mapped Experian score 712 (empty) Lost: the provider sent it, but it never reached the payload

The comparison does this for every application in the hour and every mapped field, and reports how often the two copies disagree. It works on two levels:

  1. The keys. Is the application present on both sides?
  2. The data. For each mapped field, does the payload value equal the raw value?

What 'raw' means is an assumption

The email says only "MRD stores the raw data into Snowflake". These pages read that as the data before MRD's mapping. Whether it is the providers' untouched responses or something MRD has already partly processed is not stated, and it decides how much the comparison can prove.

docs.title: The three checks
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    RAW[("Raw data<br/>MRD")]:::raw --> J{"Join on the<br/>application key"}
    PAY[("Input payload<br/>A1 or A2")]:::pay --> J
    J --> C1["<b>Coverage</b><br/>in one, missing in the other"]:::chk
    J --> C2["<b>Value match</b><br/>same field, different value"]:::chk
    J --> C3["<b>Lost values</b><br/>raw has a value,<br/>payload is empty"]:::chk
    C1 --> R[("Results table")]:::out
    C2 --> R
    C3 --> R

    classDef raw fill:#8a6d1c,stroke:#5e4a12,color:#fff;
    classDef pay fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;
    classDef chk fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3e10,color:#fff;
    classDef out fill:#54802D,stroke:#3a5a1e,color:#fff;
Check Question Typical mapping issue it catches Coverage Does every application in the payload have raw data, and the reverse? A source's data never reached the payload, or raw data was not stored Value match For a mapped field, is the payload value equal to the raw value? A value mapped to the wrong field, a unit or code changed, truncation Lost values Is the payload field empty where the raw field has a value? A field dropped in the mapping. The payload looks "missing", but the provider did send it

The third check matters most for the existing Missing Values checks. A missing score in the payload can mean "the provider had no data" or "the mapping lost it". Only the raw data tells them apart, and the two need different people to fix them.

docs.title: What it needs
docs.text:
A mapping sheet, one row per field to compare. This is a third template next to the two that already exist.

Column Meaning Example (inferred) PAYLOAD_TABLE, PAYLOAD_FIELD The field as the model service received it <A2_PAYLOAD>, EXPERIAN_SCORE RAW_TABLE, RAW_FIELD The same value as MRD stored it <MRD_RAW_EXPERIAN>, SCORE KEY The column that identifies one application in both APPLICATION_ID COMPARE How to compare: exact, numeric with a tolerance, or text ignoring case and spaces NUMERIC MAX_BAD_PCT Share of applications allowed to differ 0 ALERT Send an alert when it starts failing Yes

docs.title: How it is built in the POC
docs.text:
It is built, and it needed no new engine. The mapping columns went into the same template as the other checks, as three check types (details):

Check type Level A row is bad when SOURCE_COVERAGE Keys It has no partner in the other table MATCHES_SOURCE Data Both sides have a value and the values differ LOST_IN_MAPPING Data The raw side has a value and the payload is empty

One query joins an hour of the payload to the raw table and marks each row 0 or 1 per check. A standard GX expectation then measures the share of 1s, so every comparison reports a percentage. Results, alerts and the report needed no change: a comparison is one more row per window.

Three things decide whether this works

  • A shared key. Both sides must carry the same application identifier.
  • Timing. MRD stores the raw data at the end of its flow. If it lands later than the payload, comparing the newest hour reports false gaps. Compare a window that ended an hour or more ago.
  • Intended transformations. If MRD converts a value on purpose (units, codes, rounding), the comparison must apply the same rule, or every row "differs". The mapping owner has to state these.

docs.title: New requirement 2: alert on the absence of activity
docs.text:
"Our A1 analytic dataset did not get any applications from 10-10-2026. Could we make sure we get alerted to this?"

This is a real incident that monitoring would have caught. It is also the strongest case for the framework so far: a dataset went quiet and nobody noticed for at least a day.

docs.title: Does the POC catch it today?
docs.text:
Partly. Three gaps:

Gap Why it matters here The POC's VOLUME check counts rows in one hour A dataset that normally has quiet hours (nights, weekends) fails every quiet hour, or the limit is set so low it catches nothing Freshness was left out of the POC "How long since the last application?" is the direct question, and it has no check type yet An alert is sent once, when a check starts failing A dataset that stays empty for three days sends one email on day one, then nothing. The problem can be forgotten

10 October 2026 was a Saturday, which makes the first gap concrete: a rule must know whether a quiet weekend is normal for this dataset.

docs.title: What to add
docs.text:
Check Rule Catches In the POC No activity (freshness) Fail if the newest application is older than N hours. Looks at the whole table, not one hour The 10 October case: nothing arriving at all Yes Reminder While an alert stays open, send it again every 24 hours The alert being sent once and forgotten Yes Daily volume against normal Fail if a day's count is far below the usual count for that weekday A partial drop: one channel or client stops, the rest continue Not yet Decision needed Why How long without applications is too long? Sets N. It may differ for weekdays and weekends Is a quiet weekend or holiday normal for A1? Avoids a false alert every Saturday Who gets this alert? An empty input is usually an upstream (MRD or pipeline) problem, not a modelling one Did the applications not arrive, or did they arrive and not load into the dataset? "From 10-10-2026" may mean "since" or "for" that date. Comparing with the raw data answers which side failed

The blueprint already describes both checks (Phase 1 check catalog: Freshness, and Volume against the trailing median for the same hour of the week). Freshness and the reminder are now in the POC (details). The daily-volume comparison is not: it needs a few weeks of history first.

A quick win

A1 exists today and has a current problem. A no-activity alert on the A1 analytic dataset is a small, real first delivery: one table, one timestamp column, one rule. It needs only the A1 table path and the answer to "how long is too long".

docs.title: What to monitor
docs.text: In the 1:1, you asked where the Snowflake tables are in the UW architecture. The deployment work starts from the config tables, but the diagram shows no table for the request data. The manager's answer settles which tables input monitoring actually reads.

docs.title: Not the config tables
docs.text:
The config tables hold reference data: thresholds, MCC statistics, lookup values. They change rarely, through a governed admin console. They are not what data quality monitoring tracks.

Config tables still need some care

The support guide notes that an empty or malformed config file can break every request. That is an operational check: did the config pipe run, is the S3 file valid. It belongs with deployment and support, not in the DQ input reports.

docs.text:
flowchart LR

A later email added the raw data to this picture and named the caller (MRD). The Implementation Support Document names the Day 1 tables: an A1 output Snowflake table and a full response Snowflake table, live since 15 October 2026. The table below is from the 1:1; "API request table" there is the input payload.

Table What's in it Monitored by Status API request table Every request from step 1 (the input fields the models use) Input monitoring (Phase 1) Working assumption: it exists. Working assumption

The docs now assume each API request is stored in Snowflake with its payload data, and that input monitoring runs there. The payload comes from several sources, so it is probably stored in more than one table, roughly one per source. On this page "the API request table" means that set of tables. Their paths are placeholders such as <DB>.<SCHEMA>.<UW_REQ_APPLICATION>. Replace them when the real names are known. Several tables need more template rows, not more code: see More than one request table.

A later email refines this: the raw data stored by MRD may be split by source, and the payload is one aggregated structure (A1 today, A2 from January). See Requirements update. The POC is built on this assumption.

The modelling contact (Srayasee Chakraborty) will list the exact tables and fields for the new models in the two templates. That's what the Jira ticket asks for.

Answered by a later email

A1 is the API structure MRD sends today; A2 replaces it in the January timeframe. Both are the model service's input payload. There is also MRD's raw data in Snowflake, to be compared with the payload. See Requirements update. The tip below is kept for the record.

How this relates to A1

The kickoff named A1, a consolidated dataset, as the Day 1 source. For Underwriting, the 1:1 is more specific: the API request table is the input. Treat A1 as the general Day 1 idea and the request table as the UW answer. Confirm with the manager whether A1 and the request table are the same thing (inferred: likely related).

docs.title: Auto-decisioned vs manually reviewed applications
docs.text:
The manager also explained a second kind of table, which the stand-in table belongs to.

flowchart TB
    APP["Application arrives<br/>(API request)"] --> MODEL{"Model + rules<br/>can decide?"}
    MODEL -- "yes (~80%)" --> AUTO["<b>Auto-decision</b><br/>approve or decline in real time<br/><i>locked: never changes afterwards</i>"]:::auto
    MODEL -- "no (~20%)" --> MAN["<b>Manual review</b><br/>routed to the underwriting team"]:::man
    MAN --> S1["Pending"] --> S2["In review"] --> S3["Approved / declined"]
    AUTO --> T1[("Request + output tables<br/>one row, point in time")]:::auto
    S3 --> T2[("<b>Manual-review status table</b><br/>status changes over time")]:::man

    classDef auto fill:#127EA6,stroke:#0b5a78,color:#fff;
    classDef man fill:#BC5618,stroke:#8a3e10,color:#fff;
Auto-decision Manual review Share of applications ~80% ~20% (the share that "goes for manual review") When decided Real time, inside the API call Later, by an underwriting analyst Does the record change? No. Locked at the point of decision Yes. Status moves over time until approved or declined Where it's stored Request table (input) + 5c output A separate status table

The status table complements the auto-decision data. Without it, monitoring sees only the applications the model decided. It still matters to track, so it isn't throwaway work.

docs.title: The stand-in table
docs.text:
The real UW tables depend on Srayasee's input. So the manager picked a table to start building on now: "I'd rather not have you wait."

Property Value What it is The manual-review status table described above (inferred from the call) Where The team's sandbox / analytics databases. The names are garbled in the transcript, so use the link the manager sent Size ~800 columns, including a final-status field Refresh Every 15 minutes. Not truly real time, but "good enough" for hourly alerts Access You already have access (your earlier access request was approved) Scope for the MVP ~10 variables. The manager will try to fill in the template for them before Friday

docs.title: Choosing the 10 variables
docs.text:
Simplified in the check-in

You don't need to find the important columns first. "Take a few columns" and write one check of each type with tight criteria. See the test plan.

Pick variables that exercise every check type in the template, so the MVP proves the whole parser, not just one rule.

Pick at least one… Exercises Likely candidate (inferred) Status field (categorical) Accepted Values; new-value detection Final status Timestamp Freshness (is the table still updating?); Expected Format Last-updated / decision date Application or merchant ID Duplicate Values; Value Length; Expected Format Application ID Amount (numeric) Acceptable Range; Placeholder Value (-999) Requested amount / average ticket Often-empty field Missing Values; Field Population Analyst comments / reason code Field used by a model or rule Proves the "monitor what matters" rule Any score or bureau field present

Watch the 15-minute refresh

A table that updates in place (status changes) behaves differently from an append-only log. - Volume checks should count rows changed in the window (by a last-updated timestamp), not rows created. - Duplicate checks must use the table's key (for example application ID + status timestamp), or every status change looks like a duplicate. - Expect up to a 15-minute lag. Run the hourly checks a little after the hour (for example at :20) and check the previous full hour.
